was a need of raising the credit ceiling in view of inflation, it must also be borne in view that
majority of beneficiaries of this Scheme were in the credit bracket of Rs. 10 lakh credit and an
extension of credit ceiling may dilute the participation of small and micro units. The Additional
Secretary from the M/o MSME however cautioned and informed that the Ministry with assistance
from the World Bank, on the exoperimental basis has enhanced ceiling to Rs. 2 crores.
34. In view of inflation, the Committee concurred with the view of Ministry to enhance
the credit ceiling to Rs. 2 crores from existing Rs. 1 crore.
SIDBI/India Microfinance Equity Fund (IMEF)
35. The Committee noted that another Rs. 100 crores were being provided to SIDBI for the
IME Fund Scheme .
36. In this regard the Ministry informed that to enhance credit flow to Micro and Small
Enterprises (MSEs) by augmenting refinancing capability of SIDBI, a fund would be made available

6
to SIDBI out of the contribution made by scheduled commercial banks having shortfall in

margin money subsidy for a given state is released is two instalments of 50% each. The first
instalment is released when the State has utilized at least 50% of the margin money subsidy
released to it during the previous year after fully utilizing all previous years’ releases. The second
instalments is released after the State has utilized 50% of the current years’ release after fully
utilizing all previous years’ releases. These releases are made by the Ministry to KVIC which in
turn transfer the funds state-wise to the concerned PMEGP accounts in nodal bank branches.
Financing branches after sanctioning and making the first disbursement to the beneficiary, submits
the claims to its nodal branch. The nodal branch then settles the claims and transfers the fund to
the financing branch. Financing branch then keeps the entire subsidy in the name of beneficiary
in his TDR account. However, the Committee also came across the instances like Tamil Nadu
were no fresh applications were being entertained for last few years for the need of
adequate funds. The Committee takes strong view over such instances which will defeat the
very objective of the Scheme and bring it down in the esteem of people. Instead of turning

Interaction with Select Industry Associations
152. The Committee had useful interaction with the representatives of select industry
associations, who expressed their concerns and gave suggestions.
Difficulty in doing the business
153. There Associations impressed upon the Committee that despite its socioeconomic
importance, the growth of sector has remained stunted due to multiple constraints which has been
recognized in the Economic Survey 2012-13 which states “India has not improved significantly in
terms of the ease of doing business and ranks very low in comparison to other industrial peers.
The MSME sector in particular faces multiple approval and operational restrictions. The process of
setting up and exiting business is time consuming and complicated requiring expensive third party
assistance. Since states have the major role in administering MSME sector, the prevailing ecosystem
therefore varies from state to state.” It further acknowledges that the MSME sector suffers due
to costly finance, “Sourcing of finance at competitive cost is another major constraint for both the
organized and the unorganized MSME enterprises. Financing other than internal accruals is costly
and prohibitive.” The Survey also recognized the technological constraints faced by sector.
“Research and technology upgradation activities also need to be scaled up. Presently only a small
number of incubators operates in the country which is very low relative to other countries. New
incubators will need to be set up on a Public-Private Partnership basis.”
154. DC, MSME concurred and suggested Self certification by entrepreneur instead of recurrent
inspections by multiple inspectors. He particularly pointed out inspections by Departments pertaining
to pollution control and labour.

Summing up
177. The Committee reiterates the pivotal role MSME Sector will play to bring about
inclusive and equitable development, and in giving opportunity to self employed
entrepreneurs to express their skills and innovation. In the spectre of overall economic slow
down, only MSME could be a redeeming factor. With little support, it shows resilience to
withstand the recession. This sector provides the foundation on which new corporate sector
will be built. There are innumerable inspiring success stories, where small entrepreneurs
have achieved exemplary and inspiring success with their sheer resilience and acumen. As
the spectre of jobless growth and informalisation of job market continues, the Government
has recognized the vitality of this sector. Several Committees and instruments have been
set up to suggest ways to support this Sector. Government has increasingly been proving
budgetary support to schemes. The Committee has always supported the demand of the
Ministry for higher funds. However, the constraints not only about money, it is more about
management, monitoring and delivery of the schemes. It is issue of implementation and
financial discipline, which rests squarely on the Ministry and implementing agencies. The
structure of Schemes is complex and involves multiple funding agencies who more often
lack coordination. Scarce Finds remain unutilised for most part of the year, there is year-
end rush to spend. Balance unspent money is carried forward to subsequent year. Whether
there is a approval of Ministry of Finance, to roll over the unspent balance of a continuing
scheme to next year. Money is deposited in joint Bank accounts and remains un-used. Yet
the Budget estimates for next year are retained at same level. Umbrella allocations are
made in Budget, under which independent schemes are allocated independent meagre funds,
but same is not reflected in the Budget document. These funds remain unutilized supposedly
for lack of demand as indicated in Outcome Budgets. Yet the allocation is retained at same
level. As the Ministry seeks more funds for the MSME sector, the Committee is circumspect
about the argument of lack of demand.  There is a prevalent practice of seeking allocations
for successive years, for Schemes like Special Scheme on PM’s Task Force, Virtual SME
Univerisity etc. which does not have the approval of Planning Commission or other
competent authority. Also, there are recurrent discrepancies in figures provided by the
Ministry vis-a-vis the Budget figures.

27. The Committee expresses its disappointment over repeated under-utilization of funds
meant for critical S&T projects. The Committee apprehends year-end expenditure. The
Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry must make Planned expenditures more
discreetly. (Para No. 91)
28. The Committee expresses reservation over the practice of retaining meager ‘Token
allocations’ for successive years for Planned schemes, without approval of Planning
Commission. Such practice obviously violates the very concept of Parliamentary approval
and oversight of Budget. (Para No. 94)
29. The Committee suggests that the Ministry too should intervene in resolving the long
pending issues of MGIRI. (Para No. 97)
30. The Committee notes that annual allocations are being made to meet only committed
obligations, yet there has been gross under-utilisation in successive years. The money is
deposited in joint bank accounts of representatives of institutions, which is carried forward
to next years. The Committee wonders if the nodal agencies or Scheme Steering Committee
can monitor the expenditure from joint bank accounts. The Ministry should specify if such
practices of depositing money in joint accounts and carrying the unused funds over to
subsequent year, have the approval of the Ministry of Finance. (Para No. 102)
31. The Committee notes that there was no expenditure during half the Financial Year
and that unspent balance has been carried over this year. The Ministry may clarify if it
adhered to the norms set by the Ministry of Finance in this regard. (Para No. 106)
32. As per the Outcome Budget (2013-14), till 31.12.2012, no money was spent nor any
achievement was reported. The Committee has observed a persistent trend of under
achievement of targets and under-utilisation of funds. Yet the allocation in BE 2013-14 has
been retained at Rs 7.42 crores. The Committee expresses its anguish over general
prevalence of underutilisation of Planned funds, despite budgetary support remaining at the
same level. The Committee expects the Ministry to make proactive intervention to reach
out to intended beneficiaries. (Para No. 109)
33. The Committee recommends that the views of stakeholders in Khadi sector should
be factored while formulating the implementation. (Para No. 113)
34. The Committee expresses its reservation over repeated difference in figures
contained in Budgetary documents that are presented to Parliament. The Ministry should
explain the recurrence of this difference in figures. (Para No. 116)
35. The Committee insists that the core objective of the scheme is to provide
opportunities to self employed entrepreneurs and to generate job opportunities. The success
of the scheme shall always be judged in terms of these parameters and not in terms of
utilization of margin money only. The Committee expresses its anguish over under
achievement. (Para No. 120)
36. However, the Committee also came across the instances like Tamil Nadu were no
fresh applications were being entertained for last few years for the need of adequate funds.
The Committee takes strong view over such instances which will defeat the very objective
of the Scheme and bring it down in the esteem of people. Instead of turning the applicant
away, implementing agencies including Banks should proactively reach out to them.
(Para No. 123)

29
37. The Committee finds that these proposal regarding financing the expansion of
existing PMEGP Units and synergizing PMEGP with schemes of rural development in the
naxal effected areas, should be acceptable to the Ministry, provided that implementation
should be efficient and target oriented. (Para No. 128)
38. The Committee considers that PMEGP is an important scheme. In view of significant
under-achievements in meeting physical targets, the Committee recommends that efforts
should be made to simplify the procedure and streamline the processes. There appears to
be disjoint at every level of approvals. The Committee recommends that DTFC should
mandatorily meet and approve the applications at quarterly basis. And should evaluate the
applications after due diligence. The application should be considered against determined
check-lists and benchmarks. There should be time bound approval at every level. It would
be helpful if the DTFC assigns local Udyami Mitras for this scheme. In case of rejection the
reasons should be communicated to the applicant in writing within a time-limit. The KVIC
alongwith the Banks should use Bank’s publicity platforms to publicise PMEGP. So far only
KVIC has been publicizing the PMEGP. The PMEGP should be promoted and publicized as
a viable Banking product. The Committee also recommends that issue of relaxing Service
area norm should be settled and notified expeditiously. This procedural issue must not
hamper the Scheme. For PMEGP entire district should be considered as one unit. Every
approved project should automatically stand covered under CGTMSE. However, the
guarantee fee should be absorbed by the Bank. The Committee also suggests that Ministry
may consider having a Sub-Plan for the revivable sick PMEGP units. (Para No. 129)
39. For better and more efficient performance of the PMEGP, there was suggestion that
was discussed in Committee that instead of giving the margin money, the Government
should provide interest subvention beyond a certain rate. Considering that there is a ceiling
on the value of project, the total liability on interest rate subvention can be estimated. The
Committee would like the Ministry to consider this suggestion, for better performance of
scheme. (Para No. 130)
40. The Committee wonders reduction in Non-Planned allocation considering that
committed expenditures including salary and other statutory dues of employees are met out
of this allocation. In view of increase in the Non-Planned allocations over RE 2012-13
pertaining to other agencies under the Ministry, reduction in respect of Coir Board is
noticeable. The Ministry may clarify if these obligatory expenditures are being duly met.
(Para No. 132)
41. The Committee notes that the target for 2012-13 was 900 units, however, till
31.12.2012, only 63 units (7% of the target) could be assisted. Almost 10 fold increase in
last quarter without spending any money under the scheme. However, the Secretary, Coir
Board in his presentation before the Committee stated that the target of 900 was surpassed
and 934 units were established. The Committee seeks explanation on such difference in
figures. (Para No. 135)
42. There is a difference between the figures for 2012-13 as provided by the Ministry and
those given in the Budget documents. The Committee reiterates its reservation over this
recurrent trend. The Ministry ought to reconcile its figures as given in the Expenditure
Budget (II) for the Ministry. Further the Committee notes significant reduction in Planned
allocation at RE stage to Rs. 32.51 crores. However, the Ministry released only Rs. 19.31
crores to Coir Board. It has been stated that the Coir Board spent unutilized balance of
previous year. Whether this recurrent practice of utilizing unused balance of previous year,

30
in the Ministry, has the approval of Ministry of Finance. At RE stage only in case of Coir
S&T the allocation was retained at Rs 7 crores. However, no money was spent in I and III
quarters and total expenditure was Rs 2.31 crores uneven expenditure of Planned allocation.
No money was spent under the important REMOT scheme through out the year. The
Committee feels that Coir industry is a promising sector for employment generation and
export market. While the Committee supports greater allocation for this Sector, it can not
ignore the less than optimal performance on the part of Ministry and concerned agencies.
These issues pertain the management, monitoring and financial efficiency by the Ministry
and concerned agency. (Para No. 140)
43. The Committee appreciates the export performance in Coir sector particularly
considering the structural, technological and financial limitations. The Committee impresses
that efforts should be made to realize full potential of this Sector. (Para No. 142)
44. The Committee finds the scope and prospects in NE promising. The MSME and KVIC
could prove to be most important vehicles for inclusive development of this region which
has immense scope and skill. However, as per the Expenditure Budget (II) of the Budget
document, the actual expenditure in 2010-11 and 2011-12, has been Nil. Even for year
2013-14 the Planned allocation is shown as Rs 31.83 crores, instead of Rs 297.70 crores as
indicated above. The Committee would like clarification on the yet another difference in
figures between Budget documents and those furnished by the Ministry. (Para No. 151)
45. The Committee found its interaction with select industry associations a useful
experience. It received feedback from the ultimate consumers of these schemes. The
Committee recommends that the Ministry may consider and respond to their suggestions
and concerns. (Para No. 176)
46. The Committee reiterates the pivotal role MSME Sector will play to bring about
inclusive and equitable development, and in giving opportunity to self employed
entrepreneurs to express their skills and innovation. In the spectre of overall economic slow
down, only MSME could be a redeeming factor. With little support, it shows resilience to
withstand the recession. This sector provides the foundation on which new corporate sector
will be built. There are innumerable inspiring success stories, where small entrepreneurs
have achieved exemplary and inspiring success with their sheer resilience and acumen. As
the spectre of jobless growth and informalisation of job market continues, the Government
has recognized the vitality of this sector. Several Committees and instruments have been
set up to suggest ways to support this Sector. Government has increasingly been proving
budgetary support to schemes. The Committee has always supported the demand of the
Ministry for higher funds. However, the constraints not only about money, it is more about
management, monitoring and delivery of the schemes. It is issue of implementation and
financial discipline, which rests squarely on the Ministry and implementing agencies. The
structure of Schemes is complex and involves multiple funding agencies who more often
lack coordination. Scarce Finds remain unutilised for most part of the year, there is year-
end rush to spend. Balance unspent money is carried forward to subsequent year. Whether
there is a approval of Ministry of Finance, to roll over the unspent balance of a continuing
scheme to next year. Money is deposited in joint Bank accounts and remains un-used. Yet
the Budget estimates for next year are retained at same level. Umbrella allocations are
made in Budget, under which independent schemes are allocated independent meagre funds,
but same is not reflected in the Budget document. These funds remain unutilized supposedly
for lack of demand as indicated in Outcome Budgets. Yet the allocation is retained at same

31
level. As the Ministry seeks more funds for the MSME sector, the Committee is circumspect
about the argument of lack of demand. There is a prevalent practice of seeking allocations
for successive years, for Schemes like Special Scheme on PM’s Task Force, Virtual SME
University etc. which does not have the approval of Planning Commission or other
competent authority. Also, there are recurrent discrepancies in figures provided by the
Ministry vis a vis the Budget figures. (Para No. 177)

(i) 

 
INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamen tary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this Two Hundred 
and Forty Fifth Report on Review the implementation  of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises Development Act, 2006 pertaining to Min istry of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises. 
 
2.  The Committee heard the representatives of Mini stry of Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises, organizations under the adminis trative control of Ministry of 
MSME and received valuable inputs from select MSME Associations on the issue.   
 
3.  The Committee in its meeting held on 2
nd  July, 2013 considered and adopted the 
report. 
 
 
 
 
 
TIRUCHI SIVA        
Chairman 
Department -related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Industry 
 
 
New Delhi,  
July, 2013 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(ii) 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Report  
 
The MSME Sector accounts for 45% of the country’s m anufacturing output, 40% 
of the exports and 8% of our GDP. The 26 million enterprises employing some 60 million 
people, have investment to the tune of Rs. 6.89 lak h crores, yet about 94% remain 
unregistered with large number of them being establ ished in unorganized and informal 
sector. The Report of Prime Minister’s Task Force o n MSME brings out the  largest 
significant of MSMEs for economy and states :  
 
“….   The labour to capital ratio in MSMEs and the over all growth in the MSME 
sector is much higher than in the large industries.  The geographic distribution of 
the MSMEs is also more even. Thus, MSMEs are import ant for the national 
objectives of growth with equity and inclusion. 
 
…. The MSME sector in India is highly heterogeneous  in terms of the size of the 
enterprises, variety of products and services produ ced and the levels of 
technology employed. While one end of the MSME spec trum contains highly 
innovative and high growth enterprises, more than 9 4 per cent of MSMEs are 
unregistered, with a large number established in th e informal or unorganized 
sector.”  
 
2. Until 2006, the small scale industries sector wa s being regulated by two sections 
of Industries (Development & Regulation) Act, 1951.  There was absence of an 
institutional regulatory and consultative mechanism  to capture and guide the organic 
progress of the sector from a micro enterprise to s mall scale enterprise to eventually a 
medium scale one. It also excluded the fast emergin g service sector. It was therefore 
considered essential to provide an exclusive legisl ation for the micro, small and medium 
enterprises. Such Bill was introduced in Lok Sabha on 12 
th  May, 2005 and was referred 
to this Committee. The Committee had held extensive  consultations on the provisions of 
the legislation which  included provisions pertaining – 
 
• statutory definitions of “small enterprise” and “medium enterprise”; 
• establishment of a National Small and Medium Enterp rises Board, a high-level 
forum consisting of stakeholders for participative review of and making  
 
• recommendations on the policies and programmes for the development of small 
and medium enterprises; 
 
• Classification of small and medium enterprises on the basis of investment in plant 
and machinery, or equipment  
 
• establishment of an Advisory Committee to recommend on the related matter; 
 
• The Act also sought to empower the Central Governme nt to notify programmes, 
guidelines or instructions for facilitating the pro motion and development and 
enhancing the competitiveness of small and medium enterprises; 
 
 
 

• The Act  also made provisions for ensuring timely a nd smooth flow of credit to 
small and medium enterprises to minimize the incide nce of sickness among and 
enhancing the competitiveness of such enterprises; 
 
• The Act also provided that the Central and State Go vernments may notify 
preference policies in respect of procurement of goods and services, produced and 
provided by small enterprises, by the Ministries, d epartments and public sector 
enterprises; 
 
• The Bill had a provision for the Central Government to create a Fund or Funds for 
facilitating promotion and development and enhancin g the competitiveness of  
small enterprises and medium enterprises; 
 
• It made further improvements to ensure timely payme nts to Small Scale 
enterprises.  
 
3. The Committee had acknowledged that the Bill was  an important and forward 
looking initiative. In its discussions with various  stake-holders, Industry associations and 
representatives of State Governments, there was gen eral approval for the Bill. In its 
Report to the Parliament, the Committee made follow ing recommendations for the 
Government:  
 
“…. certain States and industry associations sought  greater elaboration of the 
provisions of Bill particularly on the enabling Cla uses for promotion, 
development and enhancement of competitiveness of t he tiny, small and medium 
enterprises.   
 
….the Ministry of SSI should hold wide consultation s with the industry 
associations and State Governments while framing th e rules, so as to incorporate 
the views of the State Governments who shall be exe cuting the provisions of the 
Bill.  
 
….Having formulated the enabling rules, the Ministr y should continue to monitor 
their execution by agencies at local level and shou ld ensure that the agencies 
evolve processes / procedures that are simple and i n consonance with the 
objectives of the Act.  
 
….in order to encourage tiny, small  and medium ent erprises to adhere to 
pollution control norms, as per the Order dated the  10 
th  December 1997 of the 
Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, the cost of pollution control and 
R&D devices should not be included while calculatin g the investments in plant 
and machinery. Similar exemption should be made wit h respect to industrial 
safety devices to promote such units to adopt industrial safety norms.  
 
… The Industrial Facilitation Council should evolve  into an effective forum of 
arbitration, to resolve the issue of delayed paymen ts to small and tiny enterprises, 
conferred with sufficient mandate to execute its aw ard, appeal against which 
could be filed only in the High Court of the State where IFC is located” 
 

 
4. The Act was passed and notified on 16 th  June 2006. The Act provided advisory 
and regulatory framework and had enabling provision s which needed subordinate 
legislations in form of Rules, Regulation and polic ies on the part of Union and State 
Governments.   
 
5. After passage of six years of the notification o f the MSME Development Act, 
2006, the Committee decided to review the implement ation of the Act in July, 2012. The 
Committee held four meetings on the subject on 6 
th  July, 13 th  July, 20 th  July and 27 th  July, 
2012 with the representatives of select industry associations and the representatives of the 
Ministry of MSME. The Committee also received a lar ge number of written 
representations. The Ministry of MSME was asked to furnish their comments on the 
suggestions made by the representatives of  industry associations.  
 
6. In its written submission to the Committee, the Ministry of MSME informed that 
in order to provide greater efficacy to some import ant provisions of the MSMED Act 
particularly in respect of delayed payments,  a pro posal to amend the relevant Sections of 
the Act was under consideration. It also submitted that in pursuance of different 
provisions of the Act the Government has been issui ng periodic notifications regarding 
operationalisation of the Act from 2 
nd  October 2006, constitution of National Board of 
MSME and Advisory Committee, classification of the micro, small and medium 
enterprises and exclusion of items while calculatin g the investment in plant and 
machinery. The Government has also notified the aut hority in the States/UTs with whom 
the medium enterprises are to be registered and the Format of memorandum to be filed by 
the micro, small and medium enterprises. The Govern ment has also notified rules for 
National Board of Micro, Small and Medium Enterpris es. However,  the Committee 
notes that the National Board of MSME had so far he ld only nine meetings at 
random intervals as against the statutory requireme nt of one meeting every three 
months.  The  Committee also  expresses reservation over the proposal to amend th e 
relevant Section of the Act which provides for quar terly meetings of the Board and 
placing it under the Rules which would fall within the scope of subordinate 
legislation.  The Committee unable to comprehend the rationale be hind such 
proposal.  It only reinforces the apprehension that the role of statutory Board would 
be further diluted.  The Committee strongly recomme nds for creating a Monitoring 
Cell for Delayed Payment in office of the Development Commissioner, MSME.   
 
7. In addition, the Advisory Committee set up under  Section 7 (2) of the Act too has 
discussed the issue of modifications in Entrepreneu rs Memoranda, issue related to 4 
th  
MSME Census and the prospects of separate SME Exchange.  
 
8. The Committee was also informed that the Governm ent has issued notifications 
regarding filing of Entrepreneurs Memorandum by the Medium Enterprises under Section 
8 of the Act. The State Governments are expected to  issue notifications in respect of 
small and micro enterprises. The Committee notes that the number of enterprises who 
had filed memoranda has increased exponentially from about 1.75 lakh in 2007-08  
 
 
 
 

 
to 2.82 lakh in 2011-12. However, the Committee obs erves reduction in number of 
registrations in successive years in case of certai n States. The Committee would like 
to explore the reasons for such reduction.  
 
9. The Committee was informed that as per the Secti on 11 Act, the Government has 
notified Procurement preference policy in March 201 2, wherein minimum 20% of 
procurement of annual requirement of goods and serv ices by all the Central 
Ministries/Departments/PSUs from MSEs, of which 4% should be sourced from the 
enterprises owned by SC/ST entrepreneurs.  
 
10. The Committee observes that the said notification does not cover the 
Autonomous organizations/Societies/ Trusts/Institut ions/ Universities and other 
Government aided organizations under the various Ce ntral Government 
Ministries/Departments. The Committee also wonders if the notification includes the 
Constitutional bodies.  The Committee recommends that the said notification  should 
include such institutions. The Committee also recom mends that the Central 
Government should persuade the State Governments to  adopt similar policies, for 
which Government can use the National Board as a fo rum where State 
Governments are also represented by rotation.  
 
11  The Committee recommends that like the Central Ministries/Departments/PSUs, 
the private sector companies should also procure a minimum of 20% of annual 
requirements of goods and services from MSEs. 
 
12. Section 20 of the Chapter V of the Act provide for the establishment of Micro and 
Small Enterprises Facilitation Council (MSEFCs) by the State Government. The Central 
Government had formulated and circulated to the States, the model rules regarding filling 
up of the vacancies of such Councils and for discha rging their functions. The Committee 
was informed that while 34 States and Union Territo ries had notified the rules, 34 
States/UTs had set up such Facilitation Councils. The Committee takes note of the 
performance of the Facilitation Councils in States. It is rather strange that in certain  
States/UTs no fresh cases were filed during year 20 11-12. Also there is large 
pendency of cases and disposal rate is rather slow.  This is clear violation of Section 
18 (5) of the Act which make disposal of references  within Ninety days, obligatory. 
The Committee also apprehends that decline in the f iling of fresh cases may be due 
to dwindling faith in the efficacy of this mechanis m. The Committee therefore 
suggests that the rate of disposal of cases should be faster. Further, it appears that 
as per Section 19 the supplier does not have right to appeal against the Award given 
by an IFC.  Considering that the IFC do not have po wers to enforce the award, the 
suppliers too should have the right to appeal.  It also reiterates its previous 
recommendation that “The Industrial Facilitation Co uncil should evolve into an 
effective forum of arbitration, to resolve the issu e of delayed payments to small and 
tiny enterprises, conferred with sufficient mandate  to execute its award, appeal 
against which could be filed only in the High Court  of the State where IFC is 
located.” The Committee also takes note of the amen dments to make IFCs more 
effective, that are under consideration of Governme nt. These amendments pertain 
to bringing earnest money/security deposit submitte d during tender and falls within 
the ambit of provisions related to delayed payment.   The amount of award given by 

the Facilitation Council should be realizable as ar rears of land revenue.   The 
amount of award given by the Facilitation Council w ould be made enforceable and 
should include earnest money and securities submitt ed during the tender . The 
Committee recommends that by brining earnest money scrutiny deposit within the 
ambit of provisions related to delayed payment in MSMED Act 2006, this delay may 
be checked and regulated.   
 
13. Apart from the inputs from the administrative M inistry of MSME, the Committee 
also received inputs from select industry associati ons. During the course of its interaction 
with the representatives of industry associations t he following major concerns were 
raised : 
 
Definition of MSME 
 
14. In view of inflation there was demand to enhanc e the limit on the investment in 
plant and machinery in micro and small scale enterp rises. It was also underscored that it 
was difficult to differentiate between private and business assets of MSMEs, hence it was 
difficult to assess the investment in assets with required exactitude.  
 
15. The Ministry in its reply generally agreed with  the contention but expressed 
constraint stating “ The present definition is in t he Act itself. These need to be defined in 
Rules rather than in Act itself. The definition sho uld be dynamic to enable the MSME to 
avail the benefits as well as handle global competition.” 
 
16.  Considering the inflation and dynamic market  sit uation, the Committee 
feels that definition of MSMEs as provided in the A ct may be revised every five 
years. 
 
Entrepreneurs’ Memorandum 
 
17. It was suggested that the filing of the Memoran da should be simplified by making 
it online. 
 
18. The Ministry agreed with the suggestion that th e filing of the Memorandum 
should be made online. It was informed that a consu ltation meeting with the States in this 
regard was held in January 2012.  
 
19. The Committee notes that the Report of the Working  Group on the MSME 
for the 12 
th  Plan, too recommended that the States should encou rage ‘online’ filing 
of Memoranda. Considering the consensus on the issu e, the Committee expects that 
necessary steps should be taken to resolve the issu e expeditiously .  The MSME 
Ministry should encourage the Micro and Small Enterprises to register themselves.     
Delayed Payment 
 
20. The Committee notes general dissatisfaction ove r the issue of delayed payment. 
The Committee also believes that this issue is crit ical for the survival of micro and small 
enterprises who work with limited working capital a nd any interruption in cash flow puts 
their survival at stake. The Committee also notes t hat the mechanism of Industrial

Rehabilitation and Exit Policy 
 
Section 25 of the MSMED Act provides for the exit policy for the closure of micro, small 
or medium enterprises. The Committee was informed that units that are not Companies or 
Limited liability partnerships, are largely governe d by provincial Insolvency Act, 1920, 
where there is no separation of personal and busine ss assets, which leads to lengthy 
litigation. The Ministry recognized the need for a separate and much simpler mechanism 
for the revival or exit of MSMEs. The Committee was  informed that the Ministry was 
working on a Draft framework in this respect which provides for setting up of Revival 
and Exit Committee of MSME Facilitation Council through which a MSME or a Creditor 
can initiate filing for either revival or exit route.  
 
The Committee also took note of the recommendations  made by the PM’s Task Force on 
the MSME in this regard, some of which are as under : 
 
 
…. The Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008 (LLP) pr ovides for enabling schemes of 
revival as well as liquidation and winding up. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs has also 
introduced the Companies Bill 2009 which includes a  provision for a ‘one person 
company (OPC)’. The MSMEs need to be encouraged/ in centivised to convert to these 
forms.  
(Action: MoCA/ DoR/MoMSME – no time lines) 
 
… Banks have existing mechanism/ procedures for rehab ilitation/ restructuring of 
potentially viable sick MSMEs. However, as the track record of the sick units is generally 
poor, the bankers are often reluctant to rehabilita te such units. Consequently, very few 
units are being rehabilitated by banks. Moreover th ese mechanisms do not provide 
protection from statutory dues or other creditor ac tion. There is, therefore, a need for an 
alternate mechanism to re-examine the viability of such units and implement a 
rehabilitation package in a time bound manner. It is suggested that for MSME units found 
to be unviable by the banks, an administrative mech anism may be put in place at district 
level, under the GM (DIC) to re-examine the viabili ty and implement a rehabilitation 
package, wherever necessary. The rehabilitation pac kage may comprise, besides 
additional lending by banks, of relief and concessi ons in statutory dues by the State 
Governments/autonomous bodies, Power Supply Company etc. Since the promoters often 
find it difficult to infuse fresh funds to the exte nt required by the Banks, Rehabilitation 
funds specially set up by the State Governments cou ld part-finance promoters margin 
money requirement. The Central Government may support the setting up of rehabilitation 
funds  in  the States to  facilitate  and  encourage  rehabilitation  of  potentially viable sick  
units. An appropriate scheme should be formulated b y Ministry of MSME with an 
estimated outlay of Rs.1,000 crore. District Level Committees will be convened by GM, 
DIC. The rehabilitation Cell set up in DICs will fo rm the Secretariat of these committees. 
It will receive and monitor the applications and wi ll also draw up a panel of Technical 

Officers/ Chartered Accountants to provide assistan ce in the preparation of the 
rehabilitation packages. The Rehabilitation cell in  consultation with the entrepreneur 
shall prepare the rehabilitation packages and place  before the Committee for approval. 
The entire process of preparation of rehabilitation plan to finalization of the rehabilitation 
package should be completed in 2 months time. Till the rehabilitation package is 
finalized, all statutory and bank payments will be kept in abeyance. This will be binding  
on all parties by issuance of Government order by t he State Government. The banks 
should devise a liberal One Time Settlement  policy  for small enterprises particularly 
micro enterprises found unviable by the District level Committee. 
(Action: Ministry of MSME/State Governments/Banks – 6 months) 
 
…. In place of the outdated Provincial Insolvency Act,  1920, action may be initiated to 
formulate and circulate a model Insolvency Act with in 6 months which will have 
enabling provisions for time bound revival and exit  for the unincorporated firms. The 
model Act should take into consideration the following 4 critical elements:  
 
(a) a specialized quasi-judicial body, to appraise viability and set up time bound revival/ 
closure plans;  
(b) enabling provisions for a holding period for revival;  
(c) segregation of business assets from personal assets based on reasonable norms; and  
(d) speedy winding up in case the business is determined as non-revivable. 
 
(Action: Ministry of MSME in consultation with M/o Corporate Affairs & 
Ministry of Law & Justice – 6 months)

43. In addition to above, the Committee also recommend s that the following 
suggestions merit due consideration and should, the refore, be incorporated in the 
proposed amendments to the Act – 
 

• As the MSE Facilitation  Councils do not consider complaints other than bills 
for supply of goods or services, they need some sta tutory body which 
provides quick relief in the matters like that of p enalty, price variation, 
earnest money and security deposit. 
 
• After Section 2 (p), 2 (q) may be added to extend t his Act to J&K. This will 
enable the supplier to supply in that State without risk. 
 
• The Facilitation Councils should be revitalized, th ey should meet regularly 
and their recommendations should be given due weightage. 
 
• There should be uniformity in awarding same rate of interest by the IFCs for 
the amount due under the provisions of delayed payment. 
 
• In  case of decree given by the Court too, provision should be made in the Act 
that the buyer will have to deposit 75% of the amou nt of decree in the Court 
before filing the appeal.  
 
• In case a buyer is found harassing a MSE supplier, provision should be made 
for a reference to be made to IFC. If the IFC finds  the reference to be true, it 
should pass the appropriate order. The IFCs should be a watchdog to 
prevent undue harassment by bigger buyers.  
 
• IFCs should have a code of dos and don’ts. 
 
• The life of the National Board should be extended f rom current two years to 
‘till the next Board is constituted’.  
 
44. The Committee is of opinion that the MSMED Act,  2006 was a positive 
beginning which provides a really enabling environm ent for the MSME sector. The 
efficacy of its provisions should be tested periodi cally and upgraded as per the ever 
changing economic scenario and the demands of the s ector. In this regard the current 
review by the Committee was   one such exercise by a Parliamentary Committee. The 
Committee also had the benefit of the prior reviews  made by the Task Force (2010) and 
the Working Group (2012) and largely concurs with t heir concerns.   Committee believes 
that the Ministry will give due consideration to th e issues raised by it in the Report 
and incorporate the same in the proposed amendments.

a specific mention of the compliance with the prefe rence policy in its Annual Report 
to be tabled in Parliament. Progressive Association s of MSEs should be associated 
with monitoring implementation and suggesting appro priate revision of the 
policies.’ 
(Para No. 24) 
 
 13. The  Committee notes that the Press Note 5 of ( 20 th  September 2012) 
mentions only the Small Industries and not enterprises thereby excluding the service 
sector. Further the Micro and medium enterprises have largely been excluded in the 
Press Note. The Committee recommends that Ministry of MSME may take up the 
issue with Department of IPP in this respect. The C ommittee also notes that the said 
Press Note defines a Small Scale Industry as having  an investment of US $ 1 Million 
in Plant and machinery. And that “ if at any point of time, this valuation is 
exceeded, the industry  shall not qualify as ‘ smal l industry’ for this purpose.” This 
will put severe cap on the growth prospects of smal l  supplier,  which  goes  against  
the  intent  of the  MSMED  Act.  However, the Comm ittee notes the Budget 
proposal for the year 2013-14 which proposes to restore the benefits and preferences 
enjoyed by the MSME units for another three years a fter they grow out of their 
category. The Finance Minister said that “ to begin  with, I propose that the non-tax 
benefits may be made available to a MSME unit for t hree years after it graduates to 
a higher category” The Committee also notes that th e Department of Industrial 
Policy and Promotion, is in the process of seeking necessary approvals to amend the 
Policy in this regard. 
 (Para No. 26) 
14. Furthermore, going by the current FDI policy, ther e could be possibility of 
global retail companies setting up their subsidiari es for sourcing the supplies, 
instead of sourcing the supplies from Indian SSIs.  
(Para No. 27) 
15 . Committee is aware of the fact that while this Se ctor is largely unorganized, 
the new giants will set a well organized supply cha in. Therefore there is inherent 
dichotomy in existing MSE sector in India and the i ntended retail trade. There is a 
vast difference in the business processes, structur e and philosophy of the two 
sectors. The Committee therefore recommends that the Government should monitor 
the impact of FDI in retail trade on the MSE sector. There should be biennial survey 
to see the incidents of sickness/ takeovers/ mergers and other effects on the Sector.  
(Para No. 28)  
 

16     The Committee recommends that a monitoring mechani sm should be set up to 
effectively monitor 30% procurement from small industries.  
(Para No. 29)   
17.  The Committee shares the concerns of the Working G roup on MSME for 
12 th  Plan  which states that “The reduction in Net Bank  Credit to the SSI in the last 
decade and in the number of SSI accounts is a cause  of serious concern . This needs 
to be monitored periodically through effective meet ings of the Standing Advisory 
Committee of RBI .” 
(Para No. 30) 
 
18.  Considering the benefits MSEs get in interest rate ,  t he Committee would like 
to know the coverage of the Performance and Credit rating Scheme and steps taken 
to expand the coverage.  The Committee suggests tha t the MSEs should be 
encouraged to adopt credit rating. In view of simil ar suggestion of the Task Force, 
the Committee would like to know from the Ministry about Government’s response 
to the suggestion of interest rate subvention in re spect of MSEs. However, the 
Committee again notes that the Scheme excludes the Medium enterprises, which 
goes against the inherent intent of the MSMED Act t hat considers MSME sector as 
an organic progression. 
(Para No. 34) 
19    The interactions of Committee with various associat ions and banks revealed 
that interest rates charged by banks  differ. The Ministry of Finance should 
intervene to fix the upper limit of rate of interes t which must be adhered to by the 
banks while extending the credit to MSMEs. The Mini stry of Finance must ensure 
its implementation.    
(Para No. 35) 
20.   The Committee too feels that the Banks too should b e more responsive and 
sympathetic towards any new prospective entrepreneu r.  The Banks should 
prescribe time bound disposal of applications and t he reasons for rejection should 
be communicated in writing so that the applicant ma y after fulfilling the conditions 
re-submit the application. The Committee recognizes  the similar recommendation 
given by the Task Force which was to be complied wi thin 2 months. Committee 
would like to know the status of compliance.     The Committee recommends that 
Banks should aggressively publicise their products for MSMEs and the Government 
sponsored schemes. A certain part of their annual e xpenditure on publicity must be 
earmarked for publicity of such programmes/products targeted for MSMEs. 
(Para No. 36) 
21.  The Committee notes that the burden of insuring the  bank credit through 
CGTMSE ultimately falls upon the entrepreneur who i n any case pays higher 
interest rate to Bank.  The Committee recommends th at cost of insuring the credit 
should be borne by the Bank and not by the entrepre neur. In this regard, the 
Committee would also like to know the recommendatio ns of the Working Group 
under the Chairmanship of the Executive Director, RBI.  
(Para No. 37) 
22. The Committee also appreciates the concern regardi ng shorter repayment 
period to banks. The SMEs face huge pressure of per formance and work under 
constant threat of defaulting on repayment, which may eventually leads to sickness.  
 
(Para No. 38) 

23. The Committee takes note of the suggestion that th e repayment period may  
be increased up to 15 years and recommends that RBI  should take note of such 
suggestions in view of increasing sickness in the s ector. The Committee would also 
expect that RBI dilutes NPA norms for micro and sma ll enterprises most of whom 
often suffer constraints in cash flow from their re spective buyers or face severe 
vagaries of market.  
(Para No. 39) 
 
24. The Committee also takes note of new concepts like  factoring services. The 
Act must provide for such mechanisms so as to enabl e the MSME units to avail 
these mechanisms for easy access to institutional credit.   
(Para No. 40) 
 
25. The Committee takes note of the recommendations of  the Task Force, which 
has identified the concerned Ministries and set the  timelines for the implementation 
of its recommendations. The Committee would like to  know the status of 
implementation of these recommendations. In this re spect, the Committee also took 
note of the observation made by the Task Force whic h stated “ None of these 
measures will work unless their implementation stat us is monitored regularly at the 
highest level. The issues are simply too diverse to  be handled by a single line Ministry. 
The Task Force accordingly recommends the establish ment of Prime Minister’s Council 
on Micro and Small Enterprises in the Prime Ministe r’s Office which may oversee 
implementation of these recommendations on a half yearly basis. The Ministry of MSME 
shall   be   the   servicing  arm  for  the  Counci l.” The  Committee though  shares  the 
apprehensions and concern of the Task Force regardi ng implementation of its 
recommendation, it is convinced that the implementa tion should be monitored by a 
Ministry that is answerable to the Parliament and i ts Committee, directly and not a 
Task Force. The Ministry must make use of the avail able statutory forum like 
National MSME Board where concerned Ministries, Ban kers/ financial institutions, 
State Governments and select associations are repre sented. Side tracking a 
Statutory Board shall only dilute the eminent force  of a law passed by the 
Parliament.  
(Para No. 42) 
 
26.   Committee believes that the Ministry will give due  consideration to the 
issues raised by it in the Report and incorporate t he same in the proposed 
amendments.  
(Para No. 44)

Report   
 
The Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company Limited located  in Tuli in 
Nagaland State is a classic case of a state owned c ompany which became a 
non-starter from its very inception.  The founders of this company 
articulated a bold, forward looking and lofty visio n by stating that it would 
be the market leader in the manufacture of world cl ass eco-friendly paper by 
adopting innovative technologies for sustainable development and to strike a 
harmonious relationship between nature and industry .  Established as a joint 
venture company of the Government of Nagaland and H industan Paper 
Corporation Limited (A Government of India Enterprise) it was incorporated 
on 14 th  September 1971 for production of pulp and paper by  using abundant 
bamboo of the north-eastern region.   
2. It took ten years for the completion of the proj ect and the original cost 
estimated at Rs.18.72 crores went up to Rs.83.73 cr ores.  The four fold 
increase in the cost of construction of the project  was indicative of the 
problem of cost overruns which plagued the company and became awe of 
the major factors behind its collapse.   
3. It started commercial production on 1 
st  July 1982 in face of 
insurmountable challenges and difficulties.  It is well known that the State of 
Nagaland faced insurgency problem and the insurgent s through their anti-
national activities posed a threat to India’s unity  and integrity.  The NPCC 
being located in Nagaland was seriously affected by  the law and order 
problem arising out of activities of the insurgents .  Besides, the poor 
performance of boilers and inadequate power availab ility paralyzed its 
operation and functioning.  The company did not hav e its captive power 
plant.  The 6 mega watt of power required by the pl ant could not be assured 
by the NED Grid.  As a result, the company within t he range of 3 per cent 
and 20 per cent. such low capacity utilization was a barometer of its sordid 

performance belying its vision and mission.  The pr oblem was further 
compounded when the skilled and experienced manpowe r bid good bye to 
the company.  Such depletion of human resources and  expertise struck a 
fatal blow to the very existence of a company which  is the only one of its 
kind in the State of Nagaland.  As a result, the Mi ll operations were 
suspended from 1 st  October, 1992.   
4. But, six months before the suspension of operati on, the company was 
returned to the BIFR.  It was done so on April 17, 1992.  As a result the 
financial restructuring of the company its net wort h became possible and the 
BIFR discharged the company from its purview on 13 th  November, 1995.   
5. However, within two years the net worth started declining and by 31 st  
March, 1997 it yet again became negative.  As a res ult, for the second time 
the company was referred to the BIFR in May 1998.  On exploring 
numerous options and possibilities and finding the non-viability of the 
company the BIFR issued orders on 4 th  March, 2002 for winding up of the 
company.  The Committee was informed that “The Government of Nagaland 
and the Company appealed before the Appellate Autho rity for Industrial and 
Financial Reconstruction (AAIFA). 
6. In April 2002, the Department-related Parliament ary Standing 
Committee on Industry examined the issue of NPCC an d recommended for 
its revival.  As part of the exercise to revive it the Committee recommended 
for preparation of a Draft Project Report.  The M/s  Development Consultant 
Limited, Kolkata, was commissioned by the HPC to pr epare a Draft Project 
Report which was submitted to DHI in December 2002 for its consideration.  
It recommended the projected cost of Rs.552.44 cror es for the revival of the 
company.  The background note supplied to the Commi ttee stated the 
following:                
 

7. “The DPR was updated several times along with th e corresponding 
financial appraisal by M/s UTI Bank Ltd. with the l ast such exercise 
undertaken in June 2006.   
 
8. The revival plan as approved by the Cabinet Comm ittee on Economic 
Affairs was conveyed on 5 
th December, 2006.  Based on the Government of 
India’s approval, BIFR sanctioned the Rehabilitatio n Scheme on  27 th  June, 
2006. 
 
9. The Committee was informed that increase in glob al prices of paper 
manufacturing plant & machinery as also increase in  interest rate on term 
loan resulted in cost escalation of the project to Rs.1102.85 crores.  With the 
augmented production capacity of 66,000 TPA, the pr oject was found to be 
unviable.  
 
10. However, the revival of the NPPC was again refe rred back to the 
earlier consultant M/s DCPL to ascertain the viabil ity of the project.  To 
retain its viability, a technically feasible maximu m production capacity of 
89,100 TPA was envisaged by the Consultant DCPL and  estimated revised 
project cost worked out to be Rs. 1479.54 crores.” 
 
11. The Committee was informed that “A review was t aken at the level of 
Minister of State (HI&PE) in February, 2010 wherein  it was decided to 
explore the possibility of turning NPPC to a pulp producing factory.” 
 
12. It is also mentioned in the background paper, “ Accordingly, 
HPC/NPPC engaged another consultant M/s. SPB-PC, Ch ennai in  October 
2010 to re-visit of existing DPR with various optio ns to be considered for 
rehabilitation of NPPC.  M/s. SPB-PC, Chennai submi tted its report in 

January 2011 with a projected cost of Rs.679 crores  to be accomplished in 
two phases.  The production envisaged in first phase is 50000 tonnes of Pulp 
and 19800 tonnes of paper with a cost of Rs 489 cro res.”  The Committee 
also understood that a captive power plant would be  set up for the 
functioning of the plant.  From the documents suppl ied to the Committee it 
is also understood that “In second phase 66000 tonn es of paper including 
16500 tonnes of unbleached glazed craft paper and 1 0097 tonnes of pulp 
(with a cost of Rs 190 crores) would be produced.  The excess pulp 
produced in NPPC will be sold to other HOC units. T he revival plan also 
envisages export of surplus power after meeting Company’s requirement.  
 
13. The proposal has been passed through Public Inv estment Board (PIB) 
in its meeting held on 5 
th  October, 2012.”   
 
14. The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA ) on 4 
th  June, 
2013 approved the Revival and Upgradation Plan of NPPC. 
 
15. T he Committee notes that with every successive Draft  Revival Plan, 
the projected cost for revival increased exponentia lly. With delay the 
accumulated liabilities increased, thereby raising the   cost of revival 
further. The Committee also notes that the original  cost of the renewed 
revival was quoted as Rs 879 crores which was reduc ed by Rs 200 
crores to Rs 679 crores. The Committee expects that this reduction of Rs 
200 crores, would not hamper the present revival process.   
 
16. As part of revival Plan, the authorized capital  of NPPC has been 
increased from Rs.150 crore to Rs.250 crore through  infusion.  The CCEA 
also gave its approval to avail Term Loan from Comm ercial Banks against 
Government Guarantee. 

 
17. In the context of failure of previous revival p lans due to procedural 
delays and with the approval of the new revival pla n, the Committee 
interacted with the representatives of the HPC, NPPC, the State Government 
of Nagaland and the Department of Heavy Industry, d uring its study visit to 
Nagaland on 19 
th  June, 2013. 
 
18. The Committee noted that proposed erection of power  plant of 
higher capacity and related sub-system too added to  cost stated that 
those huge costs have not been envisaged in the DPR .  Therefore, the 
Committee is expects that the Government will provi de every assistance 
for setting up the power plant of higher capacity a nd related sub-
systems.       
 
19.  The Committee was informed that the latest revival plan included cash 
infusion of Rs 552.44 crores through a GoI equity of Rs 261.26 crores out of 
which Rs 10 crores is to be contributed by HPC. The  Government of India 
will also give guarantee to commercial banks to giv e a term loan of Rs 
252.99 crores. Also the DHI had also sanctioned the  writing off all the dues 
towards loans and interest. The Committee sought to know the terms and 
conditions on which the Government would give its guarantee to Banks.  
 
20. The Committee was informed that in addition to infusing equity worth 
Rs 10 crores, the holding Company HPC  will  also have to write off loans 
and interest to the tune of Rs. 134.74 crores.   
 
21. Apart from cash infusion, the revival plan also  gives fiscal incentives 
to the company for 10 years from the date of commer cial production under 
NE Industrial and Investment Promotion Policy (NEII PP), 2007. It allows 

100% exemption from excise duty and corporate incom e tax, an interest 
subsidy at the rate of 3% on the working capital and reimbursement of 100% 
insurance premium on plant and machinery.  The Committee has also 
learnt that the provisions of NEIIPP have been grad ually diluted. These 
concessions have been factored into comprehensive r evival plan of the 
Company.  If this be so any further dilution of the  provisions of NEIIPP 
will adversely impact the revival of the Company.  
 
22. It was informed that of Rs 552.44 crores that w ill be infused afresh, 
major part of Rs 514.25 crores will be spent on capital expenditure, Rs 24.49 
crores will be spent of paying to creditors and Rs 3.50 crores for the VRS to 
100 employees. Rs 10.20 crores has been provided fo r the cash loss from 
production.  In the written reply the Company infor med that most modern 
equipments will be used in the mill and that Compan y proposes to induct 
skilled people in place of unskilled labour force. Preference will be given to 
local educated youth to ensure their retention for longer period. However, 
for initial period, skilled and experienced personn el from HPC will be 
borrowed on deputation. The Committee notes that there is no 
engineering college and polytechnics in the State o f Nagaland.  The 
Company may have to induct local youth trained in o ther parts of the 
country. For long term sustained supply of skilled manpower for 
industrialization and gainful self employment, there was urgent need for 
setting up quality professional institutions.  
 
23. As part of revival plan, the State Government o f Nagaland too agreed 
to increase its shareholding from 5% to 10%. It wro te off liabilities 
amounting Rs 3.31 crores and electricity dues worth  Rs 2.59 crores. A 
tripartite agreement between NPPC, HPC and the Stat e Government ensures 
uninterrupted supply of raw material from the State  for 30 years. There will 

be exemption of royalty on bamboo and other cess fo r initial 10 years.  
These gestures from the State Government  are encou raging factors for the 
revival of NPPC.  
 
24. In addition to reconstruction of plant and mach inery and clearing of 
books, the Company also required enabling surroundi ng infrastructure. The 
Company seeks that the unproductive jhum areas may be gradually 
converted into bamboo plantation. Uninterrupted sup ply of coal and lime 
stone will be required. Construction of reliable ro ad network in the vicinity 
of the Mill and feeder roads was essential for the efficient transportation of 
bamboo and other inputs. The Company was also looki ng for State 
Government’s support to purchase surplus power gene rated by its captive 
power plant. Further the Company seeks that the Tul e Railway station may 
be made operational and that the railway line may b e extended to the Mill 
for easy and cost effective transportation of raw m aterial and finished 
products. The Committee recommends that the Department of Hea vy 
Industry should take up the issues with the State G overnment, Ministry 
of Railways and other concerned Union Ministries. T he Committee also 
suggests that the State Government may extend this support to the 
Company. The Committee is of the view that the Comp any, in addition 
to being a commercial entity, is also an instrument  of inclusive 
development of the region and empowerment of local people. It will give 
an expression to the talent and skill of local prof essionals and gradually 
mitigate the residual traces of alienation among small section of people. 
 
25. The Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company is the only in dustrial 
unit existing in the State of Nagaland.  Therefore,  the Government of 
Nagaland is keen to revive this unit.  It is important to extend support to 
the State Government, the Hindustan Paper Corporati on and the 

Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company to sustain the unit .  However, close 
monitoring on the part of DHI is necessary for impl ementing revival 
plan and making the company financially viable and profitable.    
   
26. The Committee appreciates the support being offere d by the State 
Government. It was informed that there will be regu lar interaction 
between the MD of the Company, and the Chief Secret ary of State, to 
resolve remaining bottlenecks in smooth operations of the Company. 
The State Government was also keen to provide neces sary 
infrastructure and linkages and also to address the law and order issues.  
The Committee supports the resolve of the Central a nd State 
Governments in reviving the Company. Revival and su stainability of 
NPPC will improve the investment climate in the Sta te and the region 
and will expedite process of normalisation after pr olonged phase of 
disturbance. The Committee therefore, reiterates its recommendation to 
revive the NPPC.

Report   
 
 During the freedom struggle the Khadi emerged as a  symbol for our 
freedom and independence from colonial rule and eng aged communities in 
the movement to achieve economic self-reliance unde r the inspiring 
leadership of Mahatma Gandhi. Emphasis on Khadi and  its use gave 
respectability to artisans and their skills.  After  independence Khadi became 
a tool of inclusive empowerment and an expression o f enterprise.  The 
biggest challenge is to retain the competitiveness of khadi in an open market.  
The Government of India through Khadi & Village Ind ustries Commission 
has been promoting the khadi sector through its various schemes.  Till 1977-
78, the Government was providing cheap loans to kha di institutions through 
its budgetary support.  However, KVIC found it diff icult to meet the 
growing credit requirement of the Khadi institution s solely through the 
budgetary support and with the approval of Governme nt, devised a new 
scheme to mobilize bank credit. The Interest Subsid y Eligibility Certificate 
(ISEC) scheme was launched in May 1977 as the major  source of funding 
for Khadi sector.  The Committee was informed that from 1977 to 1997, the 
major khadi institutions were supported by banking institutions, whereas 
budgetary support was meant for medium and smaller khadi institutions.  
However, since 1997 almost entire working capital r equirement of all 
registered institutions under KVIC/KVIB covering all KVI activities is being 
met through the ISEC scheme.   
2. The scheme was envisaged to provide interest sub sidy on the working 
capital requirement of khadi institutions under whi ch the khadi and 
polyvastra  producers can access bank credit at a c oncessional rate of 4%. 
This interest subvention enables the khadi institutions to significantly reduce 
their cost of production.  In a recent study conduc ted by the Development 
and Research Services Pvt. Ltd. ( Delhi), it was fo und that 90% of the 
respondent beneficiaries reported average to very h igh increase in 

production and 85% accepted moderate to high increa se in their earning 
primarily due to this scheme. 70% respondents rated ISEC favorably.  
 
3.  The Committee was informed that during the XI P lan period the 
khadi production increased from Rs 543.39 crores to  Rs 716. 98 crores and 
Polyvastra production rose from Rs 58.20 crores to Rs 74.42 crores. To a 
large extent this increase can be attributed to the support offered under ISEC 
scheme.  
1 
4. However, the Committee noted that one of the maj or bottlenecks in 
the scheme was difference between KVIC and the fina ncing banks over 
assessments of working capital requirement of a Kha di institution. The 
KVIC has formulated a fairly detailed procedure of scrutiny and approval of 
working capital requirements filed by khadi institutions.  The details of it are 
given below: 
1. Khadi/poltvastra institutions submit their budge t to State level 
Budget Team for commending it to the Central office Mumbai, 
2. KVIC places fund directly with the nodal branches of Bank through 
core banking, with an instruction to release funds to the financing 
branches according to institution-wise interest subsidy due to them,  
3. Upon the approval given by the Standing Finance Committee of 
KVIC, the State /Division office issues Interest Su bsidy Eligibility 
Certificate to Khadi/polyvastra institution, 
4. On the basis of ISEC issued by the KVIC, the fin ancing branch of 
the Bank fixes the credit limit for the working cap ital and lends credit 
at the prevailing interest rate. A khadi institutio n mortgages its 
property in favour of KVIC, which provides first ch arge to the 
financing bank as a security to the bank.  
5. The Financing Branch claims interest subsidy fro m the nodal bank 
where the KVIC places the imprested amount.   

 
5. Despite such elaborate procedure, the difference  in assessment has 
resulted in sub-optimal availment of approved bank finance, as is given 
below :

6. In context of existing divergence in assessments , the Committee 
undertook the study of implementation of ISEC schem e during its visits to 
Kolkata Tiruchirapalli ( October 2010), and  Munnar  ( February 2013), with 
KVIC and the prominent Public Sector Banks in those regions.   
 
7. The Committee observes that working capital amou nt under the 
ISEC as approved by the KVIC and actual availed cre dit have 
increased over the years, however, the difference b etween the two, in 
percentage terms too has increased to about 50%. Th e Committee finds 
such a situation where Banks lend only half the amount of credit what is 
approved by the KVIC, patently unacceptable. There is a need for 
serious efforts to bridge this gap. While the Government has formulated 
enabling scheme to address the credit needs of khad i and polyvastra 
institutions, the policies and guidelines for finan cing institutions are 
either not in sync with Government's policy or the guidelines are not 
being enforced by the Banks and the RBI.  The Commi ttee was also 

informed by the KVIC officials that even though the  beneficiaries got 
the interest at the rate of four per cent, actually  some banks are 
charging more interest than prescribed.  This is a very serious matter.  
The Committee recommends that those banks which do so must be 
investigated upon and appropriate action may be tak en so that such 
gross breach of banking norms do not take place.  T he Committee 
recommends that the banks must give credit to the k hadi institution 
under the ISEC slightly above the base rate.  The C ommittee 
recommends that the banks must honour the ISEC and strict 
instructions be issued to the bank Managers to honour it.  
 
8. The KVIC informed that the issue of objectively assessing the actual 
working capital requirement have been examined by t he successive expert 
Committees like Sovani Committee (1963), Khadi Comm ittee (1973) and 
Tandon Committee (1977). On the basis of findings o f these Committee a  
formula to assess the working capital requirement o f Khadi institutions was 
developed by Vaikunth Bhai Mehta Trust under the gu idance of Prof. M.L. 
Dantwala. The latest formula prescribed by KVIC is based on these studies 
and the Kalia Committee (1994), the then M.D., NABA RD and has also 
been approved by the Government. Based on the recom mendations of the 
Kalia Committee, RBI too has issued relevant guidel ines for the banks.  The 
Kalia Committee placed greater emphasis on the asse ssment of KVIC in 
respect of working capital requirements of the khad i institutions.  The Kalia 
Committee took a view of specific nature of operati ons and financial 
requirements of the khadi institutions and accordin gly suggested that KVIC 
assessment should be accepted by the banks in case the difference in 
assessment does not exceed 10%.  However, if difference exceeded 10%, the 
issue could be resolved through mutual discussions between khadi 
institution/KVIC and the financing bank.  In 1994, the RBI also declared 
KVI as priority sector to enable KVI institution to obtain bank credit.  

9. The Committee was informed that despite these re commendations  the 
difference in assessment has grown over the years. The Committee 
observes that the banks have not complied with the RBI guidelines in 
this regard which were based on the Kalia Committee 's 
recommendations.  A mechanism must be created to mo nitor the 
implementation of guidelines.  Any breach of such g uidelines must be 
dealt with seriously.   
 
10. In its written submission the KVIC informed the  Committee about the 
reservations which banks possibly have in respect o f working capital needs 
of KVI institutions.  It was informed that bankers were often not convinced 
with the year-long utilization cycle of funds by th e khadi institutions while 
the standard  banking norms permited that the credit cycle should not exceed 
three months.  The Committee is aware of the nature of khadi busin ess. 
Unlike any other business, a typical khadi institut ions runs an 
integrated business involving spinning, weaving, we t processing, fabric 
conversion, wholesale distribution and retailing. T herefore  routine 
banking norms should not be applied in the khadi sector.  
 
11. The Committee in this respect was informed of  the pattern of 
assistance given to a khadi or Polyvastra institution, which was as following:

12. It was also informed that standard Banking norm s  prescribe Debt 
Equity Ratio of 1:4, whereas KVIC follows Debt Equity ratio of 1:10. Banks 
lend according to their norms in supersession over the KVIC assessment.  It 
was further informed that the Khadi institutions ha ve to execute stringent 
hypothecation deed with Banks for availing banking credit. Banks believe 
that the Khadi stocks can not be sold/traded even a t par value if they were to 
be auctioned in event of liquidation. Therefore ban ks insist on maintenance 
of 138% of stocks against sanctioned amount.  The Committee feels that 
such conditions of maintaining a stock of value hig her than the 
sanctioned amount, is too stringent a condition whi ch will only make a 
khadi unit unviable.   
 
 
13. The Committee also observed that the KVIC has r epeatedly sought to 
address these issues in context of evolving banking  norms and increasing 
demands for institutional credit by the khadi institution.  It was informed that 
the KVIC in 2008 commissioned an independent study by Development and 
Research Service Ltd. New Delhi, to make an objecti ve evaluation of the 
implementation of ISEC scheme.  The Study also cons ulted the banks.  The 
Study recommended that KVIC should take up the issu e of adequate 
institutional finance with RBI and NABARD to facili tate adequate credit to 
the Khadi and Village Industries institutions as pe r their requirement.  It 
observed that there was a need for banks to comply with RBI guidelines in 
letter and spirit, while assessing the working capi tal requirements of khadi 
institutions.  It was also suggested that RBI shoul d set up institutional 
mechanism to resolve the divergence  in assessment and most importantly it 
suggested bank and financial institutions should ta ke steps and interact with 
khadi institutions to appreciate their business processes and business model.   
 
14. The Committee concurs with the suggestions emer ging from the 
study.   The Committee particularly recommends that  there was a need 

that the banking institutions appreciate the busine ss cycle of khadi 
sector and the constraints faced by it.  There is a  need for alignment of 
banking/financial norms with business cycle of khadi sector.  
  
15. The Committee was informed that the based on th e outcome of this 
independent study the KVIC set up a broad based Tas k Force headed by the 
Chairman, KVIC and involving Executive Director, RB I, Chairmen SBI and 
NABARD, Chief Executive, Indian Bank Association, t o suggest the 
methods so that the Khadi institution could avail t he institutional finance. 
While agreeing with the working capital formula fol lowed by the KVIC, the 
Task Force realized that since the formula evolved by Vaikunth Bhai Mehta 
Trust needed to be updated there was a need for a r elook by an expert 
agency to convince bankers.  The Task Force accordingly referred the matter 
to the Chief Advisor (Cost), Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance 
to study and suggest the working capital norms in respect of KVI sector.  
The Committee was informed by the KVIC that the Chi ef Advisor 
(Cost) gave the following observation/recommendations:- 
i) Since the ISEC is issued for one year based on t he targets of 
production and sales fixed for the year, it is felt that the cycle needs to 
be fixed at a maximum of 100% of production. 
ii) The steps to be taken to recover the loans in a  time bound manner 
should be provided in clear terms which should form  part of the 
agreement, so that the banks will come forward to e xtend loans 
without hesitation in the event of default. 
iii) Suitable changes in the statute (the relevant Act under which the khadi 
Institutions are formed) may be incorporated so tha t KVIC can 
appoint a receiver/administrator to manage units in  case of default, if 
required. 
iv) KVIC may restrict the amount approved for issua nce of ISEC to 
annual sales projectd. 

v) The loan under ISEC may be renamed as "Annual Lo an on Subsidized 
interest to khadi" so that the same can be assessed distinctly as the SSI 
category by banks/lending institutions. 
vi) All the loans disbursed by banks under ISEC sch eme may be 
guaranteed by KVIC through a suitable arrangement w ith Credit 
Guarantee Funds for Micro and Small Enterprises (CG TSME); and 
the required premium may be met by the KVIC and 
vii) For smooth flow of annual loan on subsidized i nterest to khadi, KVIC 
may examine issuing ISEC for a block of 3 years eac h time, so that 
the units as well as banks are not forced to indulg e in the elaborate 
ritual of assessment each year." 
 
16. The Committee is inclined to accept the observa tions made by the 
Chief  Advisor ( Cost). Still, the Committee hopes that the detailed 
norms should facilitate the KVI institutions to acc ess the institutional 
finance at affordable rate. The Committee also obse rves that while the 
Government and RBI has put the sector under priorit y sector category, 
yet the terms and conditions are too stringent and defeat the entire 
purpose of placing them in the priority sector. The  purpose of 'priority 
sector' is not merely to provide greater access to institutional credit, 
rather to provide greater access to it at affordabl e terms.  While 
financing Khadi, the Banks should not look at it as  a commodity, they 
should also look at the noble legacy and philosophy  which sustain it. 
Howsoever intangible it may be, Khadi remains a pro ud heritage of 
freedom struggle invoking the ideals for which Maha tma Gandhi lived 
and sacrificed his life. 
17. The Committee notes that the ISEC is a very goo d scheme.  
However, it regrets to note that banks are issuing fifty per cent loans to 
the total ISEC issued.  The RBI guidelines based on  Kalia Committee, 
governing ISEC mandate that if less than ninety per  cent ISEC issued 

are honoured by banks then the tripartite meeting a mong the bank, 
beneficiary and the State level Director must be or ganized.  The 
Committee notes with concern that hardly any such tripartite meeting is 
organized.  It is a very serious matter.  In the ab sence of such tripartite 
meeting, the ISEC scheme is not being implemented p roperly and 
effectively.  Such tripartite meeting would provide  opportunities for 
discussing the problems affecting the khadi institu tions and for 
coordinating the implementation of the scheme which  involves banks, 
KVIC and the beneficiaries.  The Committee recommen ds that the 
KVIC must ensure that such tripartite meetings take  place in every 
State.  Besides, the Committee recommends that the State level 
Directors of KVIC must also take the initiative to organize such 
tripartite meetings.
