INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamen tary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this Two Hundred 
and Sixty Eighth Report on Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development 
(Amendment) Bill, 2015 pertaining to the Ministry o f Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises.   
2. The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Developm ent (Amendment) Bill, 2015 
was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 20 
th  April, 2015 and referred to the Committee on 
21 st  May, 2015 for examination and report.  
3.  The Committee heard the representatives of Mini stry of Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises, Ministry of Law and Justice (De partments of Legal Affairs and 
Legislative Department), Ministry of Panchayati Raj  and received valuable inputs on the 
issue.   
4.  The Committee in its meeting held on 30 
th  July, 2015 considered and adopted the 
report. 
 
 
K.C.TYAGI 
Chairman 
Department -related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Industry 
 
New Delhi,  
July, 2015 
 
 
 
(ii) 

 
 
Report 
 
The MSME Development (Amendment) Bill, 2015 (Annexure)  was 
introduced in Lok Sabha on 20 th  April 2015 and has been referred to this 
Committee on 21 st  May 2015 for examination and Report within 3 months.   
2. The Bill has two substantive clauses seeking to amend Sections 7 (1) 
and 7 (9) of the Act.  The Bill also proposes to in troduce a new clause as 
Section 7 (1 A) in the parent Act.  By amending Sec tion 7 of the Act, this 
Bill seeks to increase the investment limits for Mi cro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises in view of inflation and evolving market dynamics.  Through the 
proposed new Clause i.e., Section 7(1A), the Bill s eeks to empower the 
Government to further enhance investment limits in future through 
notification.   
3. The proposed Amendment in Section 7 (9) of the A ct defines the 
criterion of higher investment for small and medium  enterprises and will  
enable the Government to classify Village Enterpris es as Medium 
Enterprises which were earlier classified as small enterprises. 
4. A consequential amendment to Section 29 (3) is a lso proposed in 
order to give power to Government to frame Rules as per the amendments in 
Section 7(1), (1A) and (9). 
5. The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill  states : 
The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development  (MSMED) 
Act, 2006 was enacted to address policy issues affe cting MSMEs as 
well as to classify the enterprises as micro, small  or medium based on 
their investment in plant and machinery/equipments.   The existing 
limits under the MSMED Act  were fixed in 2006.  Si nce then, there 
has been a significant increase in the price index and cost of inputs.  
There has also been a change in the business enviro nment with many 
MSMEs becoming part of the domestic and global valu e chains.  
Hence, it is proposed to amend the MSMED Act to enh ance the 
existing limit for investment in plant and machiner y considering 

 
 
changes in price index and cost of inputs consistent with the emerging 
role of the MSMEs in various global value chains. 
2. The MSMED Act, at present, states that the Centr al 
Government may, while classifying any class or clas ses or 
enterprises, vary, from time to time, the criterion  of investment and 
also consider criteria or standards in respect of e mployment or 
turnover of the enterprises.  These provisions enab le the Central 
Government to classify micro tiny enterprises or th e village 
enterprises as part of small enterprises.  The curr ent proposal is to 
enable Central Government to classify micro or tiny enterprises or the 
village enterprises not only as small enterprises b ut also as medium 
enterprises.  This may also be based on criteria of  higher investment 
and also on consideration of criteria or standard i n respect of 
employment or turnover of the enterprises.  It will  open the doors of 
growth to MSMEs and will enable them to go to next level of value 
chain. 
3. Since the MSMEs are defined in the Act, any vari ation could be 
done only by way of an amendment.  Considering the inflation and 
dynamic market situation, there is a need to period ically revise the 
criterion of investment.  Revising the investment l imits by way of 
notification will facilitate timely action.  Hence,  it is proposed to 
amend the MSMED Act to empower Central Government t o vary by 
way of a notification, the investment limits, which  shall not exceed 
thrice the limits, specified in clauses (a) and (b)  of sub-section (1) of 
section 7 for the purposes of development of micro, small and medium 
enterprises. 
4. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.” 
6. In his presentation before the Committee, the Se cretary, M/o MSME 
explained the objectives of the Bill and submitted as under : 
“Let me submit before the Chairman and the hon. Memb ers of the 
Committee that this is one of the smallest amendmen ts possible 
because you must have, as law makers, come across v arious types of 

 
 
bills which suggest amendment.  Very rarely an amendment is brought 
in where the amendment is only for two sections of that. In Section 7, 
the amendment that is being proposed is actually on  the monetary 
limits.  That means we are not touching the heart b y the amendment.  
We are touching some outer things. Why? Because a certain monetary 
limit, which was prescribed several years ago, may not be valid today.  
In fact, the correct procedure would have been, at that point of time, 
to suggest or plead before the Parliament saying th is monetary limit 
must be something which should be left to the infla tionary tendencies 
and a periodic adjustment should be possible. That way, a short 
request has been made that we may also be permitted  to enhance this 
limit or vary this limit but there is an upper limit placed not exceeding 
three times.  So, one is in Section 7 and the other is in Section  9.  In 
Section 9, Sir, because it is a smaller issue, let me plead that first.  All 
that has been done is that to permit the Government of India that such 
of the village industries which were earlier being classified as small 
enterprises can also be classified as medium enterp rises It is not 
changing the whole scenario. It is only expanding where we are trying 
to have a play.  ” 
7. The Secretary, Ministry of MSME further elaborat ed on the rationale 
of the proposed amendments in context of the dynami c market conditions in 
his submission before the Committee on 17 th  June, 2015: 
“the MSMEs are characterised by very low levels of t echnology.  In 
the MSME Development Act itself, as well as from th e industry 
perspective, there have been demands for enabling s mall enterprises 
to improve their technology.  When we improve the t echnology, which 
is in the context of MSME, it is not necessarily do ne by internal 
innovation but by bringing in better machinery for purposes of 
production or service delivery.  Then, that machine ry has to be 
purchased at the current cost and in doing so, many  of the MSMEs 
would cease to be MSMEs.  The micro would become sm all, small 
would become medium and medium would  cease to be in that domain.  
That was the second consideration. 
The third consideration was the emergence of value chains in global 
economy.  In a given value chain you have the Origi nal Equipment 

 
 
Manufacturer, Tier-1, 2, 3 and below the suppliers,  who support that 
value chain.  These value chains have to be globall y competitive if we 
have to stand anywhere in the global market.  The c ompetitiveness of 
the value chain would depend on each of the element s, not only the 
OEM being competitive, but     even Tier-1, 2, 3 an d all other 
ancillary and service providers to that value chain  being competitive.  
Therefore, there is a need to improve the productiv ity of the value 
chain in which the MSMEs constitute a big part and also with 
productivity, the competitiveness vis a vis other countries.   
The bigger part of the value chain, the top-most la yers like Tier-1 and 
mostly the Tier-2 suppliers are already outside the  domain of the 
MSMEs.  In some cases, Tier-3 is within the MSME se gment but 
MSMEs are actually falling even below the Tier-3 le vel .  As a result, 
what has happened is that, many of the Tier-3 or Ti er-2 suppliers are 
actually engaging the so-called MSMEs as a kind of outsourced 
agencies to fulfil certain jobs which are required in the manufacturing 
process.  There is another difficulty in the outsou rcing part which is 
imposition of the Service Tax.  If a job connected with the 
manufacture of a particular product is outsourced, then, that entity to 
which it is being outsourced will have to pay the S ervice Tax also.  
The Service Tax is  levied on it.   So the integration of the MSMEs in 
the value chain has been a problem and it is import ant that in the 
given value chains, at least the MSMEs come to occu py the level of 
Tier-3 and Tier-2.” 
8. He further stressed: 
“Now, if the whole nature of the manufacturing is ac tually turning 
from manufacture of individual components to sub-as semblies and 
system integration by the OEMs, in that context, it  becomes important 
in our opinion to at least keep pace with the techn ology and to enable 
the MSMEs to access technologies through developmen t programmes 
of the Government, whether it is at the State level  or at the Central 
level, Sir.”  
 Committee’s earlier discussion on the issue : Empha sis on 
delivering Government Schemes to Micro sector  

 
 
9. The Committee had in its 245 th  Report  has extensively examined the 
implementation of the MSMED Act, 2006 and had given  recommendations 
pertaining Chapters IV and V of the parent Act.  Th e Committee had 
generally agreed to enhance the investment limits f or the classification of 
MSME sector in view of inflation. It had observed : 
“Considering  the inflation and dynamic market situation, the Committee 
feels that definition of MSMEs as provided in the A ct may be revised 
every five years.” 
 
10.  Subsequently, the Committee in its 264 
th  Report on the Demands for 
Grants (2015-16) of the Ministry of MSME, took a more nuanced position as 
it enquired about the accessibility of the Governme nt’s schemes to the 
unregistered and unorganized sector mainly consisti ng of micro enterprises. 
The Committee observed: 
 
“On being asked whether the Ministry’s schemes were reaching to 
remaining unregistered and unorganized sector, the Committee was 
informed in a written reply that the Ministry has n ot done any survey 
whether its Schemes are reaching to unorganized sec tor nor has it taken 
steps so far to facilitate doing business for the unorganized sector.” 
 
11. The Committee had also raised the issue of inac cessibility of 
Government schemes for the unorganized sector and r ecommended as    
under  – 
 
“…. Considering the Ministry’s admission that its s chemes are mostly 
targeted to Registered Units, and that only a miniscule minority of MSMEs 
is registered, the Committee finds the situation un acceptable. The 
MSMED Act, 2006 does not make it obligatory upon mi cro enterprises to 
register. In excluding unorganized sector, the Mini stry has gone against 
the statuary provisions of the Act in respect of re gistration. Unorganised 
sector is at the margins of even marginalized MSME sector. The Ministry 
should do a comprehensive survey if its Schemes are  reaching to 
unregistered micro enterprises who essentially seek ease of doing business. 
The Ministry has highlighted involvement of multipl e Ministries and State 
Governments for facilitating conducive business env ironment. The 
Ministry has conveniently confined itself to the role of advocacy. However, 
the MSMED Act provides for National MSME Board with  representation 
from all the relevant Ministries and the State Gove rnments. The Ministry 

 
 
has not informed that this issue was ever discussed  or likely to be 
discussed in future, in the National Board so that a comprehensive 
actionable national policy on “Ease of Doing Busine ss” particularly for 
the unorganized unregistered sector, could be evolved. ” 
 
12. The Committee was of the view that the benefits  of Ministry’s 
Schemes had not reached unorganized sectors and any  further increase in 
limits of investment, may further marginalise the u norganized units with 
micro investment. It had recommended: 
 
“The Committee therefore recommends that the Minist ry must survey that 
its Schemes must reach the largely unorganized micr o sector even as it 
proposes to increase the investment limit.” 
 
The Bill 
 
 
13. The Committee held three meeting on the Bill, w ith the 
representatives of M/o MSME and the Legislative Dep artment and 
Department of Legal Affairs ( M/o Law and Justice) and M/o Panchayati 
Raj.  
 
 
Need for greater inclusion of Micro Sector 
 
 
14. As the Committee awaited the Action taken note on its 
recommendations/observations contained in its 264 
th  Report, the 
Government brought the new MSME Development (Amendment) Bill, 2015 
in Lok Sabha which was referred to the Committee for examination. 
 
15. In his remarks the Chairman of the Committee  o bserved : 
 
“While Ministry has chosen to act upon Committee’s recommendation 
selectively, it has not followed-up  with the Commi ttee’s observations 
contained in its recent report on Demands for Grant s (2015-16) for the 
Ministry.  The Committee had asked the Ministry if it had conducted any 
survey to ensure whether its scheme reached the uno rganized unregistered 
micro sector.  In its reply, the Ministry had infor med that no such survey 
was done nor had it taken any steps to facilitate s uch micro units in doing 
business.  In his presentation before the Committee , the Secretary defended 
the exemption given to micro units from registratio n as it may bring them 

 
 
into the ambit of multiple inspections.  The Commit tee noted that while 
exemption from registration was given to facilitate  the micro unit in doing 
their business, however, without registration these units remained effectively 
excluded from the Government’s schemes.  The Committee in its Report had 
observed that the exclusion of micro units from Gov ernment’s Schemes was 
contrary to statuary position as prescribed in the Act.”  
 
 16. The Committee was inclined to recommend making  registration 
mandatory and convenient even for micro units based  on PAN or ADHAR 
numbers.  Specific provision may be incorporated to  exempt micro units 
from any inspections.  If registration is necessary  to avail the Government’s 
Scheme then it should be made easier and least intrusive. 
 
17. In this regard the Secretary, M/o MSME submitte d before the 
Committee: 
 
” If we submitted before you that mandatory registrat ion  will send a 
wrong signal, please emphasise the word "mandatory" .  If you 
mandate anything, then, the next step is the follow  up  and regulation.  
Then, what will happen?  If registration becomes ma ndatory, my 
officers will go and check.  If we do not go and ch eck, we will be 
asked questions by you, and three Organisations lik e CVC, C&AG 
and CBI…”  
 
18. He further informed the Committee: 
 
” After the K.V. Kamath Committee -- Mr K.V. Kamath  was formerly 
Chairman of the ICICI Bank and now going as the Cha irman of the 
BRICS Bank -- has made a suggestion that can there be an Adhaar  
sort of registration. And one-page registration for mat has been 
developed, it is on our website. We have written to  all the State 
Governments in this regard. After the advise by the  Standing 
Committee on this point, we have reminded them. I w ill take up with 
various State Governments to get their feeling, and  registration is 
somehow going on. “ 
 
19. In absence of any survey as recommended in the Report, the 
Committee apprehends marginalization of micro sector. 
 

 
 
20.  In this regard, the Committee during its study vis it in June 2015 
took note of PM’s MUDRA Yojna, announced in the Bud get speech 
2015-16, to meet the credit requirements for the Mi cro sector.  During 
its study visit the Committee interacted with the C MD of SIDBI, which 
is the nodal agency to implement the MUDRA Scheme a nd the select 
Public sector Banks regarding the Yojna. The Commit tee found that 
MUDRA Yojna launched in April, 2015 is designed to cater to the credit 
requirements of micro sector through a network of m icro finance 
institutions.  Same time benefits of other Governme nt schemes need to 
be delivered to the micro sector.   
 
 
Need for an Amendment Bill 
 
 
21.  The Committee considered whether there was need to bring the 
present Amendment Bill.  When Section 7 (1) of the parent Act 
empowers the Government to classify any class of En terprises through 
Notification after having the recommendations of Ad visory Committee 
and the National MSME Board.  The Government could have revised 
the classification only through the notification in stead of bringing an 
Amendment.   
 
22. On this issue, the representative of the Legisl ative Department 
informed in his submission before the Committee on 17 
th  June, 2015: 
 
“regarding the first point about classification of industries by 
notification, initially they proposed only by notif ication, they want to 
amend the Act. But the Department of Legal Affairs objected to this 
point. The Department of Legal Affairs observed tha t if some 
maximum monetary limit is specified in the Act, wit hin that limit, a 
notification can be issued. That is the observation  of the Department 
of Legal Affairs. So, accordingly, the Bill was dra fted and thrice the 
existing limit was specified in the Bill.” .  
23. In its written opinion, the Department of Legal  Affairs too underlined 
the need for an Amendment Bill to change the existi ng investment limit in 
plant and machinery as no specific power was confer red under the existing 
provisions of Section 7(1) of the parent Act. 
 

 
 
 Need to bring Village Industry under the ambit of A ct in supersession 
of the KVIC Act  
 
24. The Committee sought to know the substantive ob jective of 
Amendment proposed in Section 7 (9) to classify vil lage industries under 
Medium Enterprise, when the village industries are being governed under 
the KVIC Act which is being administered by the same Ministry.   
 
25. The Ministry in their written submission stated  as under: 
 
“Since Government has had no intention to include v illage industries 
as medium industries, this issue was not placed bef ore the National 
MSME Board or the National KVI Board.”   
 
26. The Committee in its 259 
th  Report on KVIC Act too had appreciated 
the need to enhance the investment limit in case of  KVIC Act.  Then what 
was the need to bring Village industry under MSMED Act just to classify 
them as Medium Industry.  Whether the Ministry has intention to subsume 
the Village Industry into MSMEs, then what was the relevance and need to 
retain KVIC Act? The Committee sought to know why s hould the Village 
Enterprises be administered under two Acts of the same Ministry? 
27. The Ministry stated: 
“The Ministry of MSME has no intention either to sub sume the village 
industries under the MSMEs nor, the KVIC Act under the MSMED 
Act. Village industries would continue to be admini stered under the 
KVIC Act and not under the MSMED Act.  In view of t he aforesaid 
position, Government is separately considering cert ain amendments 
in the KVIC Act, 1956.  One of the amendments relat es to change in 
definition of “Village Industry”. The amendment in the definition of 
“Village industry” has been proposed primarily for making changes 
into the fixed capital investment per head of an ar tisan or a worker 
taking into account inflation and also to widen the  reach of the 
existing schemes for providing necessary capital to  raise employment 
levels.”  
28. In this regard, the Ministry in its written rep ly also stated: 
 

 
 
‘Village Industries would continue to be classified as village industry 
as per the definition given under Section (2) (h) o f the KVIC Act, 
1956. The existing provision in Section 7(9) empowe rs the Central 
Government to classify village industries as part o f small enterprises 
only to cover the process of natural growth of a vi llage industry 
graduating to the level of small enterprises. Since  such an eventuality 
may also include the level of medium enterprises, t he words “medium 
enterprises” are proposed to be inserted.’ 
 
29. In the Committee’s meeting on 24 th  July, 2015, the Secretary read out 
the definition of Village Industry in the KVIC Act to elaborated on the issue 
further: 
“I am reading it from the KVIC Act, 1956.  It says,  ‘any 
industry located in a rural area’.  So the first co ndition is, it 
must be located in a rural area.  It further says, ‘which 
produces any goods or renders any service’.  That m eans there 
is no restriction as to what you are going to produ ce or what 
you are going to do.  There is no restriction over services.  It 
further says, ‘with or without the use of power’.  Again, there is 
no restriction, whether you are using power or not.   So the only 
condition is the rural area.  It further says, ‘in which the fixed 
capital investment per head of an artisan or a work er does not 
exceed rupees one lakh’.  So, there are two essential conditions.  
The second condition is whether it is in a rural area or not.  If it 
is not in a rural area, it is not a village industr y.  Even if it is in 
rural area and the investment per artisan is more t han rupees 
one lakh, it is out of it.  If it is less than rupe es one lakh, it is 
possible. “  
 
30. He reaffirmed before the Committee that the cha racter of Village 
Industry will not be changed : 
 
“The other point, which the hon. Member mentioned, i s that 
even a village industry, today, can be declared as a 'small 
enterprise'.  The character of the 'village industr y' will not go.  

 
 
It will be both -- a village industry under the KVI C Act and a 
small enterprise under the MSME Act.  All we are tr ying to say 
is that give us the permission to declare the villa ge industries 
without cutting the roots of village industries.  E arlier, we 
could only call that 'also a small enterprise'. Now , we are 
seeking permission to call it, if possible, 'also a small' or 'also a 
medium'.  “ 
  
31. The Committee sought to assess the proposed ame ndment in Section 
7(9) in a context. In absence of any survey on stat us of village small units, 
the Committee felt that the “Ministry has created a  hypothetical scenario for 
organic growth of village industry into a Medium en terprise. The Census 
figures recently released, pointed out that only 1. 6% of rural household are 
engaged in non-farming enterprises. 50% of the rura l households depend on 
contractual labour. ... Rural sector is under sever e distress. In such abysmal 
situation, does the Ministry realistically envisage a village enterprise of Rs 5 
crores and above?” The Committee sought to know if the provisions of the 
Act are limited only to the village industries list ed in Schedule of the KVIC 
Act?   
 
 
32. The Ministry replied: 
The MSMED Act does not define a ‘village industry”.   An industry 
located in a village and engaged in production or m anufacture of an 
item or the activity mentioned in the Schedule to t he KVIC Act is 
classified as ‘village industry’ in terms of the de finition given in 
Section 2 (h) of the KVIC Act for the purposes of the KVIC Act only. 
 
33. The issue of including village industries under  the ambit of 
MSMED Act also pertained to definition of ‘village industry’.  Under 
the MSMED Act, the classification is done on the ba sis of investment in 
‘plant and machinery’ whereas under the KVIC Act, a  village industry 
is defined in terms of investment which includes la nd and building. The 
KVIC Act also defines the ‘Rural area’ where the Vi llage industries are 
supposed to be located.  The Committee wondered if extending the 
MSMED Act to the village industry, not bring the is sue of conflicting 
definitions? And in absence of any definition of Vi llage Industry and 

 
 
Rural Area in the MSMED Act, such provisions will b e prone to 
conflicting interpretations.  
 
 
34. Regarding possible conflict in definition of Vi llage Industry, the 
Ministry in its written reply tried to justify such difference in definition: 
 
“According to the KVIC Act, 1956, a village industry  is defined in 
terms of the amount of the fixed capital investment  including 
investment in plant and machinery and land and buil ding (Section (2) 
(cc) &(h)). Since the village industries have been traditionally based 
on skills and craft of artisan with little investme nt in equipment, the 
cost of land and building is taken into consideration for the purpose of 
their categorisation. In the event, such a village industry grows in 
terms of increased business and turnover and wishes  to graduate to 
the higher scale with induction of new technologies  and equipment, it 
should be allowed to come under the umbrella of the  MSMED Act 
through the proposed amendment to the Act, instead of the KVIC Act. 
As such, there is apparently no conflict in the respective definitions .” 
 
35. During the meeting on 24 
th  July, 2015, the Secretary, M/o MSME 
conceded that there was no consultation in respect of Village Industries 
being classified as Medium Industries. He reaffirme d that the proposed 
amendment will not change the character of village industries. The Secretary 
also informed the Committee that Government will br ing a comprehensive 
Bill to amend the KVIC Act, 1956 including the defi nitions of Village 
industries to enhance the investment limit per worker/artisan. 
 
36. The Committee noted that only 4 States and 3 UTs re sponded to 
the Amendments sought in the Bill.  The Committee e xpressed concern 
whether the views of only 4 States and 3 UTs could be taken as 
representatives of remaining States.  The Committee  is of view that 
comments of remaining States may also be obtained a nd taken into 
consideration. 
 
37. The Secretary, in his submission informed the C ommittee about the 
consultative process followed before bringing the Bill: 

 
 
“We have the MSME Development Board, in which this issue was 
actually raised by the State Governments, and by th e industry 
associations. Then, we put this proposal on our web site for comment 
by anybody, including the associations, etc. Then, we requested the 
States...” 
38. He informed the Committee that he himself had w ritten letters to the 
Chief Secretaries of the States, soliciting their c omments and inputs on the 
Bill. 
39. However, the Committee has doubt whether the is sue of increasing 
the investment limit was ever conclusively discusse d in details in the 
National MSME Board. The issue was raised by two in dustry organizations 
and only one State Government of MP, who later did not even respond to the 
provisions of Amendment Bill. One industry organiza tion opposed the 
proposal. However, nothing was decided conclusively  in the Board. The 
Committee is not aware if the issue pertaining Sect ion 7(9) of the Act 
regarding Village Industries too was ever discussed  in the National MSME 
Board or the KVIC. The Committee wondered that apar t from its own 
recommendations, if adequate consultations have bee n done in the 
Government and among States on the issue. 
40. The Secretary, M/o MSME pleaded: 
“There is one question that you have raised also tha t "Did you 
consult?" The answer is yes. There was consultation  in various fora. 
The only thing is that during consultation there was unanimity, but did 
not get recorded in the shape of a conclusion, or, in the shape of a 
resolution.  But even today there is almost unanimi ty. In the last few 
days some people from the Industry Association came  and met me. 
Their view is that if you do not amend that effecti vely, quite a few 
people would be shut out of the MSMED Act.”  
 
41. However, in the meeting held on 24 
th  July, 2015, the Secretary, M/o 
MSME informed that as per the Committee’s observati ons, a meeting of 
National MSME Board was convened and that there was  general consensus 
over the issue of raising investment limit in plant  and machinery in respect 
of MSMEs.  
 
“, Sir, after the last meeting and before today’s m eeting, a meeting of 
the National Board was convened and in the meeting of the National 

 
 
Board, we, specifically, raised this point and we a lso listed out who 
the speakers are who are speaking in favour.  It is  my pleasure to 
inform you that we got almost complete support on t hat.  Some 
speakers did not mention this issue. “  
 
42. The Committee express its appreciation that the Na tional MSME 
Board considered the issue and that there was general agreement. 
 
 
Limited Amendment: Status of Committee’s earlier re commendations 
on the MSMED Act, 2006  
 
43. In addition to the proposed amendments, the Committ ee in its 
245 
th  Report had  made comprehensive recommendations per taining 
National MSME Board, for making Industrial Facilita tion Council 
more effective tool for timely recovery of dues to the MSE suppliers, 
inclusion of autonomous bodies and State Government s in the purchase 
preference policy for MSEs, protection of unorganis ed micro sector in 
wake of FDI policy and credit related issues. It wa s expected that those 
recommendations will be reflected in the Amendment Bill. However, the 
Bill is being brought only for a very limited purpo se to increase the 
investment limits. 
 
44. Regarding other steps taken by the Government, in conformity with 
the provisions of the Act, the Secretary, informed the Committee : 
 
“Sir, I would also like to point out in this contex t the other enabling 
provisions in the MSME Development Act.  There are a number of 
provisions under which Facilitation Council has bee n set up, under 
which the Ministry and the Government are empowered  to issue 
notifications for the development of MSMEs and also  for issues 
connected with the credit inflow to the MSME sector .  We have so far 
brought about two important notifications.  One is relating to the 
procurement from the micro and small enterprises.  Very recently 
another notification has been issued dealing with t he issue of relief 
and rehabilitation of the MSMEs and to address the problem of  
 

 
 
incipient sickness, its early identification and ad dressing it through a 
mechanism which has been prescribed in a notificati on in 
consultation with the Reserve Bank of India. “   
 
45. The Ministry in its written reply further submi tted: 
 
“This Ministry has proposed to amend the MSMED Act w ith the 
limited purpose to raise the investment ceiling as early as possible so

the MSMED Act in the light of the recommendations o f the Hon’ble 
Committee as well as other relevant factors may be taken up after the 
detailed examination of the issues involved.”

in its 245 
th  Report and is of the view after reading the written comments 
of the Ministry that adequate consultation has to b e done on the need to 
bring amendments in the existing parent Act.  
 
Committee’s observations  
 
47. After a detailed examination of the Bill and di scussions with the 
concerned Ministries/Departments, in addition to de tailed discussion and 
observations on above issues, the Committee also dr aws following 
conclusions: 
48. The Committee in its 259 
th  Report on KVIC Act had 
recommended amendments in the definition regarding investment limit 
for Village Industry and Rural Areas. The Committee  wonders that 
despite such recommendation the Ministry chose not to enhance 
investment limit under KVIC Act and has instead pro posed to bring

of any empirical study on the coverage of Governmen t schemes of small 
village industries and in view of recent  census fi gures reflecting severe 
economic distress in rural areas, the Committee cautions that classifying 
Village Industries as Medium Industry may not achie ve the stated 
objectives and even lead to conflicting interpretat ions of definitions 
under two Acts. The Committee is of the view that G overnment may 

 
 
consider including the definition of Village Indust ry as given in the 
KVIC Act with commensurate modifications, in the MSMED Act. 
49. The Committee reiterates its concern regarding non -accessibility 
of Government schemes to largely unregistered micro  sector and 
reaffirms its recommendation in 264 th  Report in this respect. The 
Committee acknowledges that recent PM’s MUDRA Yojna  may meet 
the credit requirements of micro sector, however, o ther Government 
schemes too should reach the micro sector.  
50. The Committee also appreciates the initiatives taken by the

intrusive inspections. The Committee therefore reco mmends that if 
registration is essential for availing Govt. scheme s then it should be 
made convenient and non intrusive. 
51. The Committee reiterates its recommendations in 24 5 
th  Report 
and feels that proposed amendments are only partial . The 245 th  report 
was the outcome of Committee’s detailed examination of actual working 
of various provisions of the parent MSME Developmen t Act, 2006, over 
last decade. The Committee had identified certain i ssues and had made 
recommendations. The Committee believes that its re commendations 
should have been incorporated in this Amendment Bil l and it feels that 
its recommendations will be a useful reference for future comprehensive 
amendment of the parent Act.  
  

 
 
Adoption of the Bill

and adopted the Bill as under:-

 Para No.15

 Out of 290 CPSEs as on 31.3.2014, 141 CPSEs has re ported a reduction in the

 During 2013-14, 1886 employees have opted for VRS in CPSEs and 3340 VRS

Further Recommendation/ observation  
 
 The Committee in their recommendation had pointed o ut a reduction of

related to those employees.  However, the reply of the Department does not mention 
anything about this large reduction in the number o f employees. The reply only 
mentions details of the VRS optees for the  year 2013-14 and other outcomes of the

Recommendation/ observation 
 
 The Committee is given to understand that the pecu liarities of the activities under 
the scheme can be concluded only at the end of a fi nancial year and as such the

 Ministry of Finance to iron out this problem. The Committee observes that utilisation of

(ii) 
 
 
 
 
 

 
REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with  the Action Taken by the 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises on the recommendations contained in the 
Committee’s Two Hundred Sixty Fourth Report on Dema nds for Grants (2015-16)  
pertaining to the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
 
2.  Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises in respect of the recommendation s contained in the Report. These have 
been categorized as follows:  
 
Chapter –I   The recommendations/observations, which have bee n accepted by the 
Ministry. 
 
 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Minis try has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report. 
 
Chapter -II   The recommendations/observations which the Commit tee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government's replies. 
 
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic and 
explanations advanced by the Ministry and therefore  do not want to pursue them for the 
present. 
 
Chapter -III    The recommendations/observations in respect of w hich the Committee has 
either not accepted replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry to review its reply. 
 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-i mplementation of 
recommendations contained in Chapter – III and desi res that the Ministry should furnish 
logical explanations therefor. 
 
Chapter -IV    The recommendations/observations in respect of wh ich final replies of the 
Ministry have not been received. 
 
 In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV , the Ministry has either 
furnished the interim replies or couched its langua ge in vague terms like noted for 
compliance/guidance, therefore, the Committee desir es that the Ministry should furnish 
Action Taken Notes in respects of recommendations c ategorized in Chapter-IV in detail and 
to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee. 
 
3. The details of the ATR are being discussed in the succeeding pages. 
 
 
 
 
 

-2- 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The  Committee  notes  that  80%  of  trainees  of  courses  run  by  the Ministry  
or its subordinate  organisations  were  from short  dur ation programme.  In such a 
situation employability and recognition of such shor t term courses, assumes importance. 
The Committee also wonders if these courses have been aligned with the National Skill 
Development framework notified in 2013. 
 
 (Para 47) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
KVIC has initiated steps for aligning the skill development p rogrammes run by 
KVIC with the National Skill Development framework. Act ion for entering into suitable 
MoU in this regard is under progress. 
Coir Board has taken initiatives to align the coir technol ogy courses offered by it with the 
National Skill Development Framework. 
In respect of Skill Development Programmes being undertaken  by other organisations 
under the Ministry, all out efforts would be made to align  the courses with the National 
Skill Development framework notified in 2013. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
In view of prevailing inflation, the Committee is inclined to r ecommend to 
Ministry to consider the demand, particularly when the  Ministry itself is proposing an 
upward revision of investment limits for MSME sector. 
 (Para 60) 
Action Taken  
 
The recommendation of the Committee has been noted. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

-3- 
 
CHAPTER-II 
 
Recommendations/Observations which the Committee do es not desire to pursue in 
view of the Government’s replies 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The  Committee  observes  that  since  January,  20 14,  the  number  and account of 
settlement has seen sudden spurt.  The Committee is ala rmed at growing cases of NPAs 
in MSE sector.  Forcing MLIs to invoke guarantees in lar ger number.   The Committee 
may also be informed about those Fixed Deposits whose gua rantee is not invoked by 
MLIs. 
 
 
(Para 58) 
Action Taken 
 
  
Ministry of MSME is keeping a close watch on the rising NPAs and outgoes on 
account of invoked guarantees. Also, there has been request to infuse the necessary amount 
of funds towards the corpus of CGTMSE. As on 31.05.201 5 the fixed deposits (i.e. total 
corpus plus interest and other incomes from corpus in vestment) stand at Rs. 4790.29 
Crore.  So far guarantees worth Rs. 1577.46 crore hav e been invoked. Remaining is the 
amount of Fixed Deposits whose guarantee is not invoked by MLIs. This is boosted further 
by service and guarantee fees collected which stand at Rs. 2497.21 Crore. 
 
  Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Committee also takes note of demand of raising the c apital investment limit 
under CLCSS from Rs. 1 crore to 2 crores.  There were  also suggestions that second 
hand plant, machineries or equipment too should be allo wed under the CLCSS Scheme. 
There was also suggestion that the scheme should be des igned on the pattern of 
Technology Upgradation Fund (TUF) meant for   textile s ector.   The   Committee   
seeks Ministry’s   view on the issues.  The Committee  found that not many 
nationalized Banks had become the nodal agencies under  the Scheme.  It recommends 
that Ministry should involve more and more banks in the  Scheme. The Ministry 
alongwith Banks should join the efforts to publisize the sche me among targeted groups 
and should also sensitize local industry associations to av ail Schemes.  
 (Para 69)    
 
 
 

-4- 
Action Taken  
CLCSS is a popular scheme of the Ministry, hence th ere is always a demand of 
raising the Capital Investment limit from Rs.1 crore to 2 crore. Though recommendation of  
the  Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) on raising  the Capital Investment  limit from 
Rs.1 crore to 2 crore and subsidy limit to 30 lakh ( max.15% of 2cr.) with enhancement of 
extra 5% subsidy to NE region, the same was not pro ceeded further due to constraint of 
additional fund requirements. 
 
The objective of the CLCSS scheme is to facilitate technology up-gradation for 
induction of well established and improved technolo gies in the specified sub-sectors 
/products approved under the scheme.  Since it is very difficult to calculate the residual life 
and  appraise the performance of second hand plant , machinery  and equipment  in a vast 
mosaic of MSEs, it is apprehended  that the very ob jective of the scheme will be defeated 
in case  such machinery under perform.  Hence, it i s advisable not to allow second hand 
plant, machineries or equipment in the scheme. The suggestion to redesign the Scheme on 
the pattern of Technology Up-gradation Fund (TUF) m eant for textile sector by Ministry 
of Textile at present can only be undertaken after independent evaluation of the present 
scheme by an Evaluation agency to assess the effica cy of the scheme and to ascertain 
fulfilment of the intended purpose of the scheme. P rior to restructuring the scheme, the 
critical parameters and constraints in implementing  the scheme are to be studied. Instead 
of focusing to a specific sector like textiles with  specific/alternate options of subsidy 
pattern , the present structure of the scheme  shou ld continue with the thrust of focusing 
on infusing  new and upgraded technology  to make MSME a vibran t sector.  Moreover, to 
ensure greater participation of MSEs, the subsidy cap may be enhanced . 
  
  Earlier there were only two nodal banks i.e. SIDB I & NABARD implementing the 
scheme. At present 12 nodal banks are implementing CLCSS, recently Indian Bank & 
Corporation Bank have been nominated. This ministry  is trying to nominate more and 
more banks especially nationalized banks as nodal b ank for better implementation of 
scheme. 
 
CLCSS being one of the flagship scheme of the Ministry, efforts are on to popularise 
the scheme in less participating states of NER. 
 
  Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee takes note of the Secretary’s submiss ion regarding  scheme and 
wonders if allocation was made without any proposal from  the Ministry. With Ministry 
having no plans or project to use the fund, such surpr ise allocation obviously led to delay. 
The Committee know the details of structures of these thre e schemes and are the 
beneficiaries identified. The Committee also cautions that th e Ministry must make use of 
funds efficiently. 
 (Para 105) 
 

-5- 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
The Ministry has notified a Scheme called ASPIRE (A  Scheme for Promoting  
Innovation,  Rural  Industry  and  Entrepreneurship).   The   objectives  of   the  
 
 
scheme are to set up business incubators so that th e eligible youth could be adequately 
incubated in various skills and provided the opport unity to set up their own business 
enterprises; to set up technology based incubators for incubation of innovative 
ideas/technology in the Agro-based industry; and Fu nd of Funds to establish Technology 
Centre Networks to promote Innovation, Entrepreneur ship and Agro-Industry.  The Fund 
of Funds will be created under SIDBI with a corpus of Rs. 60 crore and targets those 
knowledge initiatives which need support and nurtur ing to succeed in developing 
technology and business enterprise in the areas of innovation, entrepreneurship, forward 
and backward linkages etc. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee feels that the previous experience ha s told us that the Cluster based 
approach is essentially against the basic character of MSME  sector. The Units operate 
individually and independently under individual ownership o r limited partnership.   To 
ask MSME units to form Cluster will only delay the process as it involves land issues 
and would require administrative and statutory clearance s which may vary from State to 
State. 
 
 (Para 118) 
Action Taken 
 
 
Cluster based development of Traditional Industries and Villa ge Industries will 
ensure that they are more sustainable because of the stre ngthening of clusters.  This is the 
major objective of SFURTI.  Cluster development is also one model of development. 
In the 16 th  SSC held on 10.8.2015, 14 clusters (KVIC-9 & Coir-5) in volving an 
amount of Rs.2884.24 lakh worth of project cost and Rs. 2244.66 lakh as total assistance 
(including 50% of Soft Intervention, Technical Agency Cost and Implementing Agency 
Cost and 43% of Hard Intervention) under SFURTI has be en approved.  13 clusters 
(KVIC-10 & coir-3) in respect of Detailed Study Report (DS R) with total projects worth 
Rs.2530.70 lakh was approved in the 16 th  SSC meeting held on 10.8.2015. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 The Committee suggests that the possibility must be explored to use coir fibre in 
the production of paper and packaging material. 
 
 
(Para 132) 

-6- 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
The Research and Development wing of Coir Board has  already developed 
handmade paper out of coir, by which file covers, c arry bags, etc. could be produced.  
Similarly attempts were made by the wing for making packaging materials using coir.  The 
Board in collaboration with Indian Institute of Pac kaging (IIP), Mumbai, could develop 
economic packaging materials out of coir polymer co mposite boards replacing plywood, 
such as for sheathing of wooden crates for heavy eq uipments and machine tools, for pallet 
docks and for top and bottom closure for fibre board drums. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

-7- 
 
CHAPTER-III 
 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which th e Committee has either not 
accepted the replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry to review its replies 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
Instead of assisting the State Government, the Mini stry has devised its own 
Schemes and implements them through State agencies like K VIBs and DICs.   The 
Committee finds that though State Governments are involved  in consultative process 
at apex level, and execution level, the Central and Sta te agencies do not converge 
institutionally.  For example in the KVIC act, there is  no institutional arrangement for 
coordination between KVIC, State Directorate and KVIBs  to execute KVIC programmes.   
The Committee observes that with greater emphasis of cooperative federalism and 
setting up of Niti Ayog as consultative forum between Centr e and State 
Governments, the role of the Ministry may be suitably recast with respect of formulation 
and implementation of the various programmes. 
 
 (Para 3)   
 
Action Taken  
 
The KVIC Rules 32 sub-rule 3 clearly defines the relations hip between KVIC and 
the State KVI Board for implementation of Khadi and Village Industries Programme.  
 
Under the Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme  Scheme, State 
KVIB’s and DICs have been included in the implementa tion of the programme.  KVIC is 
the nodal agency for implementation of the programme at the national level.  At the State 
level, the State/Divisional Offices of KVIC, KVIB and DICs ar e involved in the 
implementation of the programme.  The budget allocation is divided among the three 
agencies in the ratio of 30:30:40 for KVIC, KVIB and DIC s respectively.  70% of the 
Budget allocation as well as the scheme targets are implemented by the State agencies. 
Coir Board has been implementing its schemes like Coir Udy ami Yojana (CUY), 
Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI), etc. in close co-
ordination with state governments and governmental agencies.  In important aspects of the 
implementation process, including selection of beneficiaries , disbursement of assistance, 
training etc., the Board seeks the assistance of the State  government and governmental 
agencies.  Under the Market Development Assistance Schem e, the states are offered a part 
of the discount amount borne by them for sale of coir pr oducts to consumers at reduced 
prices. 
Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Rural Industrialization (MGIRI) is  functioning with the 
vision of boosting and injecting innovation, quality and pro ductivity to make the rural 
products globally competitive and also to enable rural industries gets its due market share.   

-8- 
It is also conducting various awareness campaigns t hrough various channel partners at 
State level. 
Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Indu stries (SFURTI) scheme has 
been launched to spread the outreach and to establi sh competence in cluster development, 
project management and facilitation of market acces s for Traditional/Village Industries. 
Khadi & Village Industries Commission (KVIC) shall be the Nodal Agency (NA) for KVI 
clusters and Coir Board shall be the NA for Coir ba sed clusters.  National Institute for 
Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises (NIMSME), Hyderab ad, National Institute of 
Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development (NI ESBUD), NOIDA and Indian 
Institute of Entrepreneurship (IIE), Guwahati have also been assigned the status of NA.  
The selection of cluster is done jointly by the NA’s and State Governments. 
A Scheme for Promotion of Innovation, Rural Industr y and Entrepreneurship 
(ASPIRE) scheme was launched to set up a network of  technology centres and to set up 
incubation centres to accelerate entrepreneurship a nd also to promote start-ups for 
innovation and entrepreneurship in agro-industry.  The most important component is to set 
up Livelihood Business Incubators (LBI) under Natio nal Small Industries Corporation 
(NSIC), KVIC or Coir Board or any other Institution /agency of GoI/State Government.  
Private partner institutions and entities can also set up livelihood incubation centres under 
PPP mode with the aforesaid institutions, viz., NSI C, KVIC or Coir Board or any other 
Institution/agency of GoI/State Government.  The ne xt important component is to set up 
Technology Business Incubator (TBI) at twin levels,  i.e. supporting existing incubation 
centres operated currently under different Ministri es and Departments of the Government 
of India or Institutions including National / Regio nal level institutions of GoI / State 
Governments to set up such centre dedicated to incu bation and enterprise creation in the 
area of Agro based Industries and also new incubati on centres to be set up by eligible 
private institutions including Industry Association s, along with the Academic Institutions, 
R&D laboratories, Universities, Government entities  and Technology Parks. Region wise, 
Crop wise, Product wise, Process wise and Industry Vertical wise Incubation Centres will 
be promoted. 
Therefore, Ministry of MSME, ARI Division ensures t hat the schemes are 
implemented in coordination with the State Govts/ag encies in line with the spirit of 
cooperative federation. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 The Ministry tends to deny the need for any further  coordination with State 
Agencies.  The Committee believes that in absence o f institutional coordination, 
Ministry’s programmes have under performed. For exa mple, despite of passage of 
almost ten years, there are still 175 Districts in the country, that do not have even 100 
PMEGP units. The numbers of SFURTI clusters have be en reduced from 800 to 71 
for 12 th  Plan.  On the one hand there is low achievement an d on the other hand the 
budgetary allocation remains under utilized for lar ger part of financial year.  The 
Committee repeatedly found these trends disconcerti ng. The Committee apprehends 
if such under performance of Schemes and under util ization of funds has ever been 
discussed in National MSME Board where States are also represented.  

-9- 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee had raised  serious  concern  over  u nder-utilisation  of funds by 
the Ministry in its Planned schemes.   Despite repeated o bservation by the Committee 
regarding issues of under-utilisation of funds year after  year in its Reports and its 
Action Taken Reports, its concerns have been ignored. Sa me pleas of procedural delays 
in devolution of funds, approvals by Banks etc. have b een taken by the Ministry. 
Notwithstanding Government’s pronouncements towards Ea se of Doing Business, it 
appears that these procedural complexities remain insu rmountable in the Ministry. How 
else can one justify 58% utilization of funds till the end o f third quarter of Financial 
Year and then sudden jump in expenditure in the fourth q uarter?   The Committee has 
repeatedly recommended that the expenditure on the plann ed schemes should not be 
crowded in the last quarter only. Yet, no heed has been g iven to Committee’s 
recommendations. 
 (Para 16)     
Action Taken  
 
Most of the Plan Schemes of the Ministry are demand driv en schemes and the 
expenditure is incurred as per actual requirements.  Furthe r, the Ministry of Finance has 
prescribed limits of expenditure for each quarter, which i s enforced through the Financial 
Advisor.  Therefore, even on crowding of expenditure in the last quarter, the prescribed 
ceiling of 33% cannot be exceeded.

per Budget announcement. 
 
 (Para 86) 
Action Taken 
 
 
Technology Centres are conducting short term training progr ammes in the areas of 
Tool Engineering and related Upgradation of skills of the st udents who are 
pursuing/completed their degrees/diplomas/ITI trades in order to provide them hands on 
exposure.  These training programmes are also conducted for the employees of MSMEs to 
enhance their skills.  Technology Centres have observe d that most of the candidates 
undergoing short term training programmes (pursuing tech nical education or are already 
employed in the Industries) do not opt for placement.  How ever, the technology Centres 
have been advised to maintain placement records from the c urrent year onwards in respect 
of those candidates who opt for placement. 
 
Regarding performance audit by the CAG as 
 mphasized by the Committee, it is 
submitted that the accounts of the autonomous bodies are b eing audited by the CAG 
empanelled auditors, before the accounts are laid in both the Houses of Parliament. 
 
As regards the transfer of the training programmes and th e Institutions to the 
Ministry of Skill development, it is submitted that apart from conducting technical training 
programmes/skill development programmes, the Technology Centres are also engaged in a 
number of other important activities to facilitate promotion, de velopment as well as 
enhancing the competitiveness of Micro, small and Medium E nterprises as enshrined in 
the MSME Development Act, 2006.  As such, there is no pr oposal to transfer the training 
programmes and the Institutions to the Ministry of Skill Development. 
 
 

 
-36- 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee may be informed of number of trainees  in short term and long 
term courses and about employability of trainees.  The Committee reiterates its 
recommendation to have performance audit as per Ch.  7 of the Audit Regulation 
(2007) and not merely audit of accounts. If any Per formance Audit has been done 
same may be provided to the Committee.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
Yet on certain parameters, the targets were met.   This shows either figures are 
doubtful or the Ministry had inflated demands. Clubbing such varied  schemes  under  one  
umbrella    allocation,  is  obviously  going  to  be difficult to monitor yet the BE 
allocation for financial year 2015-16 have been retained at same level as previous BE 
2014-15.  Government must benchmark actual utilization whi le allocating funds.  Also 
Ministry must take a hard look of achievement figures.   To say that there are demand 
driven schemes only justify   that a l l o c a t i o n    should   have b e e n    benchmarked   
against   actual utilization. 
 (Para 89) 
Action Taken  
 
The difference between target and achievement both in t he physical and financial 
aspects depends on receiving response from various exp ert organisations as well as 
individual MSME. Most of the proposals/claims submitted by ex pert 
organisation/individual unit do not fulfil the requisite criteria  as per the scheme guidelines 
within the stipulated period, resulting delay in actual payments/e xpenditure. However, 
efforts are always being taken to improve actual utilisat ion of fund as well as achievement 
figures. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Ministry has not responded to Committee’s comm ents against clubbing up 
of different Schemes under one umbrella Scheme, making it difficult to monitor.  The 
Ministry may state the benefits of such clubbing co nsidering that there is serious 
under - utilization of allocation in each successive year yet, the BE remains the same.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
In every running Scheme, barring KRDP and new India Inn ovation 
Entrepreneurship and Agro Industry Fund, the BE (2015 -16) is lower than RE (2014-
15).  In both these Schemes the BE allocation were redu ced at RE stage and yet again 
they have been enhanced in BE (2015-16).   However, considering all other MSME 
Schemes the pattern is low BE which is enhanced at RE stage.  In the context of 
D.C.(MSME) Schemes the allocations have been enhanced  despite lower utilization, here  

-37- 
 
is case of KVIC, the budget 
allocation have  been  reduced  vis-a–vis  higher  RE.    The 
C o mm i t t e e   is  unable  to appreciate the reduction.   Th e Committee apprehends that 
such trend in allocation may force the  KVIC  to crow d its expenditure  towards  the  end  
of financial year.  KVIC is supposed to provide margin mo ney subsidy under PMEGP 
and Khadi Grant, the entire year, therefore its Budget allocation should be enhanced in 
the beginning of the financial year. 
 
 (Para 92) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
For the year 2014-15, funds to the tune of Rs. 3327.00  crore were allocated for the 
Ministry.  Out of this, funds to the tune of Rs. 2042.00  crore with Rs. 1418.28 crore alone 
being allocated for PMEGP.  During 2015-16, funds amounti ng to Rs. 2612.51 crore were 
allocated to the Ministry, out of which Rs. 1050.00 crore w as earmarked for PMEGP.  
Since the allocation of funds for 2015-16 were lower than 2 014-15, the provision for 
PMEGP was accordingly reduced in comparison to 2014-15. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 The Ministry has not informed as to why the Scheme s of DC(MSME) may get 
higher BE despite low utilization every successive year.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee has also failed to appreciate the rationa l of increasing budget 
allocation for Khadi Reform & Development Programme (K RDP) during 2015-16 as 
Rs. 66.50 crores when the scheme is not able to use the  money and allocation had to 
be reduced at RE stage. Acknowledging that the scheme is l argely funded by ADB 
assistance under certain conditions, the Committee also takes note of protests from Khadi 
Institutions against KRDP and the difficulties in getting the K hadi Institutions audited 
before availing the assistance under KRDP. 
 (Para 93) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Khadi Reform and Development Programme (KRDP) suggeste d various reform 
activities for total turn-around of the Khadi Sector.  Initially  the KIs were not coming 
forward seeking reform assistance. After conducting fi eld level sensitization programme, 
the hesitation of KIs is disappearing and the pace of the programme is gradually picking 
up.   
 
 
 
 
 

-38- 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee may be apprised of suggested reform activities under this 
KRDP Programme and actual steps being taken under this Programme for total turn 
around of Khadi sector. Details of the terms and co nditions of ADB assistance and 
also the budget allocation for KRDP is being utilized be furnished to the Committee.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee notes that the allocation for Khadi I ndustries (Grants) hiked by 
almost double at RE stage in the year 2014-15.  The Ministr y state that it was done in 
view of increased midyear demand raised by KVIC.  The  Committee finds that this has 
been the pattern of allocation in previous years also.   The Committee wonders about the 
impact on Khadi Institution if grants are allocated within second half of the financial 
year.  It will force the KVIC to   release   Khadi   Gra nt   only   after   enhanced   
Revised   Estimates.   The Committee also wonder if only 57% of the BE was spent till 
the 3 rd quarter of financial year, why the allocation was enhan ced at RE stage.  The 
Committee therefore is of the view that Ministry must stagg er the release of grant 
in installments throughout the year. 
 
 (Para 99) 
 
Action Taken  
 
During 2015-16, adequate allocation of funds to the tune of Rs. 145.95 crore has 
been made in comparison to the previous year’s BE of Rs.  93.31 crore.  Thus, necessary 
action has been taken during 2015-16 while allocating budget under Khadi grant. 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee has not been informed about quarter-w ise release of allocation 
for the financial year 2015-16. The Ministry has in formed that it had used 90% of 
allocation by August, 2015.  The Committee may be i nformed if the funds were used to 
settle the dues of previous years.  If yes, has Min istry sought additional fund for 2015-
16.  
 
  Recommendation/Observation  
 
The  Committee  notes  that  MDA  scheme  was  devised   to  sustain  the Khadi 
institutions the year long instead of seasonal rebates. Ho wever, the purpose is defeated if 
MDA is released after the passage of Financial Year. Th e  Committee  therefore  
recommends  that  the  Ministry  must  devise  the schem e so as to ensure that MDA is 
staggered and is released to khadi institutions year lon g. The Committee noted that the  
khadi   institutions   were  working  on shrinking  marg ins and depleting capital.  Any  

 
-39- 
 
delay in 
releasing the  MDA  can  result  in  sickness  and  cons equent  
unemployment  among artisans.      The  Committee  stro ngly  recommends  that  the  
Ministry  must devise method and powers to transfer the K hadi   MDA Fund.   The 
Scheme was devised to replace annual rebate, so as  to  provide assistance throughout 
the  year.     However  current  expenditure  defeats  the  objective  of  MDA. Ministry  
must  ensure  regular  release  of  funds  at  any  sta ge  of  Khadi production. 
 (Para 100) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
MDA is a component of Khadi Grant Head of Account.  Und er Khadi Grant BE 
2014-15 was Rs. 93.31 crore and BE 2015-16 has been  enhanced to Rs.145.95 crore.  Out 
of this Rs. 140.95 crore has been earmarked for MDA ( Khadi).  During 2015-16 (upto 
31.8.2015), funds amounted to Rs.127.38 crore had alr eady been released to KVIC for 
settlement of the MDA claims of Khadi Institutions.  Thus , more than 90% of the 
allocation has already been released during the current financial year. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Ministry could utilize 90% of allocation by Au gust, 2015 whether it got 
additional allocation in supplementary demands to m eet the requirement for the 
remaining part of 2015-16.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The C o m m i t t e e    noted  the  suggestion   by  represen tative   of  Khadi 
Artisans that the Janshree Bima Yojna be replaced with Rashtriya Swasthya Yojna, 
which has better medical benefits. Considering no expend iture under Janshree Bima 
Yojna due to delay in approval, the Committee recommends  the  Ministry  to  take  
appropriate  note  of  the  suggestion  given  by  the be neficiary artisans to replace 
Janshree Bima Yojna with Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojn a  and also inform the 
Committee of its view. 
 (Para 103) 
Action Taken  
 
The views of the Committee will help in providing health covera ge to the Khadi 
artisans.  
  
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee may be informed of the further actio n taken in this regard.  
 
 
 

 
 
-40- 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee noted that 800 clusters were proposed  to be developed during 
12 th    Plan.   71 cluster, majority of them Mini Clusters with less  than 500  artisans  
were  to  be  set  up  in  the  current  first  phase.    Guidelines of revamped SFURTI were 
issued only in August, 2014.  After complex and protra cted procedure only 17 proposals 
have  been shortlisted for preparation of  preparator y  project  report  and  other  
preliminary  survey  and documentation.  The Committee  in  convinced  that  going  by  
general performance of Ministry, it is highly improbable that 800 clusters could be set up 
during 1 2 t h  Plan period till 2017.  It appears that the Ministry due i t own complex 
processes, is severely constricted and hampered in a chieving its own targets. 
 
 (Para 117) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Seventeen Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) consisting of 9 p roposals from KVIC 
and 8 from Coir Board were presented before the Sche me Steering Committee (SSC) for 
obtaining final approval.  All 9 proposals from KVIC have been assigned ‘in principle’ 
approval of SSC in December 2014 and got revalidated in 1 5 th  Meeting of SSC on 
24.6.2015.  However, out of 8 proposals pertaining to Coir Board, 5 have been assigned ‘in 
principle’ approval of SSC in December 2014 and got rev alidated in 15 th  Meeting of SSC 
on 24.6.2015 and 3 proposal were put up for both ‘in p rinciple’ and final approval of the 
SSC. 
 
In the 16 
th  SSC held on 10.8.2015, 14 clusters (KVIC-9 & Coir-5) in volving an 
amount of Rs.2884.24 lakh worth of project cost and Rs. 2244.66 lakh as total assistance 
(including 50% of Soft Intervention, Technical Agency Cost and Implementing Agency 
Cost and 43% of Hard Intervention) under SFURTI has be en approved.  However, the 
releases have been restricted to Rs.968.911 lakh in resp ect of the final approvals of 
Detailed Project Reports (DPRs).  
 
As regards Detailed Study Report (DSR), 3 DSRs Coir cluster with one major cluster 
and two mini clusters have been approved in the 16 
th  SSC held on 10.8.2015.  10 proposals 
of KVIC for DSRs pertaining to different products and all in  mini category were approved 
by the SSC.  SSC also accorded financial approval of Rs. 107.21 lakhs for release to the 
Nodal Agencies in view of the ‘in principle’ approval of 13  clusters (KVIC-10 & coir-3) 
for total projects worth Rs.2530.70 lakh. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
-41- 
 
In order to achieve 800 Heritage clusters, Nodal Ag encies (NA) are also being 
increased and empanelled so that target are achieve d.  In addition to this, Asian 
Development Bank (ADB) fund was also being tied up.   
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 Of the 800 proposed SFURTI clusters for 12 th  Plan, 71 were selected for 1 st  
phase, of which till August, 2015, detailed study r eports for 13 clusters (10 khadi and 
3 coir) have been approved by Scheme Steering Commi ttee after protracted and 
complex procedure.  Entire worth of these 13 projec ts Rs. 25 crores as against 
allocation of Rs. 45 crores allocated for SFURTI-KV IC for 2015-16.  However, the 
Scheme Steering Committee has given financial appro val for Rs. 1 crore only.  The 
Committee notes that all action is happening only at the level of Ministry and none at 
ground level even after passage of half the period of 12 th  Plan.  The Committee re-
affirms its apprehension about 800 clusters.  The C ommittee may be informed of 
purpose of assistance from ADB and terms and condit ions of such assistance.  Also 
provide the details of 13 approved clusters.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee observes that the level of Non-Planne d expenditure  must be 
reduced and   scarce resources should be used for pl anned schemes for the Sector and 
coir artisans. For this the Committee had recommended to dr astically reduce the size of 
Coir Board and its Committees. The Committee reiterates i ts recommendation and asks 
the Ministry to bring a comprehensive amendment to the Co ir Act, expeditiously. 
 (Para130) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Budgetary allocation for the financial year, 2015-16 unde r the head, Non-Plan 
Grants in aid is Rs.26.45 crore which consists of grant s in aid (Salary) and Grants in aid 
(General), Rs.22.20 crore and Rs.4.25 crore respectively.  The funds under the head Grants 
in aid (Salary) are utilized for the disbursement of salari es and allowances, pension and 
other staff entitlements.  All other establishment expenditure are met out of the funds 
under the head Grants in aid (General).  Allocation has be en made by the Ministry under 
Non-Plan head based on the annual requirement of the Bo ard in the light of scarcity of 
resources on the Non-Plan side.   
 
The proposal of comprehensive amendment to the Coir Industry Act for reducing the 
size of Coir Board and its Committees is under process f or obtaining the approval of the 
competent authority. 
 
 

-42- 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Budget allocation for  Non-Planned expenditure of Coir Board belies the 
promised autonomy as envisaged in Coir Board Act.  It is therefore imperative that 
Govt. reviews the Coir Act comprehensively to minim ise overhead administrative 
expenditure like massive Board and also grant autonomy to coir Board to generate its 
own resources.  The Committee is also cognisant tha t the Coir Board has given its 
inputs to proposed amendments in Act,  in 2009.  Th e Committee wonders how much 
more time does the Ministry require to propose exte nsive amendments in view of 
emerging challenges before Coir Board and changes i n Coir Industry.  The 
Committee expects that the amendment should not be merely administrative and 
superficial.  The Govt. must bring the Amendment Bill expeditiously.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee has also learnt that domestic coir in dustries are facing shortage 
of raw material as coir is being exported to China at a  concessional duty  and  the  
finished  imported  Chinese  Coir  products  are  drivin g  the domestic producers out 
of competition in our own market. The Committee recommend s that the Government 
should address this duty imbalance. 
 (Para 131) 
Action Taken  
 
The reasons for the shortage of coir fibre faced by the domestic industry is the 
decline in production of coconuts due to the drought faced  by T.N State, the mite attack on 
coconut palm, and the exports of raw fibre to China.  Actually, the emergence of a strong 
defibering sector of coir industry is due to the high deman d of fibre from China.  The 
import of coir products from China to the tune of 35.80  lakhs in 2014-15 is found to be not 
significant.  So far the Chinese coir products are not rais ing any market threats, for Indian 
coir products, in India.  The fibre imported from India is mainly used by China for 
manufacturing boards which is used by them for manufacturing mattresses.    
Coir Board has already initiated steps for the conduct of a study on the scarcity of 
fibre.  On the basis of the outcome of study and the recommendations therein, suitable plan 
of action will be evolved and implemented to contain the present problem.    
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee may be informed of the outcome of st udy being done by Coir 
Board and recommendations thereon which should be a ppropriately reflected in 
proposed amendment. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee is dismayed to note that its repeated reco mmendations seeking 
better  and  efficient  utilization  of  scarce  funds  f or as vital sector as MSME, have been  

-43- 
 
undermined by the Ministry despite its repeated 
assurance to   improve the performance.  
Every year the Ministry seeks ever higher allocation. Keeping in view the vast scope of 
the Sector, the Committee too would be inclined to support  the demand. But utilization of 
scarce fund defeats all the arguments in favour of enhan cing the allocation. The 
Committee recommends that Year-wise Budget Estimate , Revised Estimates and the 
Actual Expenditure should be provided on the Ministry’s w ebsite. Also, the Financial 
Advisor and Chief Controller of Ministry’s Accounts shoul d post Scheme-wise Planned 
and Non Planned expenditures for every Quarter of the F inancial Year. 
 (Para 135) 
Action Taken  
 
The Ministry has requested the Chief Controller of Accounts , M/o MSME for 
posting  the BE, RE and actual expenditure figures for the  last 3 years  on the Ministry's 
web portal.  Besides, we have also requested to post scheme-wise plan and non-plan 
expenditure figures, quarter-wise, from the current financial year onwards. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee noted that expenditure only upto 1 
st  quarter of current 
Financial Year has been posted on the website.  Exp enditure for subsequent 
Quarters has not been posted.  Even in the 1 st  quarter, performance of Schemes run 
by NSIC and DC, MSME has not been up to the expecta tions. The Committee 
cautions the Ministry of possible sub optimal performance.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
In this Report, the Committee has made appraisal of the De mands of the Grants 
of Ministry of MSME and its previous performance in res pect of utilization of 
allocations.   The Committee inclined to suggest that Bud get Estimates should also take 
into account, the utilization of funds both Planned and  Non-Planned, during the previous 
years. 
 (Para 139) 
Action Taken  
 
The proforma for Detailed Demands for Grants (DDG) ha s been devised by the 
Ministry of Finance which is mandatorily applicable for a ll Central Ministries. However, 
DDG for the particular year contains the previous year's B E and RE for Plan and Non-plan 
and also actuals for last to last year. For reference of Hon'ble Committee, a copy of DDG 
for --- is being attached. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee recommends that its observation on t his Report may be shared 
with Ministry of Finance.

Introduction
The Heavy Industries in India is dominated by the Capital Good Sector (CGS) and the Auto
Sector. The Indian Capital Goods Industry has enough potential but manufacturing capacity is
underutilized to the extent of 40%.  Two major hurdles faced by the sector are cheap imports and
technology gap. The Government has come up with many initiatives/schemes to make the sector
globally competitive. The Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) with a mission to achieve high
growth in Heavy Electricals and Capital Goods Industry have announced the National Capital Goods
Policy (NCGP) on 15
th February 2016 which is a landmark initiative in this regard and has been
reflected in the Budget 2016-17 by way of enhancement of Customs Duty on Heavy Electrical
equipments from 7.5 % to 10%, imposition of Countervailing Duty (CVD) on road construction
machinery and reduction of excise duty from 12.5% to 6% on parts of centrifugal pumps.  All
these measures are expected to help indigenous producers of Capital Goods to be more cost
competitive against imports.
2.. The Auto Sector contributes 45% to the Manufacturing Gross Domestic Product (GDP),
26% to the Industrial GDP and 7.1% to the National GDP hence it is evident that this sector is
critical to the manufacturing sector. The Auto sector provides 29 million job opportunities, both
direct and indirect and has made investments to the tune of  ` 70, 000 crores in the last five
Financial Years (FYs). Considering that the industry had a turnover of USD 124 billion during
2014-15 and assuming a growth rate of 10% during 2015-16, the Government expects it to achieve
around 94% of the target set for the industry in the Automobile Mission Plan (2006-16) by 2016.
An ambitious Scheme for Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid and) Electric Vehicles in
India (FAME-India) is being implemented by the Government to support the hybrid/electrical
vehicles industry and its manufacturing ecosystem to attain self-sustenance. In the Budget
2016-17, the Government announced measures aiming to invest big in infrastructure like outlay of
` 97,000 crore for road infrastructure,  `  200 crore to FAME-India scheme & National Automotive
Testing R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP), reduction in customs duty on raw materials for
catalytic converters from 7.5% to 5%, etc that are expected to provide fillip to the Auto sector
in the ensuing years.
Department of Heavy Industry (DHI)
3. The Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, comprising the Department of
Heavy Industry (DHI) and the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), was created as per the
Presidential Notification dated the 15
th October, 1999. DHI administers 31 operating Central Public
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs), including 12 subsidiary companies and 1 JV company i.e. NTPC-
BHEL Power Projects Pvt. Ltd. (NBBPL). The Department also administers the following
autonomous organizations:
(a) NATRiP Implementation Society (NATIS) set up in July 2005, for guiding the
