not be out of place to mention that DHI should also  ensure the responsibility of the 
management of NEPA in the timely execution of RMDP and also in the follow up with 
the MoF. 
           Para No.95                 
Action Taken Replies  
 As regards RMDP of Nepa, it is likely to be comple ted by March 2017. DHI is 
closely monitoring the project to ensure timely completion of the project. 
 
Further Recommendations 
 
 
 The Committee considers the reply of the Government  regarding NEPA to 
be half-baked with only the aspect regarding expedi ting the RMDP being touched 
upon. Action taken regarding the Bank Guarantee for  securing bank loan and 
Working Capital support to NEPA have not been repli ed to by the Department. The 
Committee expresses its displeasure regarding the s eemingly careless attitude of the 
Department towards its recommendations and wants to  have a proper reply 
covering every aspect of the recommendation.  Wheth er NITI Aayog has given any 
recommendation in respect of NEPA and the views of the Department thereon?  
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee’s observation after hearing the repr esentatives of Auto & Capital 
Goods Sector associations is that the need of the h our is to focus more on urban & rural 
infrastructure, road & highways, satellite cities, etc to generate demands at home in both 

 
30 
 
these sectors. For auto industry, the Committee is of the opinion that they should start 
looking for export markets in the face of saturatin g domestic arena while formulating 
business expansion plans. Also, they should earnest ly try and develop indigenous 
technology in the field of electric vehicles. CG as sociations should come up with a 
concrete plan in tune with the NCGP, 2016 objective s of the Government to triple the 
size of Indian CGS in a decade.   
Para No.100 
Action Taken Replies  
 
 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted for compliance. 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee takes into account through the submi ssion of DHI that they have 
already taken into cognizance the areas put forth b y the industry associations seeking 
attention of the Government. Nevertheless, the Comm ittee recommends that the 
Government should look into the issues submitted by  these associations before the 
Committee and act upon them in best possible manner . This will encourage the private 
sector to be more participative in the broader initiatives of nation building. 
Para No.101 
 
Action Taken Replies 
                                        Capital Sector 
 
 As far as Capital Goods sector is concerned, the d epartment has undertaken 
extensive consultation with the industry chambers namely, CII and FICCI and core sector 
industry associations of capital goods industry in the last one year.  The National Capital 
Goods Policy has been drawn up on the basis of view s, suggestions, recommendations 
and   regular interaction with the industry, indust ry associations and chambers.  The draft

and Departments. Capital Goods Policy was submitted  for approval of the Cabinet.   
National Capital Goods Policy has been approved by the Cabinet in its meeting held on

from the current 27% to 40% of production while inc reasing share of domestic 
production in India's demand from 60% to 80%, thus making India a net exporter of 
capital goods. The Policy also aims to facilitate i mprovement in technology depth across 
sub-sectors, increase skill availability, ensure ma ndatory standards and promote growth 
and capacity building of MSMEs. 
 
 The Department is already taking steps to formulat e schemes for obtaining

development and growth of the Capital Goods sector for both private as well as public 

 
31 
 
sector.  The different schemes will help in realizi ng the vision of “Building India as a

Auto Sector

 The recommendations of Hon’ble Committee has, howe ver, been noted for

 In 2014, the Government announced “Scheme on Enhan cement of

 As regards Auto Sector, the Committee may be infor med of the

th  October, 2016 considered and adopted the 
report.

New Delhi

th  October, 2016 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(ii) 
 
 
 
 
 

 
REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with  the Action Taken by the 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises on the recommendations contained in the 
Committee’s Two Hundred Seventy Fifth Report on Dem ands for Grants (2016-17)  
pertaining to the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
 
2.  Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises in respect of the recommendation s contained in the Report. These have 
been categorized as follows:  
 
Chapter –I   The recommendations/observations, which have bee n accepted by the 
Ministry. 
 
 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Minis try has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report. 
 
Chapter -II   The recommendations/observations which the Commit tee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government's replies. 
 
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic and 
explanations advanced by the Ministry and therefore  do not want to pursue them for the 
present. 
 
Chapter -III    The recommendations/observations in respect of w hich the Committee has 
either not accepted replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry to review its reply. 
 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-i mplementation of 
recommendations contained in Chapter – III and desi res that the Ministry should furnish 
logical explanations therefor. 
 
Chapter -IV    The recommendations/observations in respect of wh ich final replies of the 
Ministry have not been received. 
 
 In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV , the Ministry has either 
furnished the interim replies or couched its langua ge in vague terms like noted for 
compliance/guidance, therefore, the Committee desir es that the Ministry should furnish 
Action Taken Notes in respects of recommendations c ategorized in Chapter-IV in detail and 
to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee. 
 
3. The details of the ATR are being discussed in the succeeding pages. 
 
 
 
 
 

-2- 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
It  is  evident  that  every  year  since  2013-14  the  Planned  allocation  has 
remained significantly under utilized by every wing  of the Ministry. And 
considering the expenditure norms prescribed by the  Ministry of Finance that not 
more than 33% of BE can be spent in last quarter of  FY and not more than 15%  
of  BE  can  be  spent  in  the  month  of  March  of FY,  it is  unlikely  that 
Ministry can stick to these norms this year (2015-1 6) as well and, therefore, 
unlikely to utilize the available resources prudent ly.  In the financial year 2015-16 
too,  as  per  the E-lekha  of  Controller  General   of  Accounts,  only  67%  of 
Planned allocation was spent by the end of January 2016, however, as per the 
above information provided  by the Financial  Advis or of the Ministry, about 
96% of Planned BE was likely to be spent by the end  of FY 2015-16 and around 
29% of the Planned BE was spent in last two months.     
   
  (Para 14) 
Action Taken :  
 
  It is true that expenditure of Plan allocation was relatively less during 
the year 2015-16 but it has considerably improved in 2016-17. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee considers these Schemes a reflection of inadequate planning 
and poor implementation. Norms of Schemes are delay ed and schemes are  
modified  the  mid-way  and  till  the  modified  n orms  are  finalized  and 
approved by the competent authority, the allocation  remains frozen. 
(Para 22) 
 
Action Taken :  
 
The observations of the Committee are noted. All th e schemes are 
implemented as per the schemes guidelines, which ar e reviewed from time to time. 
 
 
 

-3- 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
In view of 345 lakh unregistered units in the count ry as per Fourth Census 
conducted in 2006-07, registration of mere 4 lakh u nits is rather slow and tardy 
progress. The very fact that of 4 lakh registration s majority are micro and small 
entrepreneurs, shows great demand among these entre preneurs to register to 
avail of possible benefits of Government schemes.   It is also evident that in 
certain smaller, hill and remote States, the regist ration has not picked up. Even in 
larger States the progress in registration is slow compared to the scope and 
extent of this Sector. The Committee recommends tha t it will require a sustained 
campaign to register all the MSMEs under UAM and th at the registration must be 
linked with benefits.  
(Para 40) 
Action Taken:  
 
For utilization of the Udyog Aadhaar Programme, the  notifications issued in this 
regard has been uploaded in the website of this Min istry. A national web portal 
namely, http://udyogaadhaar.gov.in has also been la unched for enabling e-filing of 
Udyog Aadhar Memorandum.  States have been requeste d to issue instructions to 
the concerned Directors of industries and General M anagers of DIC for expeditious 
implementation of UAM.  In the regional meetings, S tates were requested to 
undertake steps to encourage UAM registration. The benefit of Udyog Aadhar 
Memorandum registration is ease in registering the unit and getting benefits from 
the scheme/programme run by the Government.  As of now, the registration has 
crossed 11 lakhs and, on an average, more than 4000  MSE units are getting 
registered every day. The process was, so far, slow  because of systemic  issues 
which technology has resolved.     
  
Recommendation/Observation  
The Committee apprehends that even the ASPIRE may m eet the same 
fate  as  other  entrepreneurship  development  pro grammes  being  run  by  the 
Ministry. The Committee notes that ASPIRE too is fo llowing the set stereotypes 
of considering MSMEs as low cost low technology ent erprises, that may not 
independently survive the market competition   in l onger run. The Committee 
was surprised to note that as per the Fourth Census  of MSME 2006-07, out of 
the 15 lakh registered MSME units, about 5 lakh bec ame sick. And the trades 
that are offered under ASPIRE may not improve the s ituation. ASPIRE needs to 
break this stereotype and consider MSMEs as technol ogy intensive sector that 
can survive the market competition. 
(Para 159) 
 

-4- 
 
Action Taken :  
 
 The suggestion is noted and would be followed up. However, it is the 
intention of the ministry to break the stereotype u nder the ASPIRE scheme. The 
scheme provides the much needed space for technolog y innovation and rapid 
prototyping option, which could bring the technolog ies to the market through 
commercialization under the TBI component.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

-5- 
 
CHAPTER-II 
 
Recommendations/Observations which the Committee do es not desire to pursue 
in view of the Government’s replies 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
Also, Infrastructure Development and capacity build ing includes Tool  
Rooms that are essentially training institutions an d must not be clubbed with Office 
construction. Tool Rooms and Technology Centers can  be clubbed with Skill 
Development Programmes. And the Cluster Development  may be clubbed with 
SFURTI. 
(Para 8) 
Action Taken :   
 
 It is true that Tool Rooms have separate functions and their monitoring needs 
to be more regular. That is what is happening also.   Technology Centres are being 
monitored separately and construction of office bui lding is monitored separately.  
As far as cluster development is concerned, the ind ustrial cluster development is 
different form SFURTI cluster development because u nder SFURTI, the Ministry 
promotes only artisan cluster. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The  Committee  notes  that  while  all  the  wings   have  under-utilised  the 
available  resources,  the utilization  by SME Divi sion and the DC-MSME  has 
been particularly alarming. 
(Para 15) 
Action Taken:  
 
 The issue of underutilization of the available reso urces has been brought to 
the notice of the Ministry.  The Ministry has taken  it in the right earnest and it has 
improved its performance during the year 2016-17. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The   Committee   notes   a   marginal   increase   in   overall   Non-Planned 
allocation in RE 2015-16 and would like to know the  reasons as to why Non- 
Planned allocation for DC-MSME was reduced and that  of ARI and SME was 
increased. 
(Para 17) 

-6- 
Action Taken:  
 
 The Non Plan RE allocation is done by Ministry of Finance keeping in view 
of expenditure done by each Division on pro-rata. The Expenditure figures of 
DC(MSME) for Non Plan up to Sep 2015 (six months) w as Rs. 65.67cr, so 
accordingly the RE was fixed at RE Rs. 116.61 cr.  BE was Rs. 124.33 cr. And 
expenditure was Rs. 115.92 cr.  
 
BE for Non Plan for Ministry was Rs. 394.91cr where as expenditure was Rs. 
398.50 cr. Which is within RE of Rs. 400.86 cr.   
 
The Non-Plan RE for 2015-16 in respect of ARI & SME  was enhanced on 
account of (i) number of Pensioners increased, (ii)  Two D.A. installments of 10% 
each announced and (iii) implementation of MACP. No t all these factors can always 
be guessed/ estimated correctly.  DC(MSME), because  of its large workforce could 
estimate the figures in a better manner.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee notes massive gap between Planned Rev enue and Capital 
sections. While Total of Revenue section Planned an d Non-Planned is Rs 3140 
crores and that of Capital Section is mere Rs 10.55  crores.  However, these figures 
change dramatically in terms of Planned and Non-Pla nned allocations. Whereas 
total Planned allocation is Rs 3000 crores, the tot al Non Plan is Rs. 464.77 
crores.  The  Ministry  may  explain  how  does  it   reconcile  these  four 
different sets of figures that convey diametrically  opposite scenario. 
(Para 28) 
Action Taken:  
 
Planned Revenue, Capital, Plan and Non Plan allocat ion, all the four are 
different allocation. Plan allocation comprises of Plan Revenue and Capital 
expenditure for meeting the expenditure under vario us object heads of schemes of 
the Ministry of MSME. Non Plan allocation is meant for meeting the establishment 
expenditure of the organization under Ministry of M SME. There is no relation 
between Planned Revenue and Capital Section and als o Plan and Non Plan 
allocation.  This Department does have mostly GIA a nd Subsidies rather than 
Loans.  All the GIA & subsidies are taken in revenu e side so Expenditure on capital 
side is less.  Most of the plan expenditure is done  in Revenue Section because of 
GIA & Subsidies. Plan expenditure has no one-to-one  relation/mapping with either 
capital or revenue. And, a Ministry dealing with MS ME sector cannot have much 
requirement of capital expenditure. The Total Provi sions under GIA & Subsidies 
was Rs.1484.13 crore & Rs.1479.01crore respectively in this year. 

-7- 
 
However, under the Micro Units Development & Refina nce Agency Ltd. 
(Mudra) Yojana, the maximum loan amount is Rs. 10 l akhs which is less than the 
Bank loan component of unit under PMEGP Scheme so i t might not be possible for 
financing bank loan component of a PMEGP project un der MUDRA Yojana. 
However, MUDRA authorities have been provided with the web-link of KVIC, 
wherein the data pertaining to Trainees of various skill development programme and 
beneficiaries under PMEGP have been uploaded. The r equired data can be accessed 
and downloaded by the SIDBI for providing financial  assistance to projects of upto 
Rs.10 lakhs. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
The  Committee  wonders  that  a  scheme  for  MSME   start  ups  is  not 
assigned to the Ministry of MSME and is being imple mented through SIDBI.  As 
the Committee had sought to know the details and st ructure of SMILE Scheme for 
start ups being implemented by the SIDBI, same was not provided. The Committee 
seeks details of structure and performance of SMILE  Scheme. The Committee 
notes that the Ministry has been asking for more al location for PMEGP. The 
Committee may be informed if the schemes like PMEGP  and incubators under 
ASPIRE could be linked to SMILE.  
(Para 52) 
Action Taken:   
 
SIDBI has formulated SMILE Scheme with an objective  to provide soft loan, 
in the nature of quasi-equity and term loan on rela tively soft terms to MSMEs to 
meet the required debt-equity ratio norm for new un its as also for pursuing 
opportunities for growth by existing MSMEs. The sch eme is to take forward GoI’s 
‘Make in India’ campaign and to help MSMEs take part in the campaign.  
• All new as well as existing MSME units covered unde r 25 sectors covered under 
‘Make In India’ Programme of Government of India an d few other sectors are 
eligible under SMILE. 
Special features of SMILE: 
• It is a project finance scheme; wherein, MSMEs are assisted by way of soft loan, 
which is a quasi-equity assistance to meet the requ ired debt-equity ratio and term 
loan on relatively soft terms.  
• Maximum eligible quantum under soft loan is 10% of the project cost subject to a 
maximum of Rs. 20 lakh. A higher soft loan of up to  15% of the project cost will 
be considered for the enterprises promoted by Sched uled Caste (SC) / Scheduled 
Tribe (ST) / Persons with Disabilities (PwD) and wo men, subject to a maximum 
of  Rs. 30 lakh.     

-8- 
 
• Minimum term loan size is Rs. 25 lakh.                     
• While the interest rates are fixed based on rating of the proposal, the scheme 
provides concession in interest rate during the fir st 3 years from the date of first 
disbursement. Presently, the applicable interest ra te for initial period of three 
years is 9.35% p.a. for soft loans and interest rat es for term loan under SMILE 
ranges from 9.45% to 9.95% p.a., depending on the i nternal rating of the 
borrower.  
• The soft loan is converted into term loan after 3 y ear period and would carry rate 
as per the internal credit rating of term loan assigned at the time of sanction.   
• Longer moratorium period of upto 2 years will be provided for soft loan. 
• The scheme had benefitted 419 MSMEs with cumulative  sanctions of Rs. 1323 
crore till May 31, 2016. 
1. SIDBI operates Startup Assistance Scheme out its ow n resources, wherein startup 
ventures with revenue traction of at least 6 months  and subject to compliance of 
the norms under the Scheme are extended financial assistance by way of loans. 
As on March 31, 2016, SIDBI has assisted 57 Startup s with aggregate sanctioned 
amount of  Rs. 57.48 Crore under Startup Assistance  Scheme. The Scheme does not 
cover PMEGP whereas ASPIRE is meant for rural startups by way of equity through 
AIFs. 
 
The objective of SMILE Scheme  of SIDBI is to provide soft loan, in the 
nature of quasi-equity, and term loan on relatively  soft terms to MSMEs to meet the 
required debt-equity ratio for establishment of an MSME as also for pursuing 
opportunities for growth for existing MSMEs.  The minimum term loan will be Rs.50 
lakh for new enterprise and Rs.25 for existing ente rprises going for additional 
investment.  The minimum contribution of the promot er is 15% of the project cost 
for projects upto Rs.1 crore and 20% for the rest.  Term loan will be 75% for 
enterprises with total project cost upto to Rs.1 crore and 2/3 of the project cost for the 
rest, Soft loan will be 10% of the project cost sub ject to a minimum of Rs.20 lakh 
and upto 15% for enterprises promoted by SC/ST/PwD and women subject to a 
maximum of Rs.30 lakhs.  
Whereas the objectives of PMEGP  is aimed at generating self-employment 
opportunities through establishment of micro-enterp rises in the non-farm sector by 
helping traditional artisans and unemployed youth. General category beneficiaries 
can avail of margin money subsidy of 25% of the pro ject cost in rural areas and 15% 
in urban areas. For beneficiaries belonging to spec ial categories such as scheduled 
caste/scheduled tribe /women the margin money subsidy is 35% in  rural  areas  and

25% in urban areas. The maximum cost of projects is  Rs.25 lakh in the 
manufacturing sector and Rs.10 lakh in the service sector.  The assistance under 
PMEGP scheme is available only to new projects. 
The objectives of ASPIRE  scheme is to accelerate entrepreneurship and to 
promote start-ups for innovation and entrepreneursh ip in agro-industry through 
setting up of Incubators by providing one-time gran t of cost of Plant & Machinery.  
Whereas SMILE is for promoting individual enterprises. 
 
Similarly, on comparing PMEGP with SMILE, following observations may be 
drawn: 
 
1. The project cost under SMILE is from Rs. 50-100 lak hs whereas under 
PMEGP the project cost is limited to Rs.25 lakh only. 
2. Under SMILE, assistance of Rs.25 lakh is available for existing enterprises for 
upgradation whereas PMEGP scheme is available for new enterprises. 
In view of the above, PMEGP, ASPIRE and SMILE schem es are catering to 
different segments and hence cannot be linked or inter-linked.

Action Taken:   
 
Availment of refinance by Banks, RRBs and MFIs had picked up in last part 
of FY 2016 viz. during February/March 2016.  As on March 31, 2016, MUDRA had 
sanctioned refinance assistance amounting to Rs. 37 83.20 crore, out of which 
Rs.3337.20 crore has been disbursed to 16 PSU Banks , 3 RRBs and 21 Micro 
Finance Institutions.  Although RBI has allowed exe mption from Credit 
Concentration norms in respect of refinance assista nce to Scheduled Commercial 
Banks, the same is not exempted in respect of other  partner institutions.  Hence, 
MUDRA’s refinance to MFIs/NBFCs are subject to sing le party exposure norm of 
15% of Owned Fund, which works out to Rs.112.50 cro re.  Similarly, MUDRA is 
also subject to group exposure norm of 25% of Owned  Fund, which works out to 
Rs. 187.50 crore.  Moreover, Rs.250 crore sanctione d to 3 NBFCs could not be 
disbursed, as  MUDRA’s  assistance  to  NBFCs  is  subject to an interest cap of 6%  

-63- 
 
 
over MUDRA’s refinance rate and hence MUDRA’s refin ance was not availed of

prescribed by RBI.   Similarly, in respect of RRBs and Co-operative Banks, RBI had 
stipulated that interest rate charged by RRBs/Co-op erative Banks shall be not more 
than 3.5 per cent above MUDRA’s lending rate to the m. Also MUDRA refinance is 
not exempted for the purpose of computation of CRR and SLR and same will

Action Taken:  
 
 As per RBI guidelines on Priority Sector Lending an d Classification dated 
April 23, 2015 issued to Banks, in order to classif y an advance to MFIs as Priority

also other ‘pricing guidelines’.  Accordingly, the margin should not exceed 10 
percent for MFIs, with loan portfolio exceeding Rs. 100 crore and 12 per cent for 
others, over and above their average cost of funds.    Further, interest rate on 
individual loans will not exceed the average of bas e rate of five largest commercial

 The Committee may be informed of the number of PME GP projects that

Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Committee considers this to be a violation of n orms prescribed by the

Action Taken: 
  
 
As per the instructions of Ministry of Finance the Unspent Balance on a cutoff 
date should normally be worked out on the basis of the amount that has been 
released by the Ministry by that date and the amoun t for which requisite 
confirmation of actual utilization for intended pur poses has not been received by the 
Ministry by that date.  If the confirmation has not  been received, the total amount 
released should prima facie be taken as ‘unspent’ a s far as the Ministry is concerned.  
A  statement  of  unspent  balance  regularly  forwarded  to  Ministry  of  Finance  on  
quarterly basis. As per GFR 212(1) The utilization certificate should be submitted 
with in twelve month of the closure of the financia l year by the Institution or 
Organisation concerned.  If any grantee Institute o r any organization do not submit 
all the Utilization certificates (s) due for rendit ion in respect all of the 
Scheme/Programmes/Project then further grant is not  released to that grantee 
Institute/organization by the office of . 
 Next proposal for release of funds is processed du ly considering unspent 
balance lying with the Implementing Agencies under relevant Scheme Head.  
However, the recommendation of the Committee has be en noted and approval of the 
competent authority will be obtained to carry the m oney forward to the next financial

 The Committee recognizes that Ministry has not been  taking due

Recommendation/Observation  
The Committee therefore wonders that if the previou s information given in

Action Taken:   
 
Regarding Plan S&T and Coir Vikas Yojana (CVY), the  Board could utilize

However, the utilization under CUY has not picked u p due to reluctance on the part

there is a slow pace of expenditure due to lesser i ntakes from the SCSP and TSP 
category. Since the utilization under these compone nts is not utilized at the desired

The allocation was reduced due to slow pace of expe nditure and reluctance on

under Grant-in-Aid Salaries (Non-Plan) Head, budget  allocation of Rs.22.20 crore

2015-16 upto September 2015.  As per M/o Finance’s norms, 7 months salary should 
have been disbursed upto September whereas 6 months  salary was released upto 
September.  On the basis of this, M/o Finance reduc ed the budget under Grant-in-Aid 
Salaries (Non-Plan) Head on pro-rata basis. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee feels that overall utilization by Co ir Board has been 
comparatively better.  Even in case of Coir Udyami Yojna, the Board could 
utilize the opening balance.  Therefore, there was no reason to reduce allocation 
in RE on the basis of under-utilization.  The Commi ttee fails to understand how 
could Non-Planned Grants in Aids (Salary) could be reduced which is a 
Committed obligation.  The Committee may be informe d of circumstances that 
led to violation of Ministry of Finance norms by Coir Board. .

 It appears that for long the Coir Board suffered s hortage of Non-

The Committee is unconvinced with the reply about u nder-utilisation of

liabilities were under-utilised by the Coir Board w hich inter alia warranted a

Action Taken:  
 
The reason for reduction of Non-Plan allocation at RE stage was release of 6

Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee has not been informed the circumstan ces for such breach

Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee may be informed about actual procedur e of devolution of 
subsidy to CUY beneficiary and the time taken in ac tual disbursal of subsidized 
loan. 
(Para 230) 
Action Taken:   
 
Coir Board invites the application for availing ass istance under Coir Udyami 
Yojana through the Board’s online portal – coirserv ices.gov.in.  One who desires to 
apply for assistance under CUY can register their a pplications through this portal at 
anytime from any part of the country.   The Field O ffices of the Board situated at 
different parts of the country will accept the onli ne applications coming under their 
jurisdiction.  The Officer-in-charge of the Field Office will scrutinize the applications 
and the applications which are complete in all respect will be referred to the Regional 
Level Selection Committee (RLSC) for its considerat ion. This should be done within 
21 days from the date of receipt of the application .  The Field Office will forward the 
applications recommended by the RLSC to the Financi ng Banks within 7 days of 
approval of RLSC. Once the application is received by the Financing Bank, the Bank  
 

-90- 
 
shall intimate the sanction of loan or otherwise to  the beneficiary and Coir Board 
within 30 calendar days.  On receipt of loan sancti on letter from the Financing Bank, 
the beneficiary shall deposit his contribution with in 30 calendar days to the 
concerned Bank.  The Bank shall release 1 
st  installment of loan to the beneficiary 
within 30 days of receipt of beneficiary contributi on.  The applicant should have 
undergone Entrepreneurship Development Programme be fore releasing the 1 st  
installment of loan by the Bank.  After receipt of the loan sanction letter and Margin 
Money Claim from the Financing Bank, the Field Offi ce shall submit these 
documents to Coir Board Head Office through online portal for sanction and release 
of Margin Money (Subsidy).  Coir Board Head Office shall process these online 
Margin Money Claims and intimate sanction or otherw ise to the Field Offices within 
7 days of receipt of the M.M Claims.  Within 3 days  of sanction of Margin Money 
(Subsidy), the Coir Board HO shall release the Marg in Money to the CUY Nodal 
Bank and the CUY Nodal Bank shall transfer the Marg in Money to the Financing 
Banks for depositing as TDR in the name of the beneficiary for two years.  To depict  
the devolution of Margin Money to the CUY beneficia ry the Board has prepared a 
Flow Chart indicating the time schedule, which is also annexed.  
 The actual disbursal of subsidized loan under the Scheme takes place within 
120 to 150 days.

 The Committee may be informed of total application s received during 
last year 2015-16, number of applications cleared b y RLSC and of those how 
many have been cleared by Banks.  Please provide Ba nk-wise details.  How 
many applications have actually been disbursed in 1 50 days.  Though the 
Committee feels that 150 day limit must be reduced to 100 days. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The  Committee  may  also  be  informed  about  the   purpose  of  proposed 
modification in the CUY Scheme.

Action Taken:   
 
During the Scheme implementation, the Board felt th at continuation of Coir 
Udyami Yojana during the XII Plan period with modif ications is essential for 
adoption of modern technology in the production and  processing of coir which will 
facilitate improvement in quality, improving the ma rketing opportunities thereby 
enhancing  the  earning  capacity  of the workers. The Scheme will be highly suitable  

-91- 
 
for contributing to the development of vulnerable s ections of the society especially 
the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and peopl e in North Eastern Region.  
Coir Board has conducted an independent evaluation of the implementation of the 
scheme during the XI Plan period by engaging M/s. D atamation Consultants Pvt. 
Ltd., New Delhi. In the evaluation report it was me ntioned that the purpose of the 
Scheme towards rejuvenation has been immensely serv ed.  Further, the evaluators 
have recommended for continuation of the Scheme wit h focus on extensive 
modernization and to keep the Scheme open to all ca tegories in the coir sector 
enhancing the limit of the project cost to Rs.10 la khs. Streamlining of the Scheme to 
ease Banking process for the disbursement of the lo an and subsidy, deregulation 
machine procurement so that the beneficiary has the  freedom to purchase the 
machines of their choice were also their recommenda tions. A marketing plan to 
increase the sales was also recommended to be incor porated in the scheme as this 
would lead to a chain of events as increase in sales will lead increase in production as  
well as exports and for that more coir workers woul d be needed and these changes 
will lead to employment as well as income generation. 
 
Planning Commission’s Working Group on MSME Growth for XII Plan in its 
recommendations has also stressed the need for cont inuation of the scheme during 
XII Plan period with suitable modifications and exp ansion to cover manufacturing 
units for value added products and processes, using  high-end machines and 
technologies.  The Working Group has recommended fo r enhancement of the ceiling 
of the financial assistance under the scheme so as to cover small and medium scale 
units who will be able to absorb higher investments , besides continuing the benefits 
for the tiny work sheds and spinning units.   
 
On the basis of the above recommendations, the Boar d has proposed the 
modifications in the Scheme of Coir Udyami Yojana. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 It was informed that Banks are reluctant to financ e under CUY Scheme 
despite being supported by the Government.  The Com mittee may be informed

implementation.   
 
Recommendation/Observation

enhanced the financial assistance to artisans to 40 % while reducing the share of 
producing and selling institutions. The Committee a pprehends if such reduction may 
become a dis-incentive for producing and selling un its. The Committee may also be  
 

-92- 
 
informed how does the Ministry calculate the per da y per artisan 
wage for   the   
purposes   of   overall   allocation   for   MPDA.   The   Committee   also 
recommends that the Ministry must explore the ways to transfer the wages directly

Action Taken:   
 
 Existing Market Development Assistance (MDA) schem e on production 
(Khadi & Poly) Scheme and additional components of Publicity, Marketing and

Features of MPDA are – 
• Production of incentive (PI) plan was approved by t he Commission, as 
modification to existing MDA scheme, to be name as Modified MDA plan  
• Modified MDA plan is financial assistance to Kis re quiring fiscal support to 
increase the competitiveness of Khadi Production by  improving quality as well 
as marketability and at the same time increase the artisan earning 
• MMDA to be calculated @ 30% on prime cost of Khadi i.e. cost directly 
attributable to production of Khadi  
• Under MMDA plan the Kis will have full freedom  to fix the price of the Khadi 
and Khadi Products based on market demand and acceptability  
• 40% of the amount to be distributed among the Khadi  spinners, weavers and 
karyakartas 
• MMDA Plan provides guidelines for gradual phase out  of financial assistance 
for production and marketing support through products segmentation  
• Provides flexibility to Kis to utilize alternate ma rketing channels and leveraging 
professional expertise for sales promotion.   
KVIC has already transferred the wages direct to the Bank accounts of Khadi artisans 
through DBT. The funds released an amount of Rs. 0. 03 crore as on 06.06.2016 
under MPDA. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 The Ministry has not informed how does it calculat e per day per artisan 
wage for the purposes of overall allocation for MPD A and at what rate the 
wages have been transferred by KVIC to direct bank accounts of Khadi 
artisans.  

-93- 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee also refers to the reply to Rajya Sab ha Question 1189 
(30.7.15) wherein the Ministry has stated “Khadi spinning and weaving is a 
subsidiary activity. The artisans associated with K hadi Institutions are self-
employed persons. They  operate  charkha/looms  depending  u pon  the  free  time

are  not  strictly comparable to  minimum daily wages“. The Committee on 
previous occasions during its study visits has inte racted with khadi artisans in 
presence of the representatives of KVIC and had wit nessed the abject drudgery the 
female artisans had to endure practically for long hours daily, to earn an 
uncertain meager daily wage. The Committee is convi nced that regardless  of  the  
structure  of  khadi  sector,  where  artisans  are   employed casually, the artisans 
must be classified as skilled labourer for the purp oses of wage and other benefits 
and thus recommends that to enforce this earnestly,  it should be made mandatory 
condition for the institutions availing MPDA assistance to classify khadi artisans as 
skilled worker for the wage purposes and other benefits. 
(Para 243) 
 
Action Taken:   
 
 KVIC has informed to the Khadi institutions that i t is mandatory condition for 
availing MPDA assistance. To classify the Khadi art isans as skilled worker for the 
wage purposes and other benefits. 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee may be informed if KVIC is ensuring that Khadi 
institutions availing assistance under MPDA are pay ing wages as per skilled 
workers.  If so, does not Ministry’s contradict  th e reply for Rajya Sabha         
Q. 1189 (30.7.15) reply in this regard.  
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The  Committee  while  appreciates  that  more  com prehensive  coverage 
would  be  available  to  khadi  artisans  under  n ew  social  security  schemes,  it 
however notes that no Budgetary provision has been made in this year’s Budget.  

-94- 
 
The  Committee  may  be  informed  by  when  the  m odalities  of  new

(Para 245) 
 
 
Action Taken: 
  
 
 A meeting was held under the chairmanship of Chair man, KVIC with 
Ministry officials and LIC of India, wherein following options were agreed upon. 
i) The best option would be to offer the existing AABY  with PMSBY and

ii) In the above dispensation, the artisans have to app roach host of agencies, viz.

iii) Another option could be enhancing the benefit of AA BY to three times for 
khadi artisans.  
The proposal is under examination for obtaining app roval for one of the above 
options. 
  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee may be informed of final Scheme and share of premium 
to be borne by the Ministry and insurance company i n the proposed new 
arrangement.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Committee in this penultimate year of 12 th  Plan has recommended the 
performance  audit  by  the  CAG  of  several  flag ship  schemes  like  PMEGP, 
Training Institutions and Tool Room and the NMCP fo r the entire plan period till 
2015-16. In addition, the Ministry should have its other schemes internally 
audited. And the salient findings of these audits m ust be included in the Annual 
Report. The Committee’s Reports may become the refe rence for such an audit. 
(Para 247) 
 
 

-95- 
 
Action Taken: 
 
 
Observations of the Committee have been noted for c ompliance.  In case of 
Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS), an Ev aluation Study of the

An evaluation study of CGTMSE was conducted and fin al report was

 Controller of Accounts of the Ministry will conduc t internal audit for the

         iv.       Market Development Assistance Programme

   Office of DC(MSME) have written a letter dated 0 9.05.2016 to CAG

The list of all the 18 Institutes has also been forwarded to CAG. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 The Committee may be apprised of the evaluation st udies of CGTMSE 
and CLCSS which must be incorporated in Annual Repo rt of the Ministry.  The 
Committee had asked for CAG’s Performance Audit of PMEGP, tool Rooms 
and NMCP.  The Committee insists CAG’s Performance Audit of PMEGP and

Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee is particularly concern over serious under utilization of 
funds under SCSP, TSP and NER meant for the margina lized sections of the society.  
That the funds are underutilized due to lack of dem and from these sections,   is  an   
insensitive   argument      by   the   Ministry   t o   hide   its   own shortcomings in 
reaching out to these sections. The Committee wonde rs if MUDRA Yojna could be 
successful with these very same sections, how the M inistry can blame the lack 
of demand. The Committee once again recommends that Ministry needs to 
physically expand its outreach among these sections . The Committee though finds it  

-96- 
 
ironical  that  the  same Ministry  which blames la ck 
of demand, has been entrusted  
by the Government to implement the SC/ST Hub. The Committee proposes to 
closely monitor the progress and performance of this Hub. The Committee may 
be informed of the structure and processes of proposed SC/ST Hub and the

Action Taken: 
 
 
 
    Para 57 of the Budget Speech for FY 2016 has propos ed to constitute a  
National Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe Hub in  the Ministry of Micro, Small 
and Medium Enterprises in partnership with industri es association. Ministry of 
MSME, to implement the above decision, undertook co nsultation with all the

N.E. Region and Sikkim". The salient features of the scheme are as under:

REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with  the Action Taken by the 
Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises  (Department of Public Enterprises) 
on the recommendations contained in the Committee’s  Two Hundred and Seventy- 
Second Report on the Review of the Provisions of Co rporate Social Responsibility under 
the Companies Act, 2013 pertaining to Department of Public Enterprises. 
 
2.  Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Heavy Industries 
and Public Enterprises (Department of Public Enterp rises) in respect of the 
recommendations contained in the 272 nd  Report. These have been categorized as follows: 
 
Chapter I -  The recommendations/observations, which have bee n accepted by the 
Ministry. 
 
 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Minis try has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report. 
 
Chapter -II -  The recommendations/observations which the Commi ttee does not desire 
to pursue in view of the Government's replies. 
 
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic 
and explanations advanced by the Ministry and there fore, do not want to pursue them for 
the present. 
 
Chapter -III -  The recommendations/observations in respect of w hich the Committee has 
not accepted replies of the Ministry and has asked the Ministry to review its reply. 
 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-i mplementation of 
recommendations contained in Chapter – III and desi res that the Ministry should furnish 
logical explanations thereof. 
 
Chapter -IV - The recommendations/observations in respect of wh ich final replies of the 
Ministry have not been received. 
 
 In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV , the Ministry has either 
furnished the interim replies or couched its langua ge in vague terms therefore; the 
Committee desires that the Ministry should furnish Action Taken Notes in respects of 
recommendations categorized in Chapter-IV in detail and to the point, as per the intention 
and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee. 
 
3. The details of the ATR are being discussed in the succeeding pages.

CHAPTER – I 
 
The Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee recognizes that the Act gives rule ma king powers to Central 
Government. Considering that the DPE is the nodal D epartment to provide non-financial 
guidelines to PSEs, the Committee acknowledges that  DPE guidelines have given greater 
force to the CSR related provisions of the Act by i ntroducing negative marking in MoU 
for non-CSR compiled CPSEs. The DPE may assess the performance of a PSE, against 
each of its CSR guidelines before rating the PSE.

 Under the MoU guidelines for 2016-17, DPE has incl uded compliance of CSR by 
CPSEs as provided under the Companies Act, 2013 and  Rules for obtaining higher MoU 
ratings.

 The  Committee is of the opinion that such success stori es should be published on

appreciation to these earnest efforts. The Committe e recognizes the efforts made by 
Standing Committee of Public Enterprises (SCOPE) by  compiling such success stories. 
This needs to be updated and be given wide publicity. 
Para No 41 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 
 The recommendation is noted for compliance.

CHAPTER–III 
The Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted 
the replies of the Ministry and has asked the Ministry to review its replies 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 As per the UNIDO definition CSR should be an integr al part of a Company’s 
business operation. This approach makes CSR more su stainable instead of the approach 
taken by Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 that ex clude activities undertaken in 
presence of normal course of business. This approac h will help companies to align their 
operations with sustainable development objectives,  instead of taking up unsustainable 
one off projects and tendency to make financial con tribution for CSR. The DPE 
guidelines too require the PSUs to exploit their co re competence and mobilize their 
resource capacities in implementation of CSR. PSUs have been advised to align their 
CSR with their business policies and strategies. Th is position is concurrent with the 
UNIDO but contrary to Rule 4(2) of Companies (CSR P olicy) Rules, 2014. The 
Committee finds this approach to be more effective and practicable.  
Para No. 17 
Action Taken Replies 
 Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 have been notifi ed by M/o Corporate 
Affairs under the provisions of Companies Act, 2013 on CSR contained in Section 135 of 
the Act. CSR provisions of the Act and the CSR Rule s are uniformly applicable to all 
CSR eligible companies, including CPSEs. Any change / modification to CSR Rules can 
only be considered by Ministry of Corporate Affairs.  
  
Further Recommendations 
 
 
 From the reply of the Department, it is not clear w hether the 
recommendation of the Committee has been brought to  the notice of the M/o 
Corporate Affairs for their consideration. Further,  the reply is also silent on the 
opinion of DPE on the recommendation of the Committ ee. Merely passing it to the 
M/o Corporate Affairs will not suffice.  
 
 Accordingly, it is recommended that the views of D PE with regard to the 
above recommendation and whether the recommendation  has been brought to the 
notice of M/o Corporate Affairs and if so, their op inion on the same may be 
submitted to the Committee. DPE may also inform if it stands by its own Guidelines 
that require PSUs to export their core competence a nd mobilize their resources/                           
capacities in implementation of CSR. In case it doe s not, then the rational behind 
not adopting its own guidelines may be given by DPE  despite international practices 
to this effect as reflected in UNIDO definition. 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee, while analyzing the provision that allows companies to engage 
trust/society/NGO with ‘established track record’ t o execute their CSR activities, feels 
that the term as mentioned in the Rules, ‘established track record’ needs further  
3 

specifications to avoid any possible abuse. The Com mittee also feels that it is required to 
exclude those trusts/societies/NGOs wherein relativ es of Board members of the CPSEs, 
State/Central Ministries or local administration ar e involved in undertaking CSR 
activities. DPE should issue general guidelines in this regard and not leave it to the Board 
alone. DPE should also advise CPSEs to blacklist de viant trust/society/NGO to prevent 
them from engaging in such activities in future. Th e Committee also recognized that the 
Rules have been amended to provide only 5% of the C SR budget for such overhead 
expenditure towards salary, etc. to NGOs. Also, rul es must specify that such trusts/ 
NGOs must utilize the funds in time and give Utiliz ation Certificate to the Company for 
inclusion in the annual account. 
Para No. 24 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 CPSEs while making selection of implementing agenc ies/ NGOs are required to 
apply due diligence and to look into the experience  and track record of these agencies. 
They are supposed to follow provisions of Companies  (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014. As the 
Companies Act, 2013 and the Rules apply to all corp orates, including CPSEs, it is for the 
MCA to consider the suggestions made by the Committ ee for prescribing safeguards etc. 
in the Act and Rules to be followed by all companies including CPSEs. 
 
Further Recommendations 
 
 
 The Committee is fully aware that any change in the  provisions of the 
Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 ought to be brou ght forth by M/o Corporate 
Affairs. Not withstanding  this fact, the Committee  feels that DPE, in its capacity as 
the nodal body of all CPSEs in India, can include i n its guidelines to CPSEs certain 
precautionary measures regarding the selection of i mplementing agencies/ NGOs as 
suggested by the Committee in its recommendations. Such guidelines can be 
complementary and facilitative of the CSR Rules, no t necessarily conflictive as DPE 
seems to portray in their reply. For example:-  suc h agency /trust, etc should be 
verified by company’s CVO  and its accounts should be verified by company’s 
Auditor.  
 
 Accordingly, the Committee is reiterating it’s abo ve recommendation and 
wants DPE to get back to the Committee regarding th e opinion of M/o Corporate 
Affairs on the recommendation of the Committee.

Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry

Recommendation/Observation 
 
 DPE should issue directions or guidelines, as to h ow can the CPSEs extend their 
CSR oversight to entire supply chain network to ens ure vendors comply with principles 
of CSR as per DPE guidelines. The DPE should also a llow the CPSEs to join in the 
Central and State Government’s Schemes like Mid-day  meal, Sarva Siksha Abhiyan as 
per Schedule VII. For this DPE should evolve a mode l arrangements framework between 
the CPSEs and the nodal Government Agency which sho uld ensure timely release of 
Utilization Certificate to the CPSEs so that it can  reflect the CSR expenditure in its 
annual accounts. Similarly, the Company or NGO, thr ough which CSR projects are to be 
implemented, too should furnish the Utilization Cer tificates in time. It must be ensured 
that such NGOs and Companies should actually use the funds in time. 
Para No. 9 
Action Taken Replies 
 As per Section 135 of Companies Act, 2013, the CSR Committee of the 
Company’s Board are guided by the provisions under Schedule VII of the Act and have 
functions of deciding the CSR policy including the activities and expenditure to be 
incurred thereon besides monitoring the implementat ion of CSR policy. Convergence of 
CSR activities with Central and State Government’s Schemes is to be decided by the 
Board of Directors keeping in view the permissible activities under Schedule VII of the 
Act. DPE on its part regarding implementation of CS R, has been advising CPSEs during 
the workshops organized for senior executives of CP SEs to practice due diligence in the 
implementation of CSR activities. 
 
Further Recommendations 
 
 
 The Committee recommends that in these initial yea rs, DPE must monitor 
the implementation of CSR related provisions by CPS Es to overcome the             
teething difficulties and prepare regulatory framework for the CPSEs.  
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 During its interaction with the CPSEs, the Committ ee drew the following 
inferences which needed greater clarity. DPE may include these issues in the guidelines: 
(i) Lack of provisioning for cost of maintaining a dura ble social asset created under 
CSR. 
(ii) Clarifications regarding CSR obligations of Holding  companies, like Coal India 
Ltd. considering that earning in form of dividend w ere not to be included while 
computing Net income.  
(iii) There is confusion whether PSUs can set up professi onal/ skill development 
institutions as per Schedule VII in their respectiv e area of usual business and core 
competence.  
(iv) Exclusion of para military veterans and widows from  the definition of armed 
forces. 
Para No. 12

 Observations made by Department Related Parliamenta ry Standing Committee 
(DRPSC) on Industry vide Point No. (i) to (iv)  fal l within the purview of M/o Corporate 
Affairs as amendments in the provisions of Companie s Act, 2013 on CSR or the 
Schedule VII of the Act has to be considered by Min istry of Corporate Affairs. These 
recommendations have been conveyed to Ministry of Corporate Affairs.  
 
Further Recommendations 
 
 
 DPE has merely submitted to the Committee as part of their action taken 
that they have conveyed the recommendation of the C ommittee to M/o Corporate 
Affairs. In this scenario, the Committee would like  to point out that it is also the 
responsibility of DPE to pursue the consideration o f the recommendation of the 
Committee with  M/o Corporate Affairs and update th e Committee on its outcome, 
alongwith the opinions/views of DPE as well as on the same. 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee is of the considered opinion that as  provided by the Companies 
Act, 2013 it is an obligation of a Company to be co ncerned with the well being of its 
local populace and environment, the resources of wh ich are being directly utilized by 
them. However, the Committee also holds the view th at CPSEs should take into account 
the development of remote backward areas of the country. These are areas where the pace 
of industrial development has been slow due to thei r geographic isolation. While 
neighbourhood community and local area with referen ce to company’s works have first 
claim over CSR projects, Schedule VII should also p rovide for development by 
individual company or jointly with other companies,  in backward areas like North East, 
Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep, which do not have much of 
industrialization and are in need of development. T he Committee therefore, recommends 
that some percentage of CSR be allowed to spend in such backward areas other than local 
area. Similarly, the Committee is of the opinion th at in case company contributes its CSR 
fund to the corpus for National Schemes like Swachh  Bharat Mission, a certain 
percentage of CSR fund must mandatorily be assigned  to local area around Company’s 
works/projects so that the basic ideology to start CSR policy for local area population is 
not defeated and local population do not suffer bec ause they are the first people who are 
socially and environmentally affected whenever any plant of PSUs is established. 
Para No 15 
Action Taken Replies 
 The first Proviso to Section 135 (5) of the Compan ies Act, 2013 reads: 
 
 “Provided that the company shall give preference t o the local area and areas 
around it where it operates, for spending the amoun t earmarked for Corporate Social 
Responsibility activities” 
 
 The proviso provides for preference to be given to  local area. Companies have 
enough flexibility to allot CSR funds for activities to be undertaken beyond local area,  
 
 
6 

including remote and backward areas. Any initiative  to be redefine local area besides the 
provisions contained in the first proviso of Sectio n 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 or 
any amendment / modification in Schedule VII to pro vide for development by companies 
in backward areas like North East, Andaman Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep has to be 
considered by M/o Corporate Affairs. In the worksho ps conducted by DPE, the senior 
executives of CPSEs who are involved in the impleme ntation of CSR provisions have 
been advised besides contribution to Swachh Bharat Kosh, they should also undertake 
CSR activities in local and outside local areas also. 
 
Further Recommendations 
 
 
 DPE should pursue Committee’s recommendation regard ing CSR in remote 
backward region that lack industries with M/o Corpo rate Affairs and apprise the 
Committee of their response.  
 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee feels such initiatives should become  a model for CPSEs and 
companies in other Sectors as well to come together  to set up industry specific 
technology institutes to cater to the demand of ski lled manpower for the sectors like 
defence, petroleum, etc. In this regard, the Commit tee also acknowledged the 
pronouncement made in Budget Speech (2016-17) regar ding setting up of Higher

be a not-for-profit organization that will leverage  funds from the market and supplement 
them with donations and CSR funds. These funds will  be used to finance improvement in 
infrastructure in our top institutions and will be serviced through internal accruals.’  
Para No. 18 
Action Taken Replies 
 A number of major CPSEs operating in different sec tors have their own

 The Committee believes that the concept of CSR woul d be defeated in case

/recommendation and issue supplementary guidelines for PSEs in addition to the

Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee takes note of the responses of MCA an d appreciates the fact that 
sustainability is expected to be factored into the design of CSR projects at its beginning. 
However, the Committee also takes cognizance of the  fact that a good share  of CSR 
activities are purely welfare oriented and may not strictly fit into a project/ programme 
mode where sustainability can be built in. This asp ect of sustainability of CSR initiatives 
will be even more accentuated in the case of CPSEs who are prone to fluctuating 
earnings/profits. Further, the CSR, Rules, 2014 inc lude ‘ongoing’ activities under CSR 
activities. While emphasis  is on the self sustaini ng CSR projects, the activities listed in 
Schedule VII are one off activities that do not  ge nerate revenue even to maintain these 
assets and are therefore non-self sustaining. Provi sions should be made for maintenance 
of CSR assets in successive years. Therefore, the C ommittee is of the considered opinion 
that DPE should mention in their guidelines for mai ntenance of CSR assets created under 
CSR budget. So that the assets are maintained otherwise the whole funds would go waste.

Action Taken Replies

responsibility to local bodies/users and creation o f a project specific sustainability fund 
with contribution from users are issues related to the Companies Act, 2013 and Rules and 
these are to be considered by MCA. Once amendments are carried out, DPE will act on 
them.

 As expressed earlier, the Committee is aware that the M/o Corporate Affairs 
is the Ministry in charge of the operation of the C ompanies Act, 2013 and 
Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014. However, it is of the considered opinion that 
DPE has the requisite operative space within the am bit of the Act and the Rule to 
issue guidelines to the CPSEs on implementation of issues like the steps to be taken 
to ensure the sustainability of initiatives carried  out under CSR. DPE can take 
proactive measures of advisory nature in this regar d. This may even set an example 
to companies other than CPSEs. Further, the Committ ee wants DPE to obtain the 
opinion of M/o Corporate Affairs also in this regar d and convey the same to the 
Committee.

activities after CSR has been made legally mandator y, auditing of expenditure made 
under these activities, along a guided path, would be important for streamlining of

RECOMMENDATION (PARA NO. No. 4 AND 5) 
l. The major aspect of the demand for grants of the Ministry of Mines, which m the view 
of the Committee should call for concern is its relatively small magnitude. The !11inimy is 
responsible for the exploration, developmen t and exploitation of all minerals barring atomic 
minerals, coal, natural gas and crud e petroleum. The rich ness and variety of underground 
mincr31 wealth the country possesses boggle the imaginati on. That apa rt, the country is 
stated to be on the threshold of a vastly accelerated process of industrial growth . It ts at the 
same time endeavouring to enlarge ats export potenti al. These factors together ~hould have 
persu aded the Government, the Ministry of Mines and the Planning Commission 10 place. at 
this junct ure, maximum emphasis on a massive development of mining operations. In this 
area of activity, the long·term return on investment cannot but be exceptionally high. The 
need to reduce fiscal deficits is offered as justification for economizing on budgetary outlay for 
different Ministries, including for tbe Ministry of Mines, in tbe immediate period. Such 
economizing, in the view of the Commitlee, is somewhat irrational if a "ider time fram e is 
taken into account. Whether it is zinc. bauxite, chromite, gruph ite, gold or other precious 
metu ls or stones, the pos,~ibili ties of mineral-based industri al expan>~on in the country are 
indeed immense, provided adequate technological and infrastructural support does not lag 
behind. The validity of this point of view is illustrated by the strides madi> by the alwninium 
industry in recent yeilrS. Where such domestic processing of mineral products is not yet 
considered feasible, the scope for exports to countries hungry for receiving them is practically 
limitless. And yet, in the o'·erall scheme of thing, the explora tion and exploitation of minerals 
for contr ibuting toward the notion's prosperity appear s to occupy a very modest space. The 
prop osed budgetary allocation of less than Rs. 250 crore for the Ministry of Mines is an 
eloquent testimony to the miniature scale of official thinking. 
During the span of the past five decades the authorities have mostly cont inued to lean on 
the constricted , colonial edifices or the Geological Survey of India and the Bureau of Mines 
in the matter of mineral use and exploitation. The only addition to the twosome has been 
the Mineral Exploration Corporation. Eve n if the activities of the Corporation are 
considered togetherwith those of the other two bodies , the sum total of the thrust is most 
modest. On the Government's own reckon ing, the aggregate value of extraction of minerals 
corning under the purview of the Ministry of Mines exceeds Rupees 30.000 crorc per annum. 
This return is on the basis of an annual budgetary outlay of less than 1 per cent of this 
amount. The allocation for the Ministry, in the view of the Committee, should be doubled and 
tripl ed; in case this be done, the return to the nation is likely to incre ase not just pari passu, 
but five or six times higher than what It Is at present. 
Action Taken 
The Government is fully alive to the need for stepping up budgetary allocations in favour 
of GSI and the MECL subject to the overall budgetary constra ints of the Ministry of 
Finance. It may be noted that the total budgetary allocation for GSl in 1997·98 is 
1 

proposed to be raised to Rs. 200.00 croie as compared to the provision made in the 
preceding year which was Rs. 176.92 crore. 
While enhanced allocations are welcome, it is at the same time appreciated that these 
allocations will not be enough to meet the growing requirements fully. Induction of 
investible funds from outside the budget is necessary to step up the tempo of exploration 
and exploitation of minerals in this sector. To this end in view, a new mineral policy was 
announced in M:rrch, 1993 which envisaged induction of foreign technology and foreign 
panicipation in exploration and mining of high value and scarce minerals. To ensure 
generation of adequate interest in prospecting of new reserves by aerial surveys and other 
means, the area which can now be made available to any investor, domestic or foreign will 
be 5000 Sq. Km. as compared to 25 Sq.Km. which was the position earlier. The guidelines 
also envisage that foreign direct investment in the equity participation by investors can be 
allowed up to 50% of equity. Higher equity participation may also be allowed on a case to 
case basis. However, this limit of 50% would not apply to captive mining of any mineral 
processing industry. In keeping with the new policy, the FIPB has already approved 33 
projects worth Rs. 2312.31 crore. 
Progress has also been made in the matter of processing of minerals. Steps have been 
tallen to augment export potential of raw minerals in semi-processed form like bauxite, 
alumina, chrome, ferro-chrome, charge chrome, iron ore, magnesia ore and mica. Attention 
is paid more to export or minerals in a value added form so as to maximise gains to the 
economy.

that the foreign collaboration should be governed by country's terms and conditions and in

16. A final matter, it is ent irely fair that even as the responsibility for economic and 
industrial growth in the country is shared evenly between the Union and State Governments , 
resources that enable the fulfilment of this objective is also shared in a just manner. The 
royalty on mining operations. which is a prerogative of State Governments, is supposed to 
be paid by the Centre to the States o n a regular basis and at rates that are adjustable from 
time to time. The Union Government reportedly has not been honouring this practice; the 
rates are not beiog adjusted every two yea.rs as per standing rules and there is also a certain 
reluctance to cross over to an ad-valorem system of royalty payments. The Committee feels 
that whatever is due to the States ~hould be paid in an equitable manner. The Committee 
further hopes that a part of the prOC«ds of royalty, once made available to the full 
satisfaction of the parties concerned, is made available for the welfare of the people in tile 
mining areas. It is equally important that payment to the villagers as compensation for their 
land taken over for mining activities is paid on immediate basis. The record in this respect is 
most dismal. 
Action Token 
Under Sections 9 of the MMRD Act, 1957' every holder of a mining lease is required to 
pay to the concerned State Government royalty in respect of the mineral removed or 
consumed by him at the rates specified in the Second Schedule tO the ACL ft may thus be 
seen that Royalty is not released by the Central Government to the States. It is collected by 
the States themselves at rates as notified under Sec.9 of MMRD Act, 1957 in the case of 
major minerals and at rates as decided by the State Government in case of minor minerals. 
Further Section 24A of the MMRD Act, 1957 requires the lessee to provide proper 
compensation to occupier of the surface of the land for any loss or damage which is likely lO -.. 
arise or has arisen as a consequence of mining operatio n. Compensation to be paid 01 the 
rehabilitation to be provided by the lessee is determined by the State Government as per 
Rule 72 & 73 of MCR, 1960. As regards ope n-cast mining projects, the displaced person~ 
are paid proper compensation as determined by the State Land Acquisition authorities in 
accordance with the Land Acquisition Act and Central Government Directives . Employment 
is also provided as far as possible to one of the members of the displaced families.

5.  However, the Committee also noted that ever since 4 th  Census of MSMEs, the

MSMEs. The Committee feels that Census figures are an important reference point for any 
future policy formulation initiative as it provides baseline data to measure prospective trends. 
Every year, in DFG, a separate allocation is made t o strengthen the database, survey and 
research. The Ministry may consider using this allo cation for conducting 5 th  decennial census 
of MSMEs. Also, like annual Public Enterprises Surv ey, Ministry of MSME too should 
present an annual MSME Survey on the basis of NSS Rounds.      
 
Economic Survey on prospects and challenges of MSME sector  
 
6. The Committee was informed that the  Economic Survey expressed concerns regarding the 
rise in NPA’s in the second half of 2016, which cam e from mid-size corporate and MSMEs, as 
companies that had been suffering from poor sales a nd profitability for a number of years struggled 
and remained indebted. This trend is likely to cont inue into 2017. Real loan growth to MSMEs 
slowed significantly in 2014-15, and actually turned negative during the past two fiscal years. 
 
7.  The Committee feels that an assessment should be  made of the impact if any,  of 
demonetisation, on the credit-worthiness of MSMEs and whether it has led to greater NPAs in 
MSME sector. The Committee takes note of demands pu t forth by certain industry

associations that in view of possible adverse impac t of demonetization on the business and 
overall lack of liquidity in the economy, the time limit for NPA should be extended from 
present 90 days to 180 days.  The Committee views t his demand favourably and recommends

Committee of its outcome. 
 
Evolution and Mandate of the Ministry 
 
  
8. The Government of India established the Ministry  of Small Scale Industries and Agro & 
Rural Industries (SSI & ARI) in October, 1999 as the nodal Ministry for formulation of policies and 
Central sector programmes/schemes, their implementa tion and related coordination and for 
supplementing the efforts of the States/Union Terri tories for promotion and development of small 
scale, agro and rural industries in the country.  S ubsequently, in September, 2001 the Ministry of 
SSI and ARI was bifurcated into two separate Minist ries, namely, Ministry of Small Scale 
Industries and Ministry of Agro and Rural Industrie s.  In 2006, “Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises Development Act (MSMED), 2006” was enac ted by the Parliament.  Pursuant to this 
enactment on 9 May, 2007, the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries and the Small Scale 
Industries were merged into a single Ministry, name ly, Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises.  
 
Composition of the Ministry 
 
 
9. The Ministry of Micro Small & Medium Enterprises  is having two divisions called Small & 
Medium Enterprises (SME) Wing and Agro & Rural Indu stry (ARI) Wing, besides office of the 
Development Commissioner (MSME) and other organisat ions.  The SME Wing is allocated the 
work, inter-alia, of administration, vigilance and administrative supervision of the National Small 
Industries Corporation (NSIC) Ltd., a public sector  enterprise and National Institution of Micro, 
Small & Medium Enterprises (NIMESE) an autonomous n ational level entrepreneurship 
development/training organization.  The Wing is als o responsible for implementation of the 
schemes relating to Performance and Credit Rating, Assistance to Training Institutions and 
preparation and monitoring of “Make in India” initiative among others.    
 

4 
 
10. The ARI Wing looks after the administration of two statutory bodies viz. the Khadi and 
Village Industries Commission (KVIC), Coir Board an d a society called Mahatma Gandhi Institute 
of Rural Industrialization (MGIRI).  It also superv ises the implementation of the Prime Minister’s 
Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP).  Scheme of  Fund for Regeneration of Traditional 
Industries (SFURTI) and A Scheme for Promoting Innovation, Rural Industry and Entrepreneurship 
(ASPIRE).  
 
11. The implementation of policies and various prog rammes/schemes for providing 
infrastructure and support services to MSMEs is und ertaken through its attached office, namely the 
Office of the Development Commissioner (O/o DC (MSM E), National Small Industries 
Corporation (NSIC), Khadi and Village Industries Co mmission (KVIC), the Coir Board and 
training institutes viz., National Institute for Mi cro, Small and Medium Enterprises (NI-MSME), 
Hyderabad and Mahatma Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialization (MGIRI), Wardha. 
 
12.  The Committee notes that unlike KVIC and Coir Boar d, whose allocation is made 
under ARI Division, the Office of DC-MSME though ha s same mandate and implements the 
same Schemes as SME Division, get separate allocati on in the annual Demands.  The 
Committee has been raising the issues of overlappin g and duplication of multiple Schemes of 
the Ministry.  Considering that SME Division and DC -MSME both have not been able to 
utilize their allocated funds during previous years , the Committee is inclined to recommend 
that two allocations may be merged so that the Sche mes are also consolidated with more 
money available for their implementation.  The Comm ittee recommends that like KVIC and 
Coir Board, the allocation for DC-MSME too should b e brought under SME Division for the 
efficient and economic utilization of available resources.
