Budget Proposals 
 
 
20. The Committee sought Ministry’s comments on the  impact of Budget declaration and tax 
proposals on MSME sector.  
 
21. It was informed that in order to make MSMEs mor e viable and also to encourage firms to 
migrate to company format, Union Budget 2017-18 pro poses to reduce the income tax for smaller 
companies with annual turnover upto Rs. 50 crore to  25%. As per data of Assessment Year 2015-
16, there were 6.94 lakh companies filing returns o f which 6.67 lakh companies’ fall in this 
category and, therefore, percentage-wise, 96% of co mpanies will get the benefit of lower taxation. 
This will make the  MSME sector more competitive as compared to large companies. 
 
22. The Committee is not sure that reduction in income tax rate as proposed in the Budget 
will make the MSME more competitive.  
 
23. The Committee further asked if these concession s were available only to Companies and not 
to proprietorship/partnership firms which constitute the majority of Companies in MSME sector. 
 
24. It was informed that the MSME classification wa s based on the investment criteria and not 
on the ownership of the firms. So all the MSMEs whe ther they are Private Ltd. Companies or 
proprietorship/partnership companies are eligible for this benefit. 
 
25. However, a closer reading of Budget speech sugg ests that this initiative is essentially to 
encourage MSME firms to migrate to company format.  The Finance Minister had announced in 
Budget Speech “ In order to make MSME companies more viable and als o to encourage firms to 
migrate to company format, I propose to reduce the income tax for smaller companies with annual 
turnover upto Rs. 50 crore to 25%.”.   
 
26. The Committee notes the demand expressed by one of the industry associations to 
widen the scope of this concession to proprietorshi p/partnership firms which constitute the 

9 
 
majority in MSME sector. The Ministry must take up the issue with Ministry of Finance and 
inform the Committee of the response.  
 
27. The Committee noted the Finance Minister’s Budg et Speech which stated “As against 5.6 
crore informal sector individual enterprises and fi rms doing small business in India, the numbers of 
returns filed by this category are only 1.81 crore… ..”   The Committee accordingly sought from the 
Ministry the suggestions to address the situation. 
 
28. It was informed that  demonetisation is expected and designed to bring th eir actual income 
and expenses in digital mode and thus, the taxable income would come to the fore, making the 
taxnet wider. During the presentation of DFG, the Ministry informed the Committee that it has been 
imparting training in digital transactions to MSME entrepreneurs. 
 
29. The Committee expresses concern over narrow tax ba se among informal sector 
individual enterprises.  On the one hand MSME propr ietorship/partnership firms demand 
their inclusion into proposed tax concession to sma ll enterprises, on the other hand they do 
not even file tax returns. This is an unacceptable situation and the Committee recommends 
that the Ministry of MSME must take corrective but non-intrusive action in consultation with 
Ministry of Finance. The Committee suggests that Mi nistry must seek PAN and TIN/ GST 
details of the proprietors/partners in the UAM and,  in association with the Ministry of 
Finance, link these references for better tax monit oring through data networking of direct 
and indirect taxes.  
  
  
New Initiatives by the Ministry  during 2016-17 
 
 
30. It was informed that Ministry of MSME has taken  the following various initiatives for 
strengthening and enhancing the contribution of the MSMEs in the National Economy:- 
 
(i) 
National Scheduled Caste / Scheduled Tribe Hub  
 
 The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise s was given the work of 
operationalization of National SC / ST Hub to ensur e 4% procurement from SC/ ST entrepreneurs 

10 
 
in all Central Government Ministries and Central Pu blic Sector Enterprises (CPSEs).  The High 
Powered Monitoring Committee on SC / ST Hub has alr eady met twice, which has resulted into 
more than 5000 SC / ST enterprises getting register ed on the MSME portal, namely 
msmedatabank.in. 
 
(ii) Udyog Aadhaar Memorandum  
 
 In the ease-of-doing business, the registration of  MSMEs was simplified by launching of a 
one-page online Registration methodology.   Udyog A adhaar Memorandum (UAM) was notified 
and launched on 18.9.2015 and more than 25.27 lakh Udyog Aadhaar Memorandums have been 
registered till 31.1.2017.   
 
(iii) MSME Databank  
 
 An online Census of MSMEs has started with the lau nch of MSME Databank and Micro, 
Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Furnishin g of Information) Rules, 2016 have been 
notified to make it compulsory for MSMEs to give in formation on MSME Databank.  More than 
70,590 units have already given information on MSME Databank till 31.1.2017. 
(iv)  Web portal for Micro and Small Enterprises Facilit ation Councils (MSE-FCs ) 
 The Ministry of MSME has developed a web portal wh ich will enable the States to keep 
track of the cases filed in Micro and Small Enterpr ises Facilitation Councils (MSE-FCs) under the 
provisions of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterpris es Development Act, 2006.  Ministry has also 
circulated  Draft  Model MSE-FC Rules  for consideration to revise their  MSE-FC Rules. 
(v) MSME Fund 
In exercise of the powers conferred by section 12 o f the Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises Development Act, 2006 (27 of 2006), the  Government has established a fund vide 
Notification dated 28.10.2016 to be called the Micr o Small and Medium Enterprises Fund. The 
objective of the Fund shall be promotion, development and enhancing the competitiveness of micro, 
small and medium enterprises, particularly of the micro and small enterprises.  
(vi)  Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Micro and Small E nterprises (CGTMSE) 
The Scheme is implemented by Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small 
Enterprises (CGTMSE) set up jointly by the Ggovernm ent of India and SIDBI and covers collateral 

11 
 
free credit facility (term loan and/or working capi tal) extended by eligible lending institutions to 
new and existing Micro and Small Enterprises up to Rs. 200 lakh per borrowing unit.  The 
guarantee cover provided is up to 75% of the credit  facility up to Rs. 50 lakh (85% for loans up to 
Rs. 5 lakh provided to Micro Enterprises, 80% for M SEs owned/operated by women and all loans 
to NER), and uniform guarantee of 50% of the credit  exposure above Rs. 50 lakh and up to Rs. 200 
lakh.  A composite all in Annual Guarantee fee of 1 .0% p.a. of the credit facility sanctioned is now 
being charged. 
The Government has augmented the corpus of the Trus t of CGTMSE from the present level 
of Rs. 2500 crore to Rs. 7500 crore.  The increase of corpus by Rs. 5000 crore would be entirely 
contributed by Government of India.  Government has  increased the coverage of the loans covered 
under CGTMSE from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 2 crore for th e loans to be disbursed w.e.f. 1.1.2017.  The 
loans which are being extended to Micro and Small E nterprises by National Banking Finance 
Corporations (NBFCs) have also been taken into the ambit of the Scheme.  
 (vii)  ZED (Zero Defect Zero Effect)  
 
 The ZED (Zero Defect Zero Effect) Scheme was launc hed in October, 2016 under which the 
Ministry plans to assess 22,000 units to get themse lves rated for Zero Defect Zero Effect.  ZED 
certification will be in five categories viz., Bron ze, Silver, Gold, Diamond and Platinum.  The rated 
SMEs will get better business opportunities. 
 The scheme envisages promotion of Zero Defects and  Zero Effect (ZED) manufacturing 
amongst MSMEs and ZED Assessment for their certification with the following objectives of: 
 
• Developing an Ecosystem for Zero Defects Manufacturing in MSMEs. 
• To promote adaptation of Quality tool/system and Energy Efficient manufacturing. 
• To enable MSMEs for manufacture of quality products. 
• To encourage MSMEs to constantly upgrade their qual ity standards in products 
 and processes. 
• To drive manufacturing with adoption of Zero Defect  production processes    and  without 
impacting the environment. 
• To support ‘Make in India’ campaign. 
• To develop professionals in the area of ZED manufacturing and certification.

(viii)  Technology Centre System Programme (TCSP) 
 
 The Ministry is presently running 18 Technology Ce ntres (10 Tool Rooms and 8 
Technology Development Centres) to provide technolo gical support to the micro, small and 
medium industries in the Country. Technology Centre s cater to the needs of industries located at 
those places.   
 
 To expand and upgrade the network of Technology Ce ntres in the country, the Government 
is implementing Technology Centre Systems Program (TCSP) at an estimated Projected Cost of Rs. 
2200/- crore including World Bank Loan assistance o f USD 200 million to establish 15 new 
Technology Centres (TCs) identified across the country. 
 
 13 new Technology Centres at Bhiwadi, Baddi, Rohta k, Bhopal, Durg, Kanpur, Greater 
Noida, Imphal, Vishakhapatnam, Ernakulam, Bangalore,  Sitarganj and Pudducherry are coming up 
with the assistance of the World Bank scheme.  More  than Rs.2000 crores is being spent on the 
same, besides, the Government is also upgrading the  Technology Centres at Dimapur (Nagaland)

174. The Ministry informed that MDA scheme of KVIC has been modified as Market Promotion 
and Development Assistance Scheme (MPDA). MPDA sche me is formulated as a unified scheme 
by merging different schemes/sub-schemes/components  of different Heads implemented in the 11 th  
Plan, namely, Market Development Assistance, Public ity, Marketing and Market promotion. A new 
component of Infrastructure namely setting up of Ma rketing Complexes/ Khadi Plazas has been 
added to expand the marketing net worth of Khadi & VI products.  
175. Under the erstwhile MDA scheme financial assis tance was distributed amongst Producing 
Institutions (30%), Selling Institutions (45%) and Artisans (25%).  Under Modified MDA shall be 
calculated at 30% of the Prime Cost {cost of raw ma terial plus conversion charges up to grey cloth 
plus processing charges without margins [establishm ent expenditure (25%) and trading, insurance 
& bank interest (8%)]}. The Modified MDA shall be d istributed amongst producing institutions 
(40%), selling institutions (20%) and artisans (40%).   
 
176. The Khadi institutions submit their claims thr ough DBT portal, which is  scrutinized by 
field offices of KVIC and Central office before making payment. The benefits to Khadi artisans and 
Khadi institutions are passed on to their Aadhar seeded Bank account. 
 
177. The Committee has been pursuing the issue of l ow wage remuneration to Khadi artisans.  It 
asked if KVIC is ensuring that Khadi institutions a vailing assistance under MPDA are paying 
wages at par with skilled workers.  
 
178. The Ministry replied that  linking the Minimum Daily Wage rates to Khadi artis ans was not 
correct as Khadi spinning and weaving is a subsidia ry activity.  The artisans associated with Khadi 
Institutions are self-employed persons.  They opera te charkha/looms depending upon the free time 
available to them. The artisans are paid on piece r ate basis i.e. number of hanks of yarn spun and 

47 
 
meters of cloth woven. Hence, the wages of Khadi ar tisans are not strictly comparable to minimum 
daily wages. 
179. The Committee takes strong objection to the Minist ry’s stand in respect of wages of 
khadi artisans. Khadi was a tool of Father of the N ation for self reliance. It cannot be allowed 
to become a tool of drudgery and exploitation due t o technicalities. If KVIC is unable to 
determine the daily wage for khadi artisans, it must determine reasonable wages on piece rate 
basis. The Committee may be informed as to  how oft en the KVIC has determined the piece 
rate wages. The Committee may also be informed of t he parameters on which piece rate 
prices are fixed by the KVIC. The Committee may be informed of comparative piece rates 
determined by KVIC over last five years.  
180. If wages are to be determined on piece rate basis,  then steps must be taken to improve 
productivity of artisans without drudgery. KVIC mus t ensure production and supply of solar 
charkhas at reasonable rate and any other improved version that enhances productivity, for 
which the Khadi and VI Grant for S&T may be increas ed provided its utilization too is 
improved.

MNREGA for the purposes of wages. The Ministry may expeditiously take up the issue with 
Ministry of Rural Development in this regard to fin alise the modalities. The Ministry may

General Over View  
 
268. The  MSME sector which is critical for the equitab le growth and employment and 
entrepreneurship in the economy, is a fact that can  hardly be overstated. Though the Budget 
allocation  for the Ministry of MSME is not proport ionate to the importance of this Sector, 
the Committee reiterates that the available resourc es need to be used efficiently for the 
targeted objectives. The Committee has often noted the excuse of Schemes being demand-
driven for the under-utilization of allocations. If  the Ministry is not convinced of demand, 
then it should not seek allocation. The Ministry ha s not been able to generate demand for its 
Schemes in a Sector which is wide spread over sever al sectors and is starved of any 
worthwhile policy intervention. With number of KIs reducing and low employability  of 
training courses the Committee wonders the quality of monitoring at Ministry’s level and 
efficacy of its institutional network in States and at grass root levels.  
269. The Committee observes that while utilization of f unds has increased during last two 
years, the achievement in physical target remains t epid.   The employability of training 
Schemes remains serious concern. 
270. KVIC acts as regulator, promoter and certification authority for the Khadi and 
Village Industry sector.  Its multiple rules may co me into conflict. The Committee is 
particularly concerned about the performance of Sta te Khadi networks, who are supposed to 
implement Khadi schemes, and  more particularly in the NE Region.  The Committee noted 
with serious concern that despite rising demand for  Khadi, the Khadi institutions registered 
with KVIC have shown decline in certain States.  Ye t, the allocation for MPDA has been 
increased.  The Ministry remains non-committed about the wages of Khadi artisans. 
271. Regarding PMEGP, the Ministry has not been able to set up even 75 units in every 
District.  The Margin Money remains undisbursed till the last day of Financial Year. 
272. Multiplication of Schemes with very Small allocati on vis-à-vis vast scope of MSME 
sector, do not allow efficient use of available fin ancial and human resources. The Committee 
has been emphasizing that every scheme has a cost o f outreach, implementation and 
monitoring. With as many schemes, the Budget allocations do not reflect these costs which are 
essential for effective monitoring and delivery of scheme-objectives.  Ministry therefore, must 
consolidate and rationalize its Schemes and allocations.  

66 
 
273. The Committee is particularly concerned about marg inalization of abiding 
marginalized classes of society, i.e., SC, ST and N ER regarding implementation of Schemes.  
Ministry has to make special efforts.  
274. In view of CAG’s repeated adverse observation of M inistry of MSME, the Committee 
has been asking for Performance Audit of major Sche mes by CAG and not the third party 
evaluation.  The Committee may be apprised of the o utcome of the CAG’s audit and its 
compliance.  The Committee also recommends that Aud it Paras must be appropriately 
included in the Annual Report of the Ministry.

(Para 191)

which led to earlier suspension of subsequent tranc hes of assistance from a multilateral aid

placing bulk orders for khadi products.  As the KVI C do not produce khadi themselves, the

train such Khadi Institutions with ‘Khadi Mark’ cer tification, to directly register with DG

Report 
Heavy Industries Sector in the country comprises of the heavy engineering, machine tool, 
heavy electrical, industrial machinery and the auto-industry. These industries provide goods and 
services for almost all sectors of the economy, including the infrastructure, power, rail and road 
transport. Lately, the Heavy Industries Sector has been marred by problems like absence of level 
playing field vis-a-vis imports combined with imports of second hand machinery, zero import 
duty under Project Imports, delays in project implementation, non-trade barriers faced in export 
markets, significant technology gaps across sub-sectors, lack of skill availability, cost disabilities 
due to skewed tax and duty structure, cost disadvantage due to duty structure in Free Trade 
Agreements (PTAs), etc. 
2. Indian Auto Industry, a crucial sector under Heavy Industries was at its nascent stage at 
the beginning of the 21st  century which now has become a huge industry that contributes majorly 
to growth and development of Indian Economy. As per the current statistics, the auto Industry's 
turnover is estimated to be equivalent to 7.1% of overall Gross Domestic Product (GDP). The 
auto industry currently employs more than 32 million people both directly and indirectly. As the 
Government's objective is to increase the share of manufacturing in the GDP of the economy 
from an estimated 15 percent to atleast 25 percent, so that employment gets a definite boost, the 
role of auto industry is important and it has already made investments to achieve this objective 
and have increased the capacity to levels that would be needed to achieve the objective. The 
Industry has potential to grow to become a major economic contributor. 
3. The initiatives of the Government to rejuvenate the growth of the Heavy Industries sector 
include the Enhancement of the Competitiveness .in the Indian Capital Goods Sector (CGS) 
Scheme launched in 2014 and the National Goods Policy (NGP), 2016. Likewise, the schemes 
launched by the Government to shore up the Automobile Industry are the National Mission on 
Electric Mobility, 2011 and subsequently, the National Electric Mobility Mission Plan 
(NEMMP), 2020 which was unveiled in 2013. As part of this Mission, Department of Heavy 
Industry (DHI) has notified Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid &) Electric Vehicles 
in India (FAME- India) which is intended to support the hybrid/electric vehicles market 
development and its manufacturing. Further, the Government also finalized Automotive Mission 
Plan (AMP), 2016-26 setting targets for the auto industry for the year 2026. 
1 

Department of Heavy Industry (MI)  
	
4. 	 Earlier DHI used to be one of the Departments under Ministry of Industry. With effect 
from 15 th  October, 1999, a separate Ministry viz. Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public 
Enterprises (M/HI&PE) has been created. The Ministry comprises of the Department of Heavy 
Industry (DHI) and Department of Public Enterprises (DPE). DHI promotes the development and 
growth of three sectors i.e. Capital Goods sector, Auto sector and the following 19 Industrial 
Sub-sectors 
(i) Boilers 
(ii) Cement Machinery 
(iii) Dairy Machinery.. 
(iv) Electrical Furnace 
(v) Freight Containers

(x) Oil Field Equipment 
(xi) Printing Machinery 
(xi i)- Pu 1p and Paper Machinery 
(xiii) Rubber Machinery 
(xiv) Switchgear and Control Gear 
(xv) Shunting Locomotive 
(xvi) Sugar Machinery 
(xvii) Turbines & Generator Set 
(xviii) Transformers 
(xix) Textile Machinery 
	
5. 	 As per the Annual Report (2016-17), of DHI, the Department provides administrative 
oversight to 31 Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and the following autonomous 
organizations: 
(a) NATRiP Implementation Society (NATIS) set up in July 2005, for 
guiding the implementation of the National Automotive Testing and 
R&D Infrastructure Project (N 1ATRiP); 
2 

(b) Fluid Control Research Institute (FCRI), Palakkad, Kerala which caters 
to the needs of the flow industry for calibration; 
(c) Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI), Pune, Maharashtra; 
and 
(d) National Automotive Board (NAB). 
The Annual Report also mentions that there are 25 operating CPSEs under the 
Department engaged in manufacturing, consultancy and contracting services. The list of the 25 
operating CPSEs is placed at Annexure I. 
6. The Committee takes note that the Department has quoted varying figures in its 
Annual Report regarding the number of CPSEs under it. While 31 CPSEs are under the 
`administrative oversight' of DHI, the number of 'operative CPSEs' under it stands at 25. 
Tire Committee assumes that this variance in figures is consequent to the closure of certain 
CPSEs during the preceding year. However, while perusing the status of CPSEs as 
recommended by NITI Aayog placed at Annexure II of the Annual Report (2016-17), the 
number of CPSEs recommended for closure is 7. If this figure is to be considered, the 
number of 'operating CPSEs' should be 24. The Committee observes this as a divergence 
which should have been avoided by more specific description of the status of CPSEs under 
DHI, elucidating the rationale adopted for the same. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that the Department should ensure that important documents like the Annual 
Report should be spelt out unambiguously and without deficiencies in future. 
Vision and Mission of DHI 
7. According to the presentation made by the Department before the Committee as part of 
the oral evidence related to the examination of the Demands of DHI, the Vision and Mission 
statements of DHI are as under: 
Vision 
"To have modern, healthy and robust Auto, Heavy Engineering, Heavy Electrical 
& Capital Goods. Sectors and self-reliant & growth oriented Public Sector Undertakings 
under the Department." 
3 

Mission • 
"Facilitate Automotive Industry to emerge as the destination of choice in the 
world for design and manufacture of Automobiles/ Auto components; 
Help Heavy Electrical and Capital Goods Industry to achieve high growth; 
Transform BHEL into a high growth globally competitive company; and 
Provide support to other CPSEs in order to improve their overall performance." 
8. In tune with the Vision and Mission of the Department, the Committee observes that 
schemes such as 'Enhancement of Competitiveness in Capital Goods Sector' and FAME-
India have been launched and are being nurtured carefully by DHI to facilitate the Heavy 
Industry sector. However, coming to the portion of Vision and Mission relating to CPSEs, 
the Committee finds that there is a lot of lost' ground that is- to be made up by the 
Department. The fact that the growth of Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd (BHEL) finds 
specific mention in the Mission statement underlines the crucial nature of the prospects of 
the Company to the economic interest of the nation. In this context, the Committee 
observes that by making growth of BHEL an integral of its Mission, the Department has 
entrusted upon itself the responsibilities of ensuring efficient performance of its flagship 
company. 
9. Likewise, having taken note that the list of operative CPSEs under the Department 
is lesser by 7 CPSEs this year, the Committee is of the considered opinion that the other 
Mission of DHI to 'provide support to its CPSEs to improve their overall performance' also 
requires considerable thought process and timely proactive interventions from their 
administrative Departments to ensure that the existing number of operative CPSEs are 
retained and that their numbers are not further depleted.

13. The Department submitted in this regard that this significant reform initiative in the 
budgeting process has been made to obviate the notion that had widely gained ground among the 
policy- makers and officials across all levels that Plan expenditure is good and Non-Plan is bad. 
This bias in favor of Plan expenditure and against Non-Plan expenditure has led to a situation in 
which even essential Non-Plan expenditure was being neglected. Shift of focus of Plan 
expenditure from Capital to Revenue expenditure and the process of transferring expenditure of 
old schemes to Non-Plan at the end of each five-year Plan meant that a clear correspondence 
could not be drawn between Plan and Development Expenditure. With the removal of Plan and 
Non-Plan distinction, the focus of budgeting and expenditure will shift to Revenue and Capital 
expenditure. It was also submitted that, henceforth, there will be no Five Year Plan, post 12 th  
Plan. 
14. Further, from this year onwards, Plan Finance-H (PF-H) Division; Department of 
Expenditure has been assigned the responsibility of finalizing the consolidated Demand wise 
Outcome Budget Framework in co-ordination with NITI Aayog on the basis of output/outcome 
framework submitted by each Ministry/Department. Therefore, each Ministry/ Department have 
not prepared their separate Outcome Budget. The output/outcome framework of DELI in respect of 
major Central Sector Schemes has been forwarded to NITI Ayog/ PF-II Division, Department of 
Expenditure. 
6 

15. 	 The Committee finds that the Plan and Non-Plan segregation of funds has been 
done away, with from the year 2017-18 onwards and the classification of Revenue 
expenditure and Capital expenditure has been put in place. The Committee understands 
that such bunching of funds is in alignment with the classification of funds as mentioned in 
the Constitution of India i.e., 'Revenue and other expenditures'. Also, it is not difficult to 
observe that in the era where budget allocation is being evaluated on the basis of the 
outcomes/outputs, it is only prudent to do away with the prior segmented classification in 
favour of a more holistic approach. The Committee expects that this rational step along with 
the advancement in the date of passing of the Budget will help the Department in utilizing 
the funds provided to it in a more systematic and effective manner. 
16. The Committee also finds that individual Outcome Budgets prepared by Ministries/ 
Departments of the Government has also been done away with from the current year. 
Instead, the Department has sent its output/outcome framework in respect of its major 
Central Sector Schemes to the NITI Ayog/ PF-II Division, Department of Expenditure. 
However, the Committee is of the firm opinion that linking budgetary outlays with 
deliverables/outcomes is an essential feature to ensure public accountability and 
transparency of the Government expenditure. Accordingly, the Committee recommends 
that a structured document clearly bringing out the outcomes in terms of the objectives of 
the schemes/programmes of the Department must be brought out either by the Ministries/ 
Departments concerned or by the Department of Expenditure for the benefit of the public 
and to justify the continued funding of the programmes/schemes.

Development of Automobile Industry  
27. The automotive, industry comprises of automobile and auto component sectors. 
Automotive Industry globally is one of the largest industries and is a key driver of economy. 
Owing to its deep forward and backward linkages with several key segments of industry, 
automotive industry has a strong multiplier effect on the economy. The well-developed Indian 
automotive industry ably fulfills this catalytic role by producing a wide variety of vehicles such 
as passenger cars, light, medium and heavy commercial vehicles, multi-utility vehicles, scooters, 
motor-cycles, mopeds, three wheelers, etc. 
National Automotive Testing and Research & Development Infrastructure Project 
(NATRiP).  
28. NATRiP was approved by the Government on 25 th  July, 2005 and notified by DHI on 
31g  August, 2005 with an investment of Rs 1718 cr. which was subsequently revised twice to Rs. 
2286.06 Cr in April, 2011 and to Rs 3727 Cr in July, 2016. The reasons considered by the 
Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) while upwardly revising the cost estimate 
were Forex variation, statutory levies, rise in input cost and other factors like change in scope of 
supply. The initial scheduled date of completion of NATRiP project was April, 2011, which was 
initially extended to December, 2012, then to December, 2014 and thereafter to December, 2017. 
Now, the revised timeline has been submitted by DHI as July, 2019, which means the Project has 
received yet another extension. The primary objectives of the Project are as under: 
• To setup world class infrastructure to test vehicles and components against existing and 
emerging standards mandated by the Govt. to significantly enhance vehicular safety, 
performance and ameliorate its impact on public health. 
• Deepening of automotive manufacturing in India, promoting larger value addition and 
thereby significantly enhancing employment generation in this sector. 
• India's emergence as a global outsourcing base for automobiles and auto components in 
furtherance of Auto Mission Plan. 
Automotive testing, validation, Research and Development (R&D) and homologation facilities .. 
are being created in the three principal hubs of North, West and South India under NATRiP. The 
Government of India has majority funding of the project and has 'granted full customs duty 
exemption to all project imports while the State Governments have offered land at concessionl 
rates.

view that though the modern theories of government and economics want the Government 
to withdraw from business, while deciding upon disinvestments/ closures, it is always 
prudent to keep in mind that CPSEs are also meant to serve certain larger social causes. 
The Committee would like to make a mention of an example in this regard i.e. the case of 
the decision for 100% disinvestment of HNL, a company that was classified only as 
`Incipient sick' in 2016. The Committee finds that the decision was taken despite the

(i) 	 BHEL 
66. BHEL, a Maharatna CPSE is an integrated power plant manufacturer and one of the 
largest engineering and Manufacturing companies of its kind in India. The company is engaged 
in design, engineering manufacture, construction, commissioning and servicing of a wide range 
of products and services for the core sectors of the economy viz. Power, Transmission, Industry, 
Transportation, ReneWable Energy, Oil & Gas and Defence. 
67. However, the company has not been doing well in the recent past. Further, as per the 
Guidelines of DPE on "Streamlining the mechanism for revival/restructuring of sick/incipient 
sick/weak CPSEs", BHEL has been classified as 'weak' in 2016-17. When queried about this, 
DHI submitted that the DPE has issued guidelines vide their OM dated 29.10.2015.for 
Streamlining the mechanism for revival / restructuring of sick / incipient sick / weak CPSEs. 
These guidelines are objective in nature and have been issued after due deliberations in DPE. 
DHI agrees with the guidelines. DPE has laid down certain parameters / criteria for adjudging the 
status of a CPSE under these categories. As per one of the criteria / yardstick, a CPSE can be 
categorised as 'weak' if its turnover or operational profit has declined by more than an average 
of 10 % in the last three years. This is an indication of deteriorating health of the CPSE as it is 
not able to grow financially. This condition raises an alert for remedial actions at all levels to 
arrest the declining trend and improve its health. In view of the above, the DPE guidelines signal 
an alert for timely action by the CPSE and the administrative department. DHI agrees with it. 
BHEL has accordingly been categorised as 'Weak' as its turnover and profit declined over last 
three years. It slipped into red in 2015-16 and remedial steps are being taken in association. with 
BHEL to improve its status, which has also been reflected in the current year's performance 
which has shown a marked improvement over the last year.

weighted deduction from 200 to 150% in Income Tax for investment in R&D has affected 
the prospects of the Company. Being the highest spender in R&D, as claimed by the 
management, BHEL stands to lose the most because of this move. The fact that BHEL is 
the highest investor after the GoI in the Advance Ultra Supercritical Project with an 
amount of Rs 270.00 Cr gives credibility to their said claim. Considering this, the 
Committee recommends that the Government should consider restoring the IT deduction 
for R&D investment to 200%. Further, the Committee views the Advance Ultra 
Supercritical Project as an avenue which can help BHEL make up lost ground, if 
commercialized successfully. It is expected that the Company will be executing their part in 
the project successfully. 
ii) 	 Heavy Engineering Corporation Ltd. (HEC) 
77. 'HEC is an integrated engineering complex, established in 1958 under Department of 
Heavy Industry, Govt. of India. It was originally established for manufacture of plant and 
machineries required to set up steel plants in the country. It has got three major manufacturing 
units all located at one place in Ranchi. 
1. Foundry Forge Plant (FFP) 
2. Heavy Machine Building Plant (HMBP) 
3. Heavy Machine Tools Plant (HMTP) 
4. Project Division. 
FFP and HMTP have been set up under technical collaboration from erstwhile Czechoslovakia, 
whereas HMBP has been set up with technical collaboration from erstwhile USSR. HEC's 
30 

uniqueness is in its ability to manufacture heavy components, specialized engineering products 
and. its ability to complete all the manufacturing operations like —casting, forging, fabrication, 
machining, assembly and testing at one location supported by design, engineering and project 
management functions making it an integrated manufacturing complex. 
78. In spite of valuable contributions, the financial performance of the company was not 
satisfactory due to less capacity utilization and shortage in working capital. Subsequently, the 
company was referred to Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR). Thereafter, 
government approved revival packages in 2005 and 2008. The revival package of 2005 included 
waiver of Rs 1101 Cr and cash of Rs 187.44 Cr, out of which only Rs 31.96 Cr was invested on 
Capex. While in 2008, package which was an extension of 2005, the actual receipt of cash was 
Rs 219.79 Cr, out of which only Rs 44.09 Cr was invested on Capex. Thus, as part of the revival 
package. 2005-2008, the total cash received of Rs 407.23 Cr, could provide only Rs 76.05 Cr 
towards Capex. The company could earn marginal profit from 2006-07 till 2012-13 with net 
turnover high up to Rs 682 Cr. But due to lack of modernisation and up-keeping of the plant and 
machineries performance started sliding down. 
79. Most of the plant and machineries of HEC installed during sixties have become outdated. 
The company badly needs modernization of its plant and machineries as well as infusion of latest 
technology. M/s MECON Ltd was engaged for preparation of Detailed Project Report (DPR) and 
Modernization Plan of HEC in 2014 and the same have been passed by the Board of Directors. 
Based on the same, a Cabinet note was prepared and there have been meetings at various levels 
including PS to PM in July, 2016. An expert Committee headed by Dr.V.K.Saraswat, Member, 
NITI Aayog has been appointed to examine the viability of HEC's modernization plan and 
assessment of its future potential. The Committee has since submitted its report to Go!. 
80. The Committee's report strongly recommends for discharge of all liabilities of HEC 
along with implementation of CAPEX to achieve long-term sustainability. The total fund 
requirement projected is on three heads: CAPEX, Liabilities and Working Capital. The total fund 
requirement is to the tune of Rs 2250 Cr, with Capex of Rs 1267 Crore, over next four years. It 
has recommended immediate funding of Rs. 1000 crore and Human Resource (HR) 
enhancement. The Committee has also recommended a number of measures including possible 
source of funding by monetization of additional land by transfer of the same to the State Govt. of 
Jharkhand at enhanced rate for strengthening the organization. 
31 

81. The State Government has expressed their interest in taking over 675.43 acres of liEC

engaged a professional consulting agency namely, M/s KPMG India for performance 
improvement of HEC. It has since submitted its Report and DHI is following it up with hand-
holding of HEC in proper implementation of its recommendations in operational areas of the 
Company's functioning for achieving higher levels of efficiency and effectiveness. Further, it has 
been submitted to the Committee during the oral evidence that HEC are getting orders from the 
Defence sector and are also exploring the possibility of getting orders from the Navy, under the

recommended for handing over of HEC to the State Government of Jharkhand. But DHI has held 
the view that the Company is catering to the strategic requirements of the country with its unique 
facilities and therefore, should be allowed to continue and be supported for refurbishment and

draft Cabinet Note for transferring HEC to the State Government of Jharkhand is under inter-

83. Regarding the Modernization of HEC, the Committee would like to bring on record 
its persistent recommendations for the same as contained in its reports on DFG 2013-14,

seeing light at the end of the tunnel with the signing of MoU with the Russian company 
CNITMASH for setting up niche training centres for specialized training and all-important

also lends its whole-hearted support to the same and strongly objects to the transfer of 
HEC to the State Government of Jharkhand, which might sound the death knell of a

recommended that the said move of the transfer of the Company should be summarily 
dropped and expeditious approval of the recommendation of the Saraswat —Committee for

units of HPC in the NER emanating from the fact that they are the main source of

92. The Committee also takes note of the fact that the Department have issued 
necessary instructions to the HPC to put up their procurement policy for bamboo on the

93. Still further, the Committee would want DHI to actively pursue the possibility of

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE-AT A GLANCE 
1. The Committee takes note that the Department has quoted varying figures in its 
Annual Report regarding the number of CPSEs under it. While 31 CPSEs are under the 
`administrative oversight' of DHI, the number of 'operative CPSEs' under it stands at 25. 
The Committee assumes that this variance in figures is consequent to the closure of certain 
CPSEs during the preceding year. However, while perusing the status of CPSEs as 
recommended by NITI Aayog placed at Annexure H of the Annual Report (2016-17), the 
number of CPSEs recommended for closure is 7. If this figure is to be considered, the 
number of 'operating CPSEs' should be 24. The Committee observes this as a divergence 
which should have been avoided by more specific description of the status of CPSEs under 
DHI, elucidating the rationale adopted for the same. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that the Department should ensure that important documents like the Annual 
Report should be spelt out unambiguously and without deficiencies in future. 
Para No. 6 
2. In tune with the Vision and Mission of the Department, the Committee observes that 
schemes such as 'Enhancement of Competitiveness in Capital Goods Sector' and FAME-
India have been launched and are being nurtured carefully by DHI to facilitate the Heavy 
Industry sector. However, coming to the portion of Vision and Mission relating to CPSEs, 
the Committee finds that there is a lot of lost ground that is to be made up by the

specific mention in the Mission statement underlines the crucial nature of the prospects of 
the Company to the economic interest of the nation. In this context, the Committee

entrusted upon itself the responsibilities of ensuring efficient performance of its flagship 
corn pany.

requires considerable thought process and timely proactive interventions from their

administrative Departments to ensure that the existing number of operative CPSEs are

After independence, grave socio-economic problems such as inequalities in income and 
low levels of employment, regional imbalances in economic development and lack of trained 
manpower, weak industrial base, inadequate investments and infrastructure facilities, etc. were the 
primary concerns for the Government to address. It was in this backdrop that the roadmap for 
Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) was developed as an instrument for self-reliant economic growth. 
Accordingly, India adopted planned economic development polices, which envisaged the 
development of PSUs. 
2. 	 Initially, the public sector was confined to core and strategic industries, subsequently, the 
second phase witnessed nationalization of industries, takeover of sick units from the private sector, 
and entry of the public sector into new fields like manufacturing consumer goods, consultancy, 
contracting and transportation, etc. Thereupon, protectionist Government policies envisaged active 
engagement of the State in development of industries for more than four decades. Thereafter, the 
introduction of the New Industrial Policy of 1991 was a watershed which opened up the economy 
and initiated disinvestment and privatisation. The Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) were 
also opened to competition from the private sector, both domestic and international. The World 
Trade Organisation (WTO) agreements and other Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) that followed . 
contributed to the globalised competition as well. In the present scenario, the Government now 
stresses the-need for CPSEs to .  p.eO-  orirri; to exist and the NITI Aayog has been entrusted to 
evaluate the CPSEs to determine their suitability for revival/restructuring, or closure/strategic 
disinvestment. 
An overview of CPSEs in India 
3. 	 There were 244 operational CPSEs functioning under the 22 Cognate Groups as on 
31.03.2016. The Cognate Group-wise financial performance of CPSEs for the last 3 years is 
given at Annexure- 1. The schedule-wise list of CPSEs is given at Annexure-2. Presently, there 
are 64 Schedule 'A', 68 Schedule 'B', 45 Schedule 'C' and 4 Schedule 'D' CPSEs. The 
information on categorisation of CPSEs as per the laid-out norms of Department of Public 
Enterprises (DPE) and a list of Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna CPSEs is given at 
Annexure-3.

5. The Committee notes that during 2015-16, the total number of CPSEs stood at 320, 
which was a significant increase of 22 CPSEs, compared to 2014-15 when the total number 
was 298. At the same time, the number of operating CPSEs rose only by 8 during the said 
period. Further, the Paid-Up Capital, Capital Employed, Investment and Reserves & Surplus 
by the CPSEs rose steadily during the XIIth Plan period. Similarly, the dividend paid and 
the contributions made to the exchequer also saw an increase during the Plan period. The 
indictor that decreased the most in the XIIth Plan period was the foreign exchange earnings 
by the CPSEs. Another factor that is obvious is the decline in the number of people employed. 
As submitted by DPE, due to the decline in the number of permanent employees over the 
years, CPSEs are now hiring employees on contract basis. 
6. The Committee considers the fact that the role of CPSEs in India has undergone a lot 
of metamorphosis since the beginning of planned mixed economy. After playing their part in 
nation building in a protected environment till the advent of the New Economic policy of 
1991, the era of economic liberalisation dawned upon them. Now, the Government has done 
away with planned economy and has set priority areas wherein it would continue to be 
engaged in business through CPSEs. In the remaining spheres, only CPSEs who keep 
themselves afloat by being profitable are encouraged while closure or strategic 

disinvestment, as decided by the NITI Aayog, is being used by the Government to exit loss-
incurring CPSEs in non-priority areas. This approach is expected to free up capital for 
investment in the social and infrastructure sectors. In this regard, the Committee observes 
that one of the causes for which CPSEs were envisaged, i.e. for equitable economic and social 
development - is still relevant to our country and has to be kept in mind along with financial 
and business prudence while deciding the closure or strategic disinvestment of CPSEs. The 
Committee is of the considered opinion that employment generation is one factor that CPSEs 
can facilitate for some more time especially, in areas suffering from regional imbalances, 
besides the North Eastern Region. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that CPSEs 
should be encouraged to provide permanent employment to people and may be desisted from 
hiring personnel on contract basis. 
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE). 
7. In their 52 nd  Report, the Estimates Committee of 3 rd  Lok Sabha (1962-67) stressed the need 
for setting up a centralized coordinating unit, which could also make continuous appraisal of the 
performance of public enterprises. This led to the setting up of the Bureau of Public Enterprises 
(BPE) in 1965 in the Ministry of Finance. Subsequently, as a result of the reorganization of the 
Ministries/Departments of the Union Government in September, 1985, BPE was made part of the 
Ministry of Industry. In May, 1990, BPE was made a full-fledged Department known as the DPE. 
Presently, it is part of the Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises (Mo HI &PE). 
8. The DPE is the nodal department for all the CPSEs and formulates policy pertaining to 
them. It lays down, in particular, policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, 
autonomy and financial delegation and personnel management in CPSEs. It further, collects and 
maintains information in the form of a Public Enterprises Survey on several areas in respect of 
CPSEs. 
9. In fulfilling its role, the Department coordinates with other Ministries, CPSEs and 
concerned organizations. As per the Allocation of Business Rules of the Government, the 
following subjects have been allocated to the DPE: 
• Residual work . relating to erstwhile Bureau of Public Enterprises including 
Industrial Management Pool. 
• Coordination of matters of general policy affecting all Public-Sector Enterprises. 
3 

• Evaluation and monitoring the performance of Public Sector Enterprises, including 
the Memorandum of Understanding mechanism. 
• Matters relating to Permanent Machinery of Arbitration for the Public-Sector 
Enterprises. 
• Counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees in Central Public Sector 
Undertakings under Voluntary Retirement Scheme. 
• Review of capital projects and expenditure in Central Public Sector Enterprises. 
• Measures aimed at improving performance of Central Public Sector Enterprises and 
other capacity building initiatives of Public Sector Enterprises. 
• Rendering advice relating to revival, restructuring or closure of Public Sector 
Enterprises including the mechanisms therefor. 
• Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises. 
• Matters relating to International Center for Public Enterprises. 
• Categorization of Central Public Sector Enterprises including conferring Ratna .  
status. 
• 	 Survey of Public Enterprises. 
10. The Committee notes that during the oral evidence, while making a presentation to 
the Committee, the Department submitted as part of the `CPSE highlights -2015-16' that the 
total number of CPSEs in the country to be 320, out of which 244 are operating and the 
remaining 76 are under construction. In the ensuing discussion, attention was drawn to the 
General Performance of CPSEs and the areas wherein CPSEs have excelled and the areas 
where they have failed. It was pointed out that the sectors where the top ten profit making 
CPSEs of the country operating currently were in the spheres where CPSEs can deliver and 
where they should venture more into by the Government. Likewise; when the top ten loss-
incurring CPSEs were analysed except BHEL, it was not difficult to find that they are 
operating in areas where technological changes are frequent and the market fluctuation were 
rampant due to varying factors. 
11. In view of the above, the Committee while observing the data relating to the profit 
making and loss incurring CPSEs, finds that there are certain captive sectors in the industry 
which are conducive for the Government to set up CPSEs in a profitable manner. In the 
opinion of the Committee, general parameters of such areas might iriclude stable technology, 
steady market, capital intensive nature and judicious utilization of public assets, etc. The 
Government can keep these broad principles in mind while identifying and setting up of 
A -r 

CPSEs in the future in strategic and priority areas. Besides this, the principles of social 
responsibilities of the Government should also be intertwined with the business 
considerations. 
12. Accordingly, as a preparatory step in this direction, the ComMittee recommends that 
DPE being the body in charge of the General Policy framework for CPSEs, should conduct a 
well-organized comprehensive research study to identify the areas of business wherein 
CPSEs can successfully/profitably operate and grow. A policy of public investment in CPSEs 
can be based on the findings of such a scientific study. This, in the opinion of the Committee 
should help to ensure that the 76 CPSEs that are being newly set up by the Government 
operate in a profitable environment and are not doomed to be shut due to extraneous factors 
like in case of their predecessors. 
13. As part of the examination of Demand for Grants (DFG) of DPE, the Department placed 
before the Committee the steps taken by them to facilitate the functioning of CPSEs during the last 
few years. According to DPE, while the day-to-day management of the CPSE's is being handled 
by their Boards and the respective administrative Ministries, DPE, inter-alia, coordinates matter of 
general policy, performance evaluation, corporate governance and capacity building issues of 
CPSEs and advises on the revival, restructuring and closure of CPSEs. The Department also shared 
with the Committee some of the important guidelines issued by DPE for CPSEs during the last 
three years which are placed below: 
a. Guidelines-  for 'Streamlining the mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick/ incipient., 
sick and weak CPSEs'. These guidelines would help administrative Ministries in monitoring 
those CPSEs which are moving toward sickness so that corrective measures can be taken in 
time. As per these guidelines, administrative Ministries are supposed to closely monitor the 
weak CPSEs so that they do not become sick/ incipient sick. 
b. Guidelines on 'Time bound closure of sick/ loss-making CPSEs and disposal Of their 
movable and immovable assets'. These guidelines would help in unlocking the amount 
invested in land and building as clear modalities for disposal of assets have been prescribed 
for CPSEs under closure. 
c.. Observance of transparency and due diligence in selection and implementation of activities 
under Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) by CPSEs. 
d. Guidelines on improvements in the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) process are 
being issued from time to time. Last guidelines on this subject were issued on 16.12.2016. 
5 

14. Further, in reply to the Committee's query on its Guidelines on CSR, DPE submitted the 
following- "On the issue of CSR, DPE has issued two separate advisories vide its OM dated l st  
August, 2016 to all the CPSEs on 'Observance of Transparency and due diligence in selection and 
implementation of activities. under CSR by CPSEs" and "Allocation of CSR fund by CPSEs for 
Swachh Bharat activities". 
15. The Committee had a detailed deliberation on the Guidelines regarding the utilization 
of CSR funds by CPSEs. In this context, it was brought before the Committee that there 
were certain activities like the construction of toilets which were undertaken as part of the 
Swatch Bharat activities, but funds/efforts were not spared for their upkeep or maintenance. 
The Committee notes that in many areas where such constructions where taking place were 
remote in nature and lack of upkeep rendered them useless and most unhygienic within a 
short span of time. 
16. The Committee takes note that DPE's latest advisory on CSR activities mentions only 
transparency, selection and implementation of activities under CSR by CPSEs. However, 
based on the facts brought before the Committee, it finds that there are activities under CSR 
that become redundant in the absence of provisions for their maintenance by utilizing CSR 
funds. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that DPE guidelines/advisories on CSR 
should contain provisions/instructions to ensure the maintenance of constructed toilets and 
their related -lialifies under Swachh Bharat activities. This will also be in synchronisation 
with the similar provisions as contained in Swatch Bharat Kosh guidelines. 
DPE during the XII Plan Period (2012-17) 
17. During XII th  Plan period, 3 plan schemes were in operation viz. Counselling, Retraining &

Scheme of Research. Development and Consultancies on Generic issues related to Public 
Sector Enterprises (RDC Scheme)  
31. 	 The Scheme of RDC on Generic issues of Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) was introduced 
in the year 2007-08 and is being implemented since 2008-09. In view of instructions issued by the 
Ministry of Finance (MoF) with regard to rationalization of Schemes, the Scheme for Skill 
Development/Training programme to executives/employees of State Level Public Enterprises 
(SLPEs) has been merged with the Scheme of RDC on Generic issues of Public Sector Enterprises 
(PSEs) during the year 2016-17. The objectives of Scheme are to (i) undertake thematic studies on 
the generic issues of public sector enterprises; (ii) conduct seminars and workshops on the generic 
issues to adopt collaborative and cooperative learning for experience sharing; (iii) conduct training 
programmes for capacity building and skill development; (iv) constant improvement in 
performance evaluation and management processes of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs); 
(v) incentives' best practices in focus areas through grant of awards/incentives to CPSEs and 
SLPEs; and (vi) to deal with any other pertinent issue related to DPE.

functioning of the RDC scheme since its inception. Accordingly, an intensive review in 
consultation with the other stakeholders was undertaken in DPE and a more comprehensive and 
need based scheme was finalised in February, 2016. RDC scheme was modified so that activities 
could be spread round the year and its_scope was expanded aprcraiTersified to include more . 
activities. As a measure of restructuring of Plan schemes, at the instance of MoF, Scheme of Skill

learning activities seminars, workshops, conferences, etc. on various generic issues are

MoU System for CPSEs 
42. The MoU is a mutually negotiated agreement between the Government of India/ Holding 
Company and the management of the CPSEs. Under this agreement,'the CPSEs undertake to 
. 	••• achieve the targets set in the agreement at the beginning of the year and submit themselves to • 
evaluation on the basis of its achievements at the end of the year. The Government of India 
19 

introduced the MoU system in the year 1986, based on the recommendations given by Arjun Sen 
Gupta Committee Report (1984). The report recommended that the CPSEs should enter agreement 
with their administrative Ministries for five years, with progress to be reviewed annually. The 
MoU system was given broader thrust by the Governments after the announcement of the New 
Industrial Policy of 1991. 
43. The institutional arrangements for the implementation of the MoU policy includes an apex 
High Powered Committee (HPC) headed by the Cabinet Secretary which gives guidance and 
directions with respect to the determination of the principles and parameters for evaluating the 
performance of CPSEs. Till now, there was a Task Force of experts to assist the HPC in their job. 
From the year 2016-17 an Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) has been put in place headed by the 
Secretary, DPE to approve the MoU targets and recommend its evaluated score and rating to the 
HPC. A Pre-Negotiation Committee (PNC), earlier known as the Standing Committee on MoU, is 
also there to assist the IMC in determining the most appropriate and relevant parameters for 
measuring improvement in performance and for fixing targets. 
44. The Committee asked the Department to provide an overview of the evolution of the MoU 
system for CPSEs over the years in terms of the method of implementation, evaluation parameters, 
consultative process to draw up the guidelines, etc. The Department was also sought to furnish the 
details of the modifications made in MoU guidelines during the. last three years and the current 
year, i.e., 2016-17 in response to the changes in the regulatory/ legal framework impacting CPSEs 
like, the Procurement Policy & Vendor Development Programmes and CSR. Responding to this, 
DPE submitted the following:- 
I. 	 Overview of the evaluation of the MoU System for CPSEs over the years: 
1 Method of implementation: 
Signing of MoU has been made compulsory as per the decision of the High-Powered 
Committee in 2007. Rating of MoU is used for rating Board level officials of the CPSEs, 
payment of PRP, giving Maharatna status, etc. This has resulted in increase in number of 
MoU signing companies from 144 in 2007-8 to 234 in 2015-16. 
2. Evaluative parameters: 
Evaluation of MoU of the CPSE is done after the end ofthe year and finalisation of their 
accounts. The evaluation is done based on the parameters fixed at the time of target 
setting: Evaluation of MoU, i.e., achievement of targets is .first approved by Board of 
Directors of the :CPSE concerned. Mali evaluation issent to DPE through.their .

administrative Ministry. The parameters for the targets are decided based on MoU 
guidelines for the respective years. 
3. Consultative process to draw up the Guidelines: 
For formulating the Guidelines, DPE consults administrative Ministries/ Departments and • 
CPSEs by holding workshops at various places. 
MoU 2016-17 Guidelines were finalised after consulting CPSEs in 4 workshops. These 
Guidelines were discussed in High Powered Committee (HPC) on MoU having 
Secretaries of various Ministries and Members. On the directions of HPC, these 
Guidelines were again discussed with administrative Ministries and Conveners of Task 
Forces on MoU. Thereafter, the Guidelines were again discussed and finalised in a 
meeting of High Powered Committee. 
MoU 2017-18 Guidelines were finalised after consulting CPSEs in 3 workshops, out of 
which one workshop was exclusively for senior officers of administrative Ministries/ 
Departments and Board level officers of Navratna and Maharatna CPSEs. The Guidelines 
were issued after the approval of Cabinet Secretary as Chairman of High Powered 
Committee on MoU. 
II. 	 Details of the changes made in MoU Guidelines during the last three years and the current 
year, i.e., 2016-17 in response to the changes in regulatory/ legal framework: 
1. Procurement and vendor development programme: 
Public Procurement Policy issued by Ministry of MSME was made compulsory 
parameter from the year 2014-15 onwards. Failure to comply with the Public Procurement 
Policy was given negative mark of 1 for the years 2014-15, 2015-16, 2017-18 and 
onwards. For the year, 2016-17, non-compliance of various conditions including Public 
Procurement Policy issued by Ministry of MSME would result in downgrading- of 
Excellent rated CPSEs to Very Good and 5 marks are to be deducted in respect of other 
CPSEs. 
During the year 2015-16, 131 CPSEs were given negative mark for non-compliance of 
Public Procurement Policy issued by Ministry of MSME. 
2. CSR: 
CSR has been a parameter from the year 2013-14 onwards. For the year 2015-16, non-
compliance of CSR parameter was given 1 negative mark. For the current year 2016-17, 
non-compliance of provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 which also includes 
compliance of CSR would result in downgrading of Excellent rated CPSEs to Very Good 
and 5 marks are to be deducted in respect of other CPSEs. 
During the year 2015-16, 39 CPSEs were given negative mark for non-compliance of 
CSR Guidelines.

Revival/Restructuring/Closure of CPSEs  
47. 	 The Government of India has recently taken many steps to make the mechanism and 
process for revival/ restructuring of CPSEs time bound, comprehensive, performance driven and 
efficient. The Government has decided to remove the multiple layers in the decision-making 
process to ensure timely revival/ restructuring of CPSEs. It has been decided that revival/ 
restructuring of sick /incipient sick CPSEs is to be merit based considering strategic, national and 
business concerns of the CPSEs. Accordingly, the Government has wound up BRPSE and 
administrative Ministries/Departments concerned are made responsible to monitor sickness of 
CPSEs functioning under them and to take timely redressal measures with the approval of the 
competent authority. On these lines DPE issued guidelines on 29 th  October, 2015 for 'Streamlining 
the mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick/ incipient sick and weak CPSEs: General 
principles and mechanism of restructuring' to be followed by the administrative Ministries/ 
Departments. Further, DPE issued another guideline on 7 th  September, 2016 for 'Time bound 
closure of sick/ loss-making CPSEs and disposal of their movable and immovable assets'. These 
guidelines are intended to expeditiously complete the various process and procedure related to the 
closure of CPSEs. 
48. 	 On the procedure for deciding restructuring / closure / strategic sale of a PSU and the role 
of NITI Aayog in this direction, DPE submitted that Chapter XIX of the Companies Act, 2013 
refers to Reviyal—arrd—Rehabilitation of Sick Companies and Chapter XX to Winding up of the 
Companies. The decision whether a company has become a sick company would be taken by the 
National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). The Act is administered by Ministry of Corporate 
Affairs ( MoCA). Further, a Committee has been constituted under the Chairmanship of Vice-Chairman, NITI 
Aayog to review the status of all loss making_ CPSEs. Secretaries of DPE, Department of Investment and 
Public Asset Management (DIPAM) and Department of Heavy Industry (DHI), CEO, NITI Aayog and Joint 
Secretary (Expenditure), Ministry of Finance are members of the Committee. The recommendatiohs of NITI 
Aayog with regard to revival, restructuring or closure of CPSE are processed by the administrative 	 . 
Ministry/Department concerned for obtaining the approval of the Cabinet/ Cabinet Committee on 
Economic Affairs (CCEA). The final decision of whether to accept these recommendations in part, . 
fully or with modifications, rests with the Cabinet/CCEA.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE-AT A GLANCE 
1. The Committee notes that during 2015-16, the total number of CPSEs stood at 320, 
which was a significant increase of 22 CPSEs, compared to 2014-15 when the total number 
was 298. At the same time, the number of operating CPSEs rose only by 8 during the said 
period. Further, the Paid-Up Capital, Capital Employed, Investment and Reserves & Surplus 
by the CPSEs rose steadily during the XIIth Plan period. Similarly, the dividend paid and 
the contributions made to the exchequer also saw an increase during the Plan period. The 
indictor that decreased the most in the XIIth Plan period was the foreign exchange earnings 
by the CPSEs. Another factor that is obvious is the decline in the number of people employed. 
As submitted by DPE, due to the decline in the number of permanent employees over the 
years, CPSEs are now hiring employees on contract basis. 
(Para No. 5) 
2. The Committee considers the fact that the role of CPSEs in India has undergone a lot 
of metamorphosis since the beginning of planned mixed economy. After playing their part in 
nation building in a protected environment till the advent of the New Economic policy of 
1991, the era of economic liberalisation dawned upon them. Now, the Government has done 
away with planned economy and has set priority areas wherein it would continue to be 
engaged in business through CPSEs. In the remaining spheres, only CPSEs who keep 
themselves afloat by being profitable—are encouraged while closure or strategic 
disinvestment, as decided by the NITI Aayog, is being used by the Government to exit loss-
incurring CPSEs in non-priority areas. This approach is expected to free up capital for 
investment in the social and infrastructure sectors. In this regard, the Committee observes 
that one of the causes for which CPSEs were envisaged, i.e. for equitable economic and social 
development - is still relevant to our country and has to be kept in• mind along with financial 
and business prudence while deciding the closure or strategic disinvestment of CPSEs. The 
Committee is of the considered opinion that employment generation is one factor that CPSEs 
can facilitate for some more time especially, in areas suffering from regional imbalances, 
besides the North Eastern Region. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that CPSEs 
should be encouraged to provide permanent employment to people .  and may be desisted from 
hiring personnel on contract basis. 
(Para No. 6) 

3. The Committee notes that during the oral evidence, while making a presentation to 
the Committee, the Department submitted as part of the `CPSE highlights 2015-16' that the 
total number of CPSEs in the country to be 320, out of which 244 are operating and the 
remaining 76 are under construction. In the ensuing discussion, attention was drawn to the 
General Performance of CPSEs and the areas wherein CPSEs have excelled and the areas 
where they have failed. It was pointed out that the sectors where the top ten profit making 
CPSEs of the country operating currently were in the spheres where CPSEs can deliver and 
where they should venture more into by the Government. Likewise, when the top ten loss-
incurring CPSEs were analysed except BHEL, it was not difficult to find that they are 
operating in areas where technological changes are frequent and the market fluctuation were 
rampant due to varying factors. 
(Para No. 10) 
4. In view of the above, the Committee while observing the data relating to the profit 
making and loss incurring CPSEs, finds that there are certain captive sectors in the industry 
which are conducive for the Government to set up CPSEs in a profitable manner. In the 
opinion of the Committee, general parameters of such areas might include stable technology, 
steady market, capital intensive nature and judicious utilization of public assets, etc. The 
Government can keep these broad principles in mind- while identifying and setting up of 
CPSEs in the future in strategic and priority areas. Besides this, the principles of social 
responsibilities of the Government should glso be intertwined with the business 
considerations. 
(Para No.11) 
5. Accordingly, as a preparatory step in this direction, the Committee recommends that 
DPE being the body in charge of the General Policy framework for CPSEs, should conduct a 
well-organized comprehensive research study to identify the areas of business wherein 
CPSEs can successfully/profitably operate and grow. A policy of public investment in CPSEs 
can be based on the findings of such a scientific study. This, in the opinion of the Committee 
should help to ensure that the 76 CPSEs that are being newly set up by the Government 
operate in a profitable environment and are not doomed to be shut due to extraneous factors 
like in case of their predecessors. 
(Para No. 12)

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having
been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this Two Hundred Eighty-Third Report on Action
Taken Notes furnished by the Department of Public Enterprises (Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public
Enterprises) on the recommendations contained in the Committee's Two Hundred Eighty-Second Report
on the Demands For Grants (2017-18) pertaining to Department of Public Enterprises.
2. I, thank the Department of Public Enterprises (Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises)
for furnishing the Action Taken Notes on the recommendations contained in the Committee's Two
Hundred Eighty-Second Report.
