the revival/restructuring of its CPSEs in NER from the Non-lapsable pool of resources for NER.
(Para 93)
Action Taken
Draft Note containing the proposal for revival of HPC has been circulated to concerned departments
for their comments. Based on the comments of concerned departments, draft CCEA Note is being
modified. Suggestion of the Committee to secure funds for the revival of HPC from the non-lapsable pool
of resources for NER is noted and possibility of the same will be explored.
Recommendation/observation
The Committee finds that revival of NEPA Ltd. was approved by the CCEA in September, 2012 with
a CAPEX of ` 285 crore (out of which ` 157.00 in the form of fresh equity by GoI and balance ` 128
Crore through bank loans) for RMDP. Out of the pledged Government support of ` 157 crore the
Committee has been informed that an amount of ` 104.58 crore provided during 2015-16 is to be utilized
by March, 2017 for RMDP. The Committee's expectation was that this year the remaining Government
support will be provided and NEP A is pursuing, with the help of DHI, avenues for bank loan components.

21
However, the Committee expresses its disappointment that the date of completion of the RMDP has been
extended from March to June, 2017 and no budgetary support is extended for NEP A for this year.
(Para 97)
Action Taken
Government accorded approval to the proposal for revival of NEPA Limited with CAPEX of ` 285
crore. Out of this, GoI equity infusion was ` 157 crore and balance amount of `128 crore to be raised
by the Company from Banks/Financial Institutions. Funds of ` 157 crore have already been released by
GOI in 4 instalments; last one of ` 47.91 crore was released on 31.03.2016. Therefore no budgetary
support is extended for NEPA this year.
As per contract, CPP renovation works were to be completed by June 2017, however the vendor
agreed to squeeze the schedule. Demonetisation has affected the progress of works and vendor could
not manage to squeeze the schedule. Best efforts are being made to complete the project early.
Company is still on old 1997 scales. Salary support since April 2014 is pending for release. Since
February 2016, Company is anyhow managing to release only 50-60% salary and wages advance for
sustenance of employees. This is leading to de-motivation and also affecting the progress.
The original sanctioned RMDP budget was ` 285 crore However, the revised budget estimate of
RMDP now works out to be ` 428 crore due to cost escalations and additional items for the overall plant.
Proposal for Revised Cost Estimate is being included in the CCEA Note for salary support.
The process of balance loan ` 128 crore from the Banks (SBI & BOI) is under consideration. DHI
has given approval of mortgage of Plant and Machinery and immovable property at Delhi. SBI, the lead
bank, sought a revised TEV report. For the purpose, consultant was appointed. Draft TEV report has
already been prepared and sent to SBI and is under review at their end. They have also indicated
requirement of credit rating. Tender for the same has already been floated and the work will be finished
within a month. Loan is likely to be sanctioned in May/June, 2017.
Recommendation/observation
Also, the Committee finds that NEPA has scaled up its tentative production performance to 
` 306
crore for 2017-18 compared to ` 13.75 crore (anticipated) performance during 2016-17. The Committee
appreciates optimism expressed by NEPA and presumes that the Company expects to do well during
2017-18 as RMDP is to be completed during the year. However, if that is the case the Committee finds
it difficult to comprehend why NEP A expects a tentative loss of 
` - 8.60 crore for 2017-18 despite the
projected surge in production performance. The loss figure gets stark when compared to the anticipated
profit of 
` 11 crore for 2016-17. The Committee wants the Department to go into the matter and furnish
an explanation for this ironical situation with regard to the performance of NEP A. (Para 98)
Action Taken
The anticipated profit for the Financial year 2016-17 was ` 11 crore after taking into account profit
of ` 89 crore on transfer of 803 acres Hempur Land to Government of Uttarakhand. Despite best efforts,
transfer could not be finalized during 2016-17. The process is now in final stage and funds are likely
to be received in May 2017. Excluding this exceptional item, anticipated loss for F.Y . 2016-17 is
` 78 crore, which mainly consists of salaries and wages of ` 36.50 crore, VRS of ` 5 crore, interest
of ` 22 crore on GOI loan and establish expenses of ` 11 crore.

22
After implementation of RMDP, NEPA would be able to produce quality paper/newsprint of 100,000
TPA. RMDP completion was targeted in June, 2017 and as such, operations were considered for part
of the year only, with targeted production of 74,250 MT.
During the first year with 9 months operation, company was able to contain the loss to ` 8.60 crore
only, after taking care of interest on GOI loan (salary support) and bank loan and higher depreciation
of RMDP .
Recommendation/Observation
Further, the Committee takes into account the recommendation of the NITI Aayog that the revival
process of NEP A may be permitted to complete and the Company may be reviewed for strategic
disinvestment. Firstly, the Committee disagrees with the dichotomous approach adopted by the NITI
Aayog. It is obvious that the uncertainty regarding the status of the CPSE will dangle above the
Company until a final decision is taken and is certain to affect the morale of the employees. This itself
can impinge the post revival performance of NEPA. At the same time the Committee also feels that,
NEP A can sway the decision on disinvestment, if any, in their favor by coming up with outstanding
performance after revival. The Committee recommends that DHI shall extend all support to NEPA in this
regard. (Para 99)
Action Taken
DHI is taking necessary steps to extend support to NEPA Limited. A proposal for budgetary support
for payment of salary/wages of employees of NEPA Limited is under process. For successful implementation
of RMD, Revised Cost Estimate proposal of NEPA Limited is also under consideration. NEPA will
certainly be motivated to come out with an outstanding performance.
Recommendation/observation
The Committee recommends that the above submissions made by the associations may be appropriately
considered for favourable implementation to the extent possible as creating a facilitating environment
for the private industry to prosper will be decisive in the growth of Capital goods sector in the Country.
The Committee also feels that the Capital Goods Industry should be accorded priority status while
formulating initiatives to improve 'Ease of Doing Business' in the Country. The demands put forth by
the association which does not directly fall under the purview of the Department may be taken up for
inter-ministerial consultation. (Para 102)
Action Taken
The Industry Associations were involved in formulation of the National Capital Goods Policy. The
ongoing Capital Goods Scheme, presently under implementation in the Department of Heavy Industry is
based on the recommendations of the Report of the Working Group on Capital Goods that was constituted
under the aegis of the erstwhile Planning Commission. Industry Associations participate in the Development
Councils for the CG Sub Sectors in a regular manner to air their issues. In other words, DHI actively
involves Industry Associations before planning any policy interventions and take up their issues with
other Ministries like Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Commerce etc. The issues concerning CG Industry,
which include issues raised by the Industry Associations, have been taken up in the Inter Ministerial
Standing Committee for Capital Goods. Meeting and follow up action has been initiated.
Recently Development Council meetings for Machine Tools Industry and Textile Machinery Industry
have been held on 24.05.2017 and 16.05.2017 with active participation of the Industry/Industry Associations.

REPORT
The Industrial sector in India had seen in the recent past many policy interventions by the Government
that include, measures to improve the Ease of Doing Business, Start Up India initiative, Digital India programme,
formulation of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), the introduction of Goods and Services Tax
(GST) and the umbrella promotion of domestic production under the flagship ‘Make in India’ scheme, etc.
There has been invigorated emphasis on infrastructure and tangible inroads have been made in the construction
of highways, railways, power and other infrastructure sectors. Such decisive action has resulted in impetus
to the Heavy Industries sector which broadly encompasses Machines Tools, Heavy Engineering and Electrical,
Industrial and Textile machinery, Earth Moving Equipments & Tractor and Automobile industry.
2. As per the Economic Survey 2017-18, the effect of the efforts of the Government has been reflected
in the fact that the India has leabt 30 ranks over its previous rank of 130 in the World Bank’s latest ‘Doing
Business Report, 2018’. The industry associations like Automotive Component Manufacturers Association
of India (ACMA) and Confederation of Indian Industry (CIl) are also of the opinion that the recent policy
initiatives and infrastructural ventures of the Government along with the allocations made in the Union
Budget, 2018-19 are to become beneficial in the coming days to the various sectors under Heavy Industry.
According to them, policy initiatives like GST, National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), and IBC along
with Non-performing asset (NPA) Ordinance and infrastructure projects like Bharatmala (announced in the
Budget 2018-19) aiming to build highways and roads across the country would have cascading benefits for
various Heavy Industry sub-sectors like earth moving, mining, heavy electric equipment, etc.
Department of Heavy Industry (DHI)
3. The Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises comprises of the two departments i.e. the
Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) and the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE). The allocation of
work of the DHI entails promoting engineering industry viz, machines tools, heavy electrical, industrial
machinery and auto industry and the administration of 31 CPSEs and 5 autonomous organizations. The
Department also caters to the requirements of equipments for basic industries such as steel, mining, non-
ferrous metals, power, fertilizers, refineries, petrochemicals, shipping, paper, cement, sugar, etc. The 5
autonomous organizations under the Department are:-
(i) Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI);
(ii) Fluid Control Research Institute (FCRI)
(iii) NA TRIP Implementation Society (NATIS);
(iv) National Automotive Board (NAB); and
(v) Central Manufacturing Technology Institute (CMTI).

Vision and Mission of DHI
5. According to the official website of DHI, the Vision and Mission statements of DHI are as follows:
Vision
To have Modern, Healthy and Robust Auto, Heavy Engineering, Heavy Electrical and Capital
Goods Sectors and Self-reliant and Growth Oriented Public-Sector Undertakings under the
Department.
Mission
/circle6The Department of Heavy Industry strives to bolster profit making PSEs as well as restructure
and revive sick and loss-making PSEs under its administrative control.
/circle6The DHI seeks to achieve its vision of global automotive excellence through creation of state-
of-the-art Research and Testing infrastructure through the National Automotive Testing and R&D
Infrastructure Project (NATRIP).
/circle6The DHI seeks to achieve its vision by providing necessary support to the Auto, Heavy Engineering,
Heavy Electrical and Capital Goods Sector.
6. Regarding the operating CPSEs, under the administrative control of Department of Heavy
Industry, the Committee notices that their number has begun to dwindle since 2016-17. From a
total of 31 in 2016-17, they have come down to 24 in 2017-18 and currently the number of operating
CPSEs under DHI have been reduced to 22. According to the data submitted by DPE before the
Committee, amongst the Ministries/Departments of Government of India it is DHI that has seen
the largest attrition rate of CPSEs - 10 that have been approved for closure and 6 that have been
approved for strategic disinvestment.
7. In this regard, the Committee takes into cognisance the fact that depending on the NITI
Aayog’s classification of ‘High Priority’ areas for Government Ownership, CPSEs which are in
profit or those that can very well be revived/restructured can also be strategically disinvested/
closed, if they do not fall under the priority areas. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that
DHI should start classifying CPSEs under it, in tune with the ‘High Priority’ areas identified for
Government ownership. Such classification would help the Department focus its attention and funds
on CPSEs that would be identified for retention under Government ownership as per extant policy.
In the opinion of the Committee, this would in turn give more meaning to the Department’s Mission
and Vision statements.
8. Also, the Committee is of the opinion that it would be prudent for DHI to study the goods/
services offered by the CPSEs intended/identified for closure or strategic disinvestment and
understand the manner in which the void likely to be created in the market due to the absence of
Government ownership of these CPSEs is going to get filled. If such demands are proposed to be
met by imports, including cheap second-hand machinery/goods, rather than by domestic production,
then it must be assumed that the closure/strategic disinvestment would be antithetical to national
priority of promoting domestic production and ‘Make in India’ initiative and would be a matter of
great worry. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Department should commission a
research study to find reasons as to why they are losing CPSEs dealing with goods/services under

4
the Heavy Industries Sector. The study should also focus on the market demand currently being
met by these CPSEs and how the said demand would be met in case of their closure/strategic
disinvestment.
Demand for Grants (DFG) 2018-19
9. From the year 2017-18, the Annual Financial Statement is being presented to the Parliament on 1st
February, in a departure from the past practice of presenting the same on 28th February. The Committee
sought the tangible benefits that have accrued by taking this step from the point of view of DHI. In this
regard, it was submitted that on account of the presentation of Annual Financial Statement to the Parliament
on 1st February instead of on 28th February, there was no requirement for ‘Vote on account’ for incurring
the expenditure for the first two months of the financial year. Now, a single Appropriation Bill would be
presented to Parliament for the expenditure of the Government for the full year. Further, any expenditure on
new schemes/projects included in the Budget, can be made right from the commencement of the financial
year as compared to the earlier position wherein no expenditure could be made during the first two months
of the financial year i.e. during the period of operation of’ V ote on account’.

11. While examining the Demand for Grants (2018-19) for DHI, the Committee observed that the budgetary
allocation for the Department under the Revenue Expenditure for the last five years has gone up from ` 221
crore (RE) to ` 801 crore (RE) and the Capital Expenditure, during the same period, had gone down from
` 1034 crore (RE) to ` 306 crore (RE). The Committee further observed that the increase in Revenue
Expenditure (which is considered to be non-productive) and decrease in Capital Expenditure (which is
considered to be used for asset cteation) was not a healthy financial trend. In this regard, Secretary, DHI
while agreeing that there is a general perception that Revenue Expenditure is not productive expenditure
stated that the schemes under DHI have both Revenue and Capital Expenditure. Further clarifying this, he
submitted that when a subsidy is given under a scheme, in the long run, it was considered as productive
expenditure because its end result is productive. Because of this, the expenditure on the schemes of
Department of Heavy Industry cannot be classified in the closed compartments of ‘productive’ and
‘unproductive’.

significant fluctuation between the Budget Estimates (BE) and Revised Estimates (RE) figures of the Capital
Expenditure. During 2015-16, the BE under Capital Expenditure of ` 1349 crore went down to ` 664 crore
at RE. In 2016-17, the BE for Capital Expenditure was ` 907 crore and it swelled up to ` 2354 crore at RE.
Again in 2017-18, ` 1615 crore BE went down to ` 306 crore during RE under Capital Expenditure. But the
actual utilisation of the said Revised Estimates under Capital Expenditure during all these years has almost
been complete.
13. In this regard, the Committee would like to suggest that such a wide gap between Revenue
and Capital Expenditure under Revised Estimates (RE) in the Budget allocations of DHI does not
paint an ideal financial picture and needed to be looked at with a holistic/balanced approach. From
the submission of the Department, the Committee infers that huge fluctuation in the Budget
Estimates (BE) and Revised Estimates (RE) in terms of Capital Expenditure figures is broadly due
to delays in approval for the anticipated closure/restructuring packages of CPSEs. Such unforeseen
delays in approval take out large amount of funds at Revised Estimates (RE) stage. This, combined
with the Revised Estimates ceiling prescribed by Ministry of Finance based on pace of expenditure,
which is applicable to the entire Budget allocations, affects the key projects like NA TRiP, FAME-
India, AUSC, etc. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that DHI should initiate appropriate
action and avoid such vast fluctuations between BE and RE allocations in future in consultation with
the Ministry of Finance (MoF).
Automobile Industry of India
14. Automobile Industry was delicensed in July 1991 with the announcement of the New Industrial
Policy, whereas, the passenger car got delicensed only in 1993. The norms for foreign investment and
import of technology have also been progressively liberalized over the years for vehicles manufacturers
to make this sector globally competitive. At present, 100% Foreign Direct Investment (FOI) is permissible
under automatic route in this sector including passenger car segment. The auto-industry is a key employment
generator, in which the Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) manufactures the vehicles, the inbound
auto component and logistics industry makes and delivers component and systems and the outbound
logistics and dealer network sells, maintains and distributes the vehicles. Every vehicle produced, generates
secondary and tertiary employment. The industry generates employment of 13 persons for each truck, 6
persons for each car and 4 persons for each three-wheeler and 1 person for two-wheelers. As such the
sector has multiplier effect on economic activity. If the industry produces as per its potential, it could
support employment of over 65 million people by 2026. The Government, recognizing the importance of
the automobile industry in the Indian economy, is currently working with targets set in the Automotive
Mission Plan 2016-26. The DHI is also developing an automotive policy for holistic development of the
sector in India.

vehicles, three wheelers and two wheelers in April-September, 2017 against 13.4 million in April- September,
2016 (% of growth rate is 9.18%). In April-September 2017, overall automobile exports were 1.95 million,
against the same period i.e. April-September 2016 of 1.76 million (% of growth rate is 10.71%).

(ii) Scheme for Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid and) Electric Vehicle in India —
FAME - India
26. As part of the National Mission on Electric Mobility Plan 2020 (NEMMP), DHI formulated a scheme
namely,. FAME-India, to promote hybrid/electric technology in transportation to reduce dependency on
fossil fuel. The scheme was proposed to be implemented over a period of 6 years, till 2020, wherein it is
intended to support the hybrid/electric vehicles, market development and its manufacturing eco-system to
achieve self-sustenance at the end of the stipulated period. At present, the Phase-I of the scheme is under
implementation, which was originally for a period of 2 years commencing from l “ April 2015 i.e. FY 2015-
16 and FY 2016-17 and has since been extended now till 31st March 2018. As per the original scheme, Mild
hybrid, Strong Hybrid, Plug-in Hybrid and Pure Electric technologies (collectively termed as xEV) were
covered in the Scheme. However, “Mild Hybrid” technology has been excluded from the Scheme w.e.f.
01/04/2017.
27. The scheme has four focus areas i.e. Technology Development, Demand Creation, Pilot Project and
Charging Infrastructure. Market creation through demand incentives is aimed at incentivizing all vehicle
segments i.e. 2- Wheelers, 3- Wheelers, Passenger 4- Wheeler vehicles, Light Commercial Vehicles and
Buses. The scheme, lays emphasis on providing affordable and environmentally friendly public and private
transportation/vehicular mobility for the masses. The demand incentive was available to buyers (end users/
consumers) in the form of an upfront reduced purchase price to enable wider adoption. The demand incentive
amount has been determined for each category (vehicle - technology - battery type) considering the principles
of Total Cost of Ownership (TCO), Pay-back Period on account of fuel savings, cost of maintenance, etc.
Specific projects under Pilot Projects, R&D/Technology Development and Public Charging Infrastructure
components are approved by the Project Implementation & Sanctioning Committee (PISC), under the
chairmanship of Secretary (Heavy Industry), for extending grant under the different focus areas of the
scheme.

34. As part of the examination of the Demands of DHI for 2018-19, the Committee heard Auto Component
Manufacturers’ Association of India (ACMA) who flagged certain concerns relating to the Government’s
push for transformation from the existing Internal Combustion Powertrains to Electrical Mobility. The
concerns broadly include lack of clear roadmap from Government or the OEMs, non-availability of key
technologies for e-mobility in key components like batteries/motors/power-train, with Indian manufacturers,
etc. Further, as per the Association the hasty transformation to pure electrical vehicles could result in
significant (over 50%) of component industry getting wiped out, huge loss in jobs, total dependence on
import for key technologies and components. Accordingly, ACMA had requested through the medium of the
Committee that the Government consider only gradual adoption of electric vehicles, thereby promoting
electrification of powertrains, rather than an abrupt shift to only pure EVs. With such an approach, the end
objective of EV deployment can be achieved in a gradual manner without impacting jobs, investments and
growth of the industry. To improve the FAME -India scheme, suggestions were made to broaden its scope
to include funding/grants for xEV component development and R&D along with development of components
for Charging Infrastructure.
35. During the oral evidence of DHI, as part of the examination of their Demands 2018-19, the concerns,
of the Auto Associations regarding the sudden transformation to EV s was sounded to them by the Committee,
Addressing the concern, Secretary, Department of Heavy Industry, replied that the Department has formulated
a proactive new Automobile Policy Document to deal with the problems faced by the auto industry. This
document would act as single mouthpiece to spell out the policies/decisions of various departments/agencies
of the Government having an impact on the Automobile industry. A road map regarding the transformation
to EV technology till the year 2028 would be handed over to the industry 10 years in advance, so that the
transformation could be made smooth. This document, according to DHI, is currently open to stakeholder’s
suggestions. Further, the proposed Automobile Policy Document would leave it to the consumer to decide
whether he opts for Hybrid, Electric or Bharat VI emission compliant vehicle.
36. The Committee understands that the gradual transition to pure EVs is an inevitability
considering the limited fossil fuel reserves and heightened environmental concerns. However, it
has been felt that the path of transformation needs a lot of coordinated and well thought out planning
on the part of the Government, with the partnership of the Auto Industry. A synchronized platform
involving the relevant Ministries and other stakeholders need to be set up for policy formulation
and implementation. Further, the Committee perceives that EV penetration in the Country would
critically depend on the development of indigenous battery technology and the creation/setting up
of charging infrastructure dovetailed by appropriate charging technology. Also, the Committee is of
the considered opinion that the economic ramification of transformation to pure EV technology has
to be given priority by the Government, taking into account the fact that any laxity in proper
planning and implementation could affect millions of jobs in the auto sector. Such an impact on jobs
would be unaffordable to the economy of a developing country like India. The Department should
make concerted efforts in planning a roadmap to re-deploy the emplo yees in the conventional Auto
Sector, who would be displaced with the change over to electric mobility.
37. Taking all of the above into account, the Committee recommends that the Government should
come up with a well spelt out road map based on empirical studies before pushing hard for change
over to pure EV technology. In the opinion of the Committee, gradual shift, taking the route of
promoting appropriate hybrid technology, could be one of the adoptable methods in this direction.

13
The FAME- India scheme under DHI is an ideal vehicle which could be widened in scope and magnitude
to accommodate the challenging needs of the Country’s gradual shift to the Electric Mobility. The
Committee is well aware that the stakes are high for the Country in terms of the environmental
benefit the changeover can offer and also in terms of the weaning away from import dependence on
fossil fuels.

51. The Committee sought clarifications regarding the reasons behind the below par progress of projects
and delay in receipts of pro-rata industry contributions to the project. Also, the Committee wanted to know
whether this scenario pointed to the Scheme losing its effectiveness and the steps taken by the Department
to resolve the same. In response thereto, DHI informed that the scheme was launched in the financial year
2014-15 with a financial allocation of ` 581.22 crore (including administrative expenditure of ` 7.26 crore)
over a period of five years extending up to November, 2019. Till now, projects worth `572.22 crore have
already been approved by the Competent Authority under the various components of the Scheme.

18
52. Regarding the effectiveness of the scheme, it was submitted that the Department had received large
number of project proposals under the components of the Scheme which were scrutinized in detail and
thereafter, examined by Screening Committee, set up for examination and recommending the proposals for
the approval of the Apex Committee. The project proposals worth `246.64 crore were approved by the
Apex Committee in the financial year, 2017-18. Further, all the on-going projects are being constantly
reviewed and monitored through well-structured Project Review and Monitoring Committees constituted,
separately. for all the projects. Most of the projects are taking good shape as per the physical and technical
milestones drawn in the MoUs for the respective projects. Accordingly, as per the Department, the Scheme
is very much effective as the number of approved projects would lead to almost full utilization of the funds
allocated for the Scheme and most of the projects are well on course for achieving their targets. In addition,
many proposals are in the pipeline and are expected to be considered on approval of additional funds for the
scheme.
53. Further, the Committee wanted to know the reasons for no Test Centres being approved under the
Scheme till now, as envisaged under its objectives. In response, the Department explained that a Test and
Certification Centre for Earth Moving Machinery had been proposed to be set up through a Special Purpose
V ehicle (SPV) with a cost of ` 100 crore to be funded by DHI. Setting up of such Test and Certification
Centre was under active consideration of the Department and the Automotive Research Association of India
(ARAI) had been requested to work in collaboration with Indian Construction Equipment Manufacturers
Association (ICEMA) in preparing a Detailed Project and Implementation Report (DPIR) for setting up of
the Construction, Earthmoving, Material Handling and Mining Machinery (CEMM) Equipment Test Centre
in the Country .
54. About the need of Test Centre, the Committee also noted the submission made by the CII that one of
the major problems faced by the CGS in the country was the lack of defined product standards which could
prevent our Capital Sector from going global. Setting up common testing centres/certification centres would
be primal to the process of defining the missing standards. The Confederation was, accordingly, in favour
of increasing the budgetary support for setting up common testing centres/facilities for the Capital Goods
produced in the country.
55. The Committee has an unequivocal and firm opinion about the cardinal role the Capital Goods
Sector of the country can play in improving the economy of India. The opinion is same about the
prospects of the Scheme for Enhancement of Competitiveness’s contributions to the Government’s
‘Make in India’ initiatives. While analysing the progress of the scheme, the Committee finds that
the money allocated for the scheme saw a reduction for first time, since its inception, at Revised
Estimates stage in 2017-18. The reasons quoted by the Department for this curtailment was the
delay in receipt of pro-rata industry contribution for the project in few cases and slow pace of
progress of the project. The Committee sought further clarification on the above reasons and their
impact on the effectiveness of the scheme.
56. In reply, the Department assured the Committee on the progress of the projects under the
scheme and stated that projects worth ` 246.64 crore have been approved by the Competent Authority
for the year 2017-18. But, the Committee notices that even though project proposals worth of
` 246.64 crore was approved, the allocated fund at Budget Estimates stage for the year was only
` 150.00 crore, which was again curtailed to ` 110 crore at Revised Estimates stage. Though the
Department has submitted that the progress of the projects under the scheme is satisfactory, the

19
Committee does not find that entirely convincing based on the figures shown above. Curtailment at
RE stage usually happens when the utilization of funds is not up to the expected level. Hence, it
would not be out of the place to suspect that the progress of projects under the scheme were not up
to the mark. Taking into consideration the number of approved proposals, the Committee observes
that there is no dearth of projects under the scheme, while the problem seems to be with the pace
of implementation and the fund availability. Therefore, taking into consideration the benefits that
proper implementation of the scheme can bring to the nation; the Committee recommends that the
DHI should work on both, implementation of its ongoing projects as well as to secure required funds
from the Ministry of Finance (MoF). Here, the Committee would like to mention that the Department
while answering to the queries of the Committee chose to remain silent on the reasons behind
delayed receipts of pro-rata industry contributions.
57. Regarding the setting up of Test and Certification Centre, the Committee observes that despite
being in the fourth year of the implementation of the scheme, the Department is yet to finalize the
DPIR of its first Certification Centre which is expected to cost ` 100 crore. Considering the fact
that the total financial allocation of the scheme for five years is ` 581.22 crore and projects worth
` 572.22 crore have already been approved, the Committee hopes that the Department would be
able to secure the required fund for the setting up of the proposed Test Centre. Based on the
submissions made before the Committee that, Common Testing Centres/Certification Centres are
the need of the hour, the Committee recommends that the Department should work more on
setting up such centres and should try and seek more fund from M/o Finance to rectify this lacuna
which otherwise can hinder the growth oflndia’s Capital Goods Sector.

purposes and assisting technological growth in the country. The Institute is equipped with trained manpower,

industries including machine tools and the programmes and projects executed in CMTI pertained to issues/
subjects for which mandate has been given to DHI. The transfer of CMTI would enable strengthening of

should be allocated budgetary support to strengthen its core R&D activities that could enhance

CPSEs in India
74. The era of industrialization and resultant nation building of post independent India was pioneered by
CPSEs. However, subsequent to economic liberalization, they were being looked at through the prism of the
requirements of the new market driven economy. The latest Public Enterprises Survey states that the CPSEs
had contributed 38.63% more to the Central Exchequer in 2015-16 compared to the year before. This
indicates the continuing economic relevance of CPSEs to the nation. Further, during the recent past, the
CAPEX (investment) employed in the country had been mainly by the CPSEs in comparison to the private
companies. The CAPEX investment directly aids infrastructure building of the country. Power, roads and
highways, railways, defence, petroleum mining, public health, social security, education, agriculture, etc.
still remain areas where public investments are critical. Besides this, the promotion of R&D and innovation,
balanced regional development, Make in India initiatives, etc. are also zones where CPSEs can still play
decisive roles.

76. As part of its examination of Demands 2018-19 of DHI, the Committee desired to know whether
DHI’s support to its CPSEs would depend upon the area of operation of CPSEs despite them being profit
making or loss incurring. In reply, it was submitted by DHI that the Department had been undertaking
appraisals of performance of each CPSE under its administrative control to assess its prospects and had
been taking appropriate course of action in respective cases. As a follow up of this exercise, revival effort
was made wherever possible and those assessed to be chronically sick were processed for closure as per
extant guidelines and procedure.
77. The DHI also stated that the NITI Aayog had been entrusted with the responsibility to critically review
the performance of CPSEs and give their recommendations on their future. NITI Aayog takes a holistic
view of all relevant factors viz. the sectors in which the CPSE operates, product profile, its financial and
physical performance over the years, prospects, manpower, economic environment of business, etc.
Subsequently, NITI Aayog had classified certain CPSEs as “high priority” for Government ownership if
they fit any of the following criteria:
(a) National Security: Certain CPSEs serve such national security purposes that the Government
may like to retain direct control over them. CPSEs that are performing critical functions related
to production of defence equipment or nuclear power production fall under this category. NITI
Aayog was of the view that since the defence sector has now been opened to the private sector,
this category should not include CPSEs that are producing tools that may be going into production
of defence equipment.
(b) Sovereign function at arm’s length: Certain CPSEs serve sovereign or quasi-sovereign
functions so that it just happens to be an arm’s length body performing a function that would
otherwise be performed by the Government directly. CPSEs that are in control of the natural
resources that are low on tradability, CPSEs that enjoy specific concessions from the Government
to undertake exploration to secure the country’s energy security/future, CPSEs that perform
Government functions such as minimum prices support, and CPSEs that manage core
infrastructure (airports, railway tracks) may fall under this criterion.
(c) Markets Imperfections and Public Purpose: Some of the CPSEs perform developmental
functions that the Government may consider important, but where the private sector is either
not present or is failing to perform. CPSEs catering exclusively to certain sectors, regions or
populations group with an explicit developmental mandate fall under this category. Such CPSEs
cannot be sold because they are not meant to be purely commercial in nature.
After considering the above criteria, NITI Aayog recommended the closure of some chronically sick
CPSEs under DHI and transfer of some CPSEs to the State Government concerned. They also recommended
strategic disinvestment or merger of some profit making CPSEs. However, the final decision on closure or
disinvestment was taken by the Cabinet/CCEA after detailed study and due consultations with Ministries/
Departments concerned in the larger public interest.

(i) Hindustan Paper Corporation (RPC)
81. HPC was incorporated on 29.05.1970 with the objective of establishing pulp and paper/newsprint
production in the country to make paper available for mass consumption. HPC has two units Nagaon Paper
Mill (NPM) and Cachar Paper Mill (CPM) and subsidiaries, namely, Hindustan Newsprints Limited (HNL)
and Nagaland Pulp and Paper Corporation (NPPC). The first unit of HPC, NPM, was commissioned in
October, 1985 and the second unit CPM came into operation in April, 1988. These two units are the only
100% bamboo-based paper mills in India.
82. HPC was a profit-making company earlier and had been performing reasonably well till the year
2008-09. But thereafter, the Committee had been made to understand that its capacity utilization started
declining due to various external factors beyond the control of the management. The downtrend in performance
started from the year 2009-10 mainly due to shortage of bamboo on account of large scale severe gregarious
flowering of bamboo in NER and also due to a subsequent embargo by Mizoram Government on supply of
bamboo outside Mizoram. As a result, capacity utilization of CPM Unit had been hovering around 50%.
Later, when bamboo availability normalised and HPC was set to recover, the National Green Tribunal (NGT)
put a blanket ban on mining and transportation of coal in the State of Meghalaya w.e.f. May, 2014 from
where CPM and NPM had been sourcing 100% and 60% of their coal requirements respectively since
decades and therefore, again recovery process derailed. This fluctuating capacity utilization, continued load
of salary and wages and fixed expenses has had a cascading effect on overall working of the Corporation
and it has pushed up all the associated costs resulting in HPC posting losses and leading to erosion of
working capital of the company. A proposal for revival of HPC is under consideration.

The project cost which was approved at ` 285 crore has got escalated to ` 434 crore (net of EPCG

Economic Feasibility Report (TEFR), formulated in 2010. It will be anybody’s guess that approval of
a cost estimation made in 2010, as such in 2014, plagued by further implementation delay, would
only result in further conundrum for the Company. This is exactly where NEPA finds itself today.

materializing from the banks, for which the banks were insisting on Government guarantee, the
execution of RMDP would remain incomplete. Now, the revised cost estimate is  ` 434 crore and the
process for securing an approval for this amount from the competent authority is underway. The
progress made towards securing loan, with or without Government guarantee, has not been furnished
to the Committee. Further, the Committee is aware of the recommendation of NITI Aayog with
respect to NEP A which is that the revival process of NEPA may be permitted to complete and then
the Company may be reviewed for strategic disinvestment. The Committee is of the view that if the
current state of affairs is allowed to prevail, the revival of NEPA might remain a mirage. Accordingly,
the Committee recommends that DHI should come up with proactive and fast-tracked measures,
with accelerated inter-departmental coordination, if deemed required, to revive/restructure NEPA,
taking every care to avoid any further delay. It is further recommended that the decision whether
or not to provide Government guarantee for obtaining the bank loan portion of the funds for
executing the RMDP should also not be procrastinated any further because clarity in this regard
will give a better assessment of the availability and sources of funds for the revival of NEPA .
(v) Hindustan Cables Ltd. (HCL)
103. HCL was set up in 1952 as the first telecommunication cable manufacturing unit in the country. The
Company has units in Rupnarainpur (West Bengal), Hyderabad (Andhra Pradesh) and Naini (Allahabad)
(UP). HCL became sick and was referred to BIFR since 2002. Further, its production activities had been
suspended since 2003. As per the recommendation of the BRPSE, various proposals for Joint V enture with
HCL and takeover of HCL had been examined. CCEA in its meeting dated 29.12.2014 approved closure of
the company by offering VRS/VSS at 2007 national pay scales. On 28.09.2016, as per the direction of
Union Cabinet, action pertaining to closure of Company had been undertaken in terms of guidelines issued
by DPE.
104. During the presentation in connection with examination of the DFG-2018-19, the Secretary,
DHI has stated that land assets of HCL at Hyderabad and Asansol are slated to be disposed off as per
guidelines framed by DPE. The Secretary also informed the first round of bidding process had been
completed recently, in which few Government Department had taken part, A final decision is yet to
be taken as to whom the landed assets of HCL is to be disposed off, The Committee had time and
again observed that land assets of CPSEs decided for closure should be given to Government
Department for better utility of the same. The Committee accordingly desires that DHI may in
collaboration with the authorities concerned ensure that land assets of RCL may go to proper hands
so that the larger interests of society is served.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
1. Regarding the operating CPSEs, under the administrative control of Department of Heavy
Industry, the Committee notices that their number has begun to dwindle since 2016-17. From a
total of 31 in 2016-17, they have come down to 24 in 2017-18 and currently the number of operating
CPSEs under DHI have been reduced to 22. According to the data submitted by DPE before the
Committee, amongst the Ministries/Departments of Government of India it is DHI that has seen
the largest attrition rate of CPSEs - 10 that have been approved for closure and 6 that have been
approved for strategic disinvestment. (Para No. 6)
2. In this regard, the Committee takes into cognisance the fact that depending on the NITI
Aayog’s classification of ‘High Priority’ areas for Government Ownership, CPSEs which are in
profit or those that can very well be revived/restructured can also be strategically disinvested/
closed, if they do not fall under the priority areas. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that
DHI should start classifying CPSEs under it, in tune with the ‘High Priority’ areas identified for
Government ownership. Such classification would help the Department focus its attention and funds
on CPSEs that would be identified for retention under Government ownership as per extant policy.
In the opinion of the Committee, this would in turn give more meaning to the Department’s Mission
and Vision statements. (Para No. 7)
3. Also, the Committee is of the opinion that it would be prudent for DHI to study the goods/
services offered by the CPSEs intended/identified for closure or strategic disinvestment and
understand the manner in which the void likely to be created in the market due to the absence of
Government ownership of these CPSEs is going to get filled. If such demands are proposed to be
met by imports, including cheap second-hand machinery/goods, rather than by domestic production,
then it must be assumed that the closure/strategic disinvestment would be antithetical to national
priority of promoting domestic production and ‘Make in India’ initiative and would be a matter of
great worry. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Department should commission a
research study to find reasons as to why they are losing CPSEs dealing with goods/services under
the Heavy Industries Sector. The study should also focus on the market demand currently being
met by these CPSEs and how the said demand would be met in case of their closure/strategic
disinvestment. (Para No. 8)
4. In this regard, the Committee would like to suggest that such a wide gap between Revenue
and Capital Expenditure under Revised Estimates (RE) in the Budget allocations of DHI does not
paint an ideal financial picture and needed to be looked at with a holistic/balanced approach. From
the submission of the Department, the Committee infers that huge fluctuation in the Budget
Estimates (BE) and Revised Estimates (RE) in terms of Capital Expenditure figures is broadly due
to delays in approval for the anticipated closure/restructuring packages of CPSEs. Such unforeseen
delays in approval take out large amount of funds at Revised Estimates (RE) stage. This, combined
with the Revised Estimates ceiling prescribed by Ministry of Finance based on pace of expenditure,
which is applicable to the entire Budget allocations, affects the key projects like NA TRiP, FAME-
India, AUSC, etc. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that DHI should initiate appropriate
action and avoid such vast fluctuations between BE and RE allocations in future in consultation with
the Ministry of Finance (MoF). (Para No. 13)

5. Regar ding the report of the C&AG on the performance audit of NATRiP, the
Committee desires that it be furnished with the findings thereof as and when the Report
is available. (Para No. 24)
6. Further, while analyzing the fund allocation and utilization under NATRiP in 2016-17 and
2017-18, the Committee noted that in 2016-17 the fund has been completely utilized and for the
current financial year, the utilization is 89% of RE by the end of January, 2018. Likewise, the
Committee hopes that for the year, 2018-19, the Department would take appropriate measures to
utilize the fund allocated effectively as per their submission made before the Committee. Here, the
Committee also takes into account the submission of the Department that during 2017-18 they
faced certain legal road blocks mainly due to delinquent contractors. It was also seen that the slow
take off at certain facilities is due to hitches in the bidding process. However, since most of the
facilities have now surpassed the legal problems and troubled bidding process, the Committee expects
that there shall not be any further delays in the future and the scheduled completion time of July,
2019 would be adhered to. It is for DHI to ensure this, by providing timely interventions to avoid
such roadblocks in future. (Para No. 25)
7. The Committee notes that during 2017-18, the FAME-India scheme got a hiked RE of ` 235
crore compared to the BE of ` 175 crore. Regarding the utilization of this enhanced funds, DHI has
informed that the funds would be utilized for the committed liabilities as well as for funding the
Pilot Project of Public and Shared Transpor tation involving 11 cities. However, the Committee finds
that till January, 2018, the expenditure under  the scheme along with said liabilities, amount to `
144.66 crore. That is, the utilisation during 2017-18 till date is only around 60% and has not even
reached the mark of ` 175 crore (BE). This leaves the Department with only two months in the
current FY to utilize the rest of the allocation of ` 89.34 crore. The Committee expects that maximum
funds would be efficiently utilized within the time left and in consonance with the Expenditure
Management Rules stipulated by the Ministry of Finance. The Committee also desires that for the
future, adequate, care should be taken while conceptualising a scheme initially instead of resorting
to mid-course re-conceptualising. (Para No. 33)
8. The Committee understands that the gradual transition to pure EVs is an inevitability
considering the limited fossil fuel reserves and heightened environmental concerns. However, it
has been felt that the path of transformation needs a lot of coordinated and well thought out planning
on the part of the Government, with the partnership of the Auto Industry. A synchronized platform
involving the relevant Ministries and other stakeholders need to be set up for policy formulation
and implementation. Further, the Committee perceives that EV penetration in the Country would
critically depend on the development of indigenous battery technology and the creation/setting up
of charging infrastructure dovetailed by appropriate charging technology. Also, the Committee is of
the considered opinion that the economic ramification of transformation to pure EV technology has
to be given priority by the Government, taking into account the fact that any laxity in proper
planning and implementation could affect millions of jobs in the auto sector. Such an impact on jobs
would be unaffordable to the economy of a developing country like India. The Department should
make concerted efforts in planning a roadmap to re-deploy the emplo yees in the conventional Auto
Sector, who would be displaced with the change over to electric mobility. (Para No. 36)
9. Taking all of the above into account, the Committee recommends that the Government should

39
come up with a well spelt out road map based on empirical studies before pushing hard for change
over to pure EV technology. In the opinion of the Committee, gradual shift, taking the route of
promoting appropriate hybrid technology, could be one of the adoptable methods in this direction.
The FAME- India scheme under DHI is an ideal vehicle which could be widened in scope and magnitude
to accommodate the challenging needs of the Country’s gradual shift to the Electric Mobility. The
Committee is well aware that the stakes are high for the Country in terms of the environmental
benefit the changeover can offer and also in terms of the weaning away from import dependence on
fossil fuels. (Para No. 37)
10. The Committee notices that DCCAI has been entrusted with the function of hand holding
R&D proposals in the Automobile Sector. The source of  funds for the Council till now was the Auto
Cess collected during the sale of automobiles. Going through the utilization of funds by the Council
in the recent past, the Committee finds that the utilization of funds has been below par. The same
fact was pointed out by the Committee during the last year as well. The noncommittal reply of the
Department regarding the specific action taken/proposed by them to increase the fund utilization
under DCAAI for R&D gives the Committee an indication that little has been done in this
regard. (Para No. 43)
11. The Committee also discerns the fact that Auto Cess has been subsumed after the coming
into effect of GST. That puts a stop to the hitherto available source of funds to the Council. In this
regard, the Committee takes note of the Department’s decision to seek the continuance of the
support to the ongoing projects through DCAAI by way of Budgetary Support. Pertinently, the
Committee is also aware of the need of assistance to R&D initiatives in the auto sector which is
slated for huge transformation in the wake of changing mode of mobility. Therefore, the Committee
recommends that the functions of R&D support extended by DCAAI should be continued, despite
the end of Auto Cess, as the same is one of the better avenues for R&D initiatives, alongwith other
proposed funding like Venture Capital Funding. (Para No. 44)
12. The Committee has an unequivocal and firm opinion about the cardinal role the Capital Goods
Sector of the country can play in improving the economy of India. The opinion is same about the
prospects of the Scheme for Enhancement of Competitiveness’s contributions to the Government’s
‘Make in India’ initiatives. While analysing the progress of the scheme, the Committee finds that
the money allocated for the scheme saw a reduction for first time, since its inception, at Revised
Estimates stage in 2017-18. The reasons quoted by the Department for this curtailment was the
delay in receipt of pro-rata industry contribution for the project in few cases and slow pace of progress
of the project. The Committee sought further clarification on the above reasons and their impact on
the effectiveness of the scheme.
(Para No. 55)
13. In reply, the Department assured the Committee on the progress of the projects under the
scheme and stated that projects worth ` 246.64 crore have been approved by the Competent Authority
for the year 2017-18. But, the Committee notices that even though project proposals worth of `
246.64 crore was approved, the allocated fund at Budget Estimates stage for the year was only `
150.00 crore, which was again curtailed to ` 110 crore at Revised Estimates stage. Though the
Department has submitted that the progress of the projects under the scheme is satisfactory, the
Committee does not find that entirely convincing based on the figures shown above. Curtailment at
RE stage usually happens when the utilization of funds is not up to the expected level. Hence, it

40
would not be out of the place to suspect that the progress of projects under the scheme were not up
to the mark. Taking into consideration the number of approved proposals, the Committee observes
that there is no dearth of projects under the scheme, while the problem seems to be with the pace
of implementation and the fund availability. Therefore, taking into consideration the benefits that
proper implementation of the scheme can bring to the nation; the Committee recommends that the
DHI should work on both, implementation of its ongoing projects as well as to secure required funds
from the Ministry of Finance (MoF). Here, the Committee would like to mention that the Department
while answering to the queries of the Committee chose to remain silent on the reasons behind
delayed receipts of pro-rata industry contributions.
(Para No. 56)
14. Regarding the setting up of Test and Certification Centre, the Committee observes that despite

able to secure the required fund for the setting up of the proposed Test Centre. Based on the
submissions made before the Committee that, Common Testing Centres/Certification Centres are
the need of the hour, the Committee recommends that the Department should work more on
setting up such centres and should try and seek more fund from M/o Finance to rectify this lacuna

15. The Committee finds that the funds for AUSC project during the first year i.e. 2017-18, of
` 121.00 crore (Budget Estimates) as approved by Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA)
was curtailed to ` 90 crore at the Revised Estimates stage. The initial query of the Committee
regarding the reasons for this yielded an answer that the reduction in funds was due to a Revised
Estimates ceiling imposed by MoF. However, on further  enquiry it was revealed that the Revised
Estimates (RE) ceiling had been prescribed purely based on the pace of expenditure which has been
really slack in the case of AUSC as well as other projects/schemes under DHI. So, it turns out that
lack of proper progress in AUSC project execution had resulted in funds being taken away at Revised
Estimates stage during 2017-18.
(Para No. 67)
16. For the year 2018-19, the allocation for AUSC is only ` 100 crore whereas the CCEA approved
fund for the year is ` 608 crore. Such humongous difference in the planned expenditure and the
Actual allocation compels the Committee to presume that there are enough reasons to be
apprehensive about the progress of the Mission Mode project as pace of the project execution decides
the fund allocation. Going as per the figures approved by the CCEA, till now, the fund allocation of
the project should have been ` 729.00 crore whereas the actual allocation is ` 90 crore (Revised
Estimates, 2017-18) and ` 100 crore (Budget Estimates, 2018-19) totalling to only ` 190 crore. The
Committee also takes note of the fact that the Department is confident of meeting the timeline of
the project as submitted by them. (Para No. 68)
17. Taking the above situation into account, the Committee cannot but express its displeasure at
this juncture about the way the Mission Mode AUSC supervised by the Principal Scientific Advisor
to the Government of India is progressing. The Committee accordingly recommends that DHI, as
the primary contributor to the project, should take appropriate measures to improve the pace of the
implementation of the project in coordination with other stakeholders.

areas of operation like in the spheres of national security, sovereign functions at arms length like

support from the part of the Government. Besides, by their own Mission statement, the Department
has a mandate to provide necessary support to CPSEs in order to improve their overall performance

(Para No. 80)

recommendation of Dr. Saraswat Committee which had favoured the revival of HEC by approving

REPORT
In the early 1950s, India had only five CPSEs with an investment of around ` 29 crore. Today,
the country has 320 CPSEs with ` 11, 71,844 crore cumulative investment. CPSEs were the harbingers
of industrial development, indigenisation and self reliance in India. They have played an unimpeachable
role in building infrastructure, capital intensive industries, national security, public services, etc. at an
affordable rate. The Public Sector Companies balanced social development along with economic prosperity
and brought in employment on a large scale. When the era of globalization dawned and the initial phase
of nation building was over, the Government of the day took a call to liberalize Indian Economy.
Accordingly, the New Industrial Policy, 1991 came about and it revealed the lack of market competitiveness
and inefficiency of our CPSEs in comparison to the private sector. To adapt to the new economic order,
the CPSEs underwent extensive disinvestment of Government equity, downsizing/retrenchment and other
measures of organizational recalibration. Redundant CPSEs were closed down and, now, specific areas
have been identified as "High Priority Area" for the Government to remain in business. Currently, even
profit making CPSEs face disinvestment if they do not"fall in the areas of business so identified.
However, despite extensive privatization in many areas, Government companies remain significant. There
are still many areas that have to be controlled by the Government in a country like India - basic
infrastructures like road transport and railways, electricity, banking, material recourses extraction, defence,
aerospace, shipbuilding, etc. are some. Further, promotion of R&D and innovations, delivery of public
goods and services, Make in India initiatives, balanced regional development and social security also
remain key areas for CPSEs to deliver, in the Indian context.
CPSEs in India
2. There were 320 Central Public Sector Enterprises under the administrative control of various
Ministries/Departments as on 31.3.2016. Out of these 320 CPSEs, 244 are in operation and 76 CPSEs
have yet to commence business. Further, out of 244 operating CPSEs as many as 165 CPSEs showed
profit during 2015-16, 78 CPSEs incurred losses during the year. List of Operating CPSEs with Net
Worth. Gross Revenue from Operations and Net Profit/Loss for the financial years from 2014-15 to
2016-17 is enclosed at Annexure-1. The schedule-wise list of CPSEs is enclosed at Annexure-2. Presently,
there are 64 Schedule 'A' 68 Schedule 'B'. 45 Schedule 'C' and 4 Schedule 'D' CPSEs. The list of 8
Maharatna. 16 Navratna and 74 Miniratna CPSEs is enclosed at Annexure-3. Under the Maharatna
category, there has been a new addition in 2017, namely, Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL).

Department of Public Enterprises (DPE)
4. In their 52nd Report, the Estimates Committee of 3rd Lok Sabha (1962-67) stressed the need for
setting up a centralized coordinating unit, which could also make continuous appraisal of the performance
of public enterprises. This led to the setting up of the Bureau of Public Enterprises (BPE) in 1965 in
the Ministry of Finance. Subsequently, as a result of the reorganization of the Ministries/Departments of
the Union Government in September, 1985. BPE was made a full-fledged Department as the Department
of Public Enterprises (DPE). At that time it was made part of the Ministry of Industry. Presently, it is
part of the Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises.
5. The DPE is the nodal department for all the Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and formulates
policy pertaining to CPSEs. It lays down, in particular, policy guidelines on performance improvement
and evaluation, autonomy and financial delegation and personnel management in CPSEs. It, furthermore,
collects and maintains information on several areas in respect of CPSEs.
6. As per the Allocation of Business Rules of the Government, the following subjects have been
allocated to the DPE:-
1. Residual work relating to erstwhile Bureau of Public Enterprises including Industrial Management
Pool.
2. Coordination of matters of general policy affecting all Public Sector Enterprises.
3. Evaluation and monitoring the performance of Public Sector Enterprises, including the
Memorandum of Understanding mechanism.
4. Matters relating to Permanent Machinery of Arbitration for the Public Sector Enterprises.
5. Counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees in Central Public Sector Undertakings
under V oluntary Retirement Scheme.
6. Review of capital projects and expenditure in Central Public Sector Enterprises.
7. Measures aimed at improving performance of Central Public Sector Enterprises and other
capacity building initiatives of Public Sector Enterprises.
8. Rendering advice relating to revival, restructuring or closure of Public Sector Enterprises
including the mechanisms therefor.
9. Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises.
10. Matter relating to International Centre for Public Enterprises.
11. Categorization of Central Public-Sector Enterprises including conferring 'Ratna' status.
12. Survey of Public Enterprises.
7. Regarding the publication of Public Enterprises Survey, it has been submitted to the Committee that
with a view to improve the analytical content, overall design and presentation of Public Enterprises
Survey, the Department invited bids from external agencies of national repute. The study to upgrade the

4
Public Enterprises Survey has been awarded to CRISIL. The report was expected to be received by
December 2017.
8. According to the Annual Report of the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises the
Vision and Mission statements of DPE are as follows:
Vision
"Effective, Profitable and Globally Competitive Central Public Sector Enterprises"
Mission
"To continuously improve management and performance of CPSEs through Corporate Governance,
Performance Evaluation, Human Resource Management, Research & Development so as to enhance
their global competitiveness"
9. The Committee is aware that the realm of CPSEs has recently under gone major changes,
especially, since the Government has decided to restrict itself only to a few selected priority areas
of business. Even the CPSEs that are profitable, but not belonging to specified areas of business,
are being disinvested. In this scenario, the Committee is of the considered opinion that the
CPSEs that would remain in operation, after hiving off of the earlier said non-priority companies,
would need clear guidance regarding efficient functioning and other inputs required to sustain
themselves successfully. Here, the Committee takes note that the mandate of DPE includes the
following:
'Measures aimed at improving performance of Centra! Public Sector Enterprises and other capacity
building initiatives of Public Sector Enterprises.
Rendering advice relating to revival, restructuring or closure of Public Sector Enterprises including
the mechanisms therefor."
In the opinion of the Committee, the above mentioned mandates of DPE under the Allocation
of Business Rules, entails DPE to be empowered to play a more proactive role than their current
profile. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that LPE should widen the horizon of its activities,
under the said ambit, to support and facilitate the revival/efficient functioning of CPSEs in
future. To achieve this, the Committee feels that DPE has to think beyond their current set of
activities, for which they can be well endowed with as per the business allocated to them, to
actually play the role expected of a nodal department.

10. From the year 2017-18, the Annual Financial Statement is being presented to the Parliament on 1st
February in departure from the past practice of presenting the same on 28th February. The Committee
sought to know the tangible benefits that have accrued from such a move from the point of view of
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE). In reply, it was submitted that since DPE has no Centrally

Counselling, Retraining & Redeployment (CRR) Scheme for Separated Employees of CPSEs.
21. DPE is implementing CRR Scheme since the year 2001-02 as a social safety net to provide
opportunities of self/wage employment to the employees or dependents of CPSEs separated under
V oluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS)/V oluntary Separation Scheme (VSS) or retrenched due to closure/
restructuring of the enterprises. The main elements of the CRR programme are Counselling, Retraining
and Redeployment The Scheme aims at providing short duration skill development/entrepreneurship
development training programmes to equip the beneficiaries for self/wage employment. In September,
2016, a tripartite agreement Was signed between DPE, National Skill Development Fund (NSDF) and
National Skill Development Council (NSDC) under Ministry of Skill Development & Entrepreneurship
(MSDE) to initiate a skill development project with the objective to provide skill training under National
Skills Qualifications Framework (NSQF) to the target group of the CRR scheme. NSDC being a
facilitator ensures that training programmes are as per National Occupational Standard (NOS), which
have been set forth by the Sector Skills Council (SSC) resulting in certification and augmentation of

10
redeployability of the trainees under the Scheme. This step broadened the Network of Training providers
and also introduced standardized methodology of training design and delivery. During the oral evidence,
as part of the examination of Demands. 2018-19 of DPE. Secretary, DPE informed that the process of
third party evaluation of the CRR scheme has been initiated.
22. Objectives of the CRR Scheme are:
1. Separated employees of CPSE to be brought into the mainstream economy and thereby
contribute to national income.
2. Reorientation of VRS /VSS optees / dependent to enable them to adjust to new environment
and adopt new vocations.
3. Skill development for VRS optees / dependent for their redeployment.
4. Exposure to various industry associations, which is also a component of the CRR scheme,
to help the trainee in product / service selection.
5. Awareness of various central and state government loan assistance/subsidized schemes.

C. The Recommendations of NITI Aayog on strategic disinvestment of CPSEs are based on
following criterion:
(i) Classification of CPSEs as 'high' or 'low' priority
The CPSEs have been considered 'High priority' for the Government if they fit in any of the
following criteria:
(a) National security
(b) Sovereign function at arm's length
(c) Market imperfection and public purpose
The CPSEs not covered in the above criteria are reckoned as 'low priority' for the Government
notwithstanding that they may be profit making companies. Tow priority' CPSEs have been considered
for Strategic Disinvestment notwithstanding that they may be profit earning.
(ii) Economic principles
The NITI Ayog was guided by basic economic principles that Government should have no business
to continue to engage itself in marketing/producing goods and services in sectors where competitive
market has come to age, and such entities are most likely to perform better in private hands due to
various factors e.g. technology upgradation and efficiency management practices and add GDP of the
country.
(iii) Tr eatment of subsidiaries and holding companies:
NITI Ayog has restricted its analysis to operating company for Strategic Disinvestment irrespective
of the fact whether it was holding company or a subsidiary. Where subsidiary CPSEs are tightly
connected into productions / manufacturing chain or business process of the parent company, such
entities have been considered alongwith parent company.
(iv) Unblocking the Value through Strategic Disinvestment
Further revenue optimization for the Government was also one of the factors, though not the only
guiding criteria. It was of the view that real unlocking of value through better/efficient management and/
or of latest technology by private sector may bring much higher dividends for the economy as a whole
in terms of GDP growth.
